Name: context_complexity_difficulty_contamination
Title: Guilty by Association: How Benign Surrounding Context Inflates a Model's Internal Difficulty Estimate and Wastes Reasoning Compute
Short Hypothesis: The pre-generation difficulty representation reasoning models use to allocate thinking compute is contaminated by the complexity of BENIGN, task-irrelevant surrounding context: embedding the identical target question inside a longer, more elaborate but irrelevant passage (as users and RAG systems routinely do) raises the model's internal difficulty estimate and inflates reasoning tokens on the target, independent of the target's true difficulty. 'Benign' is operationalized concretely: plausible, non-adversarial, LLM-judge-and-human-verified-irrelevant material (small talk, unrelated narrative, or genuinely-irrelevant retrieved passages) not optimized to mislead — distinguishing it from adversarial distractor-injection. We make three core claims: (1) benign context-complexity, not raw prompt length, inflates reasoning compute on matched targets at equal accuracy; (2) the inflation is decodable specifically at the pre-generation difficulty representation (the known difficulty direction/heads), not merely a generic attention-diversion/entrainment effect; (3) resetting that difficulty representation cancels the tax at equal accuracy, with patching/steering read as evidence that the difficulty representation is causally INVOLVED rather than the sole mechanism. The downstream payoff is concrete for RAG systems and chat assistants — lower latency, token cost, and context-window pressure via prompt sanitation or an inference-time difficulty-reset controller — and for benchmark protocols, which by testing questions in isolation may systematically under-estimate deployed compute.
Related Work: Difficulty-perception work (Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism, 2025) shows difficulty is linearly encoded and drives adaptive compute, but only on clean, isolated problems. Overthinking-cause work attributes waste to internal first-impression bias (2025), missing premises (MiP-Overthinking, 2025), or a length/verbosity direction, always with the target in isolation. Distractor/attack work (Distractor Injection Attacks 2025; CODE 2026; contextual entrainment 2025; LeaF 2025) studies ADVERSARIAL or spurious tokens that divert attention or are optimized to inflate compute; the mechanism is attention-diversion/entrainment and the framing is malicious. Our delta on both axes: (i) BENIGN, plausible, non-adversarial context — the kind users and retrieval naturally include — rather than optimized distractors; and (ii) contamination of the model's DIFFICULTY ESTIMATE specifically, tested by showing the difficulty probe/heads (not just attention) shift and by comparing against a generic attention-diversion/entrainment baseline, rather than an attention-diversion account. We narrow our novelty claim to exactly this combination — benign context-complexity as a compute tax, tied to the difficulty representation, and canceled by a causal difficulty reset — none of which prior clean-prompt difficulty work or adversarial distractor work establishes.
Abstract: Reasoning models allocate a thinking budget assumed to reflect a problem's genuine difficulty, which is known to be linearly encoded before the model reasons. But real questions rarely arrive alone: users paste a question into a long email, chats have scrollback, and RAG systems prepend passages. We ask whether such benign, task-irrelevant surrounding context contaminates the internal difficulty estimate and inflates reasoning compute on the embedded target, even when the target's true difficulty is unchanged. We construct matched prompts holding a math or science target and its answer fixed while varying only surrounding, verified-irrelevant benign context (none, short-simple, long-elaborate), and add human-authored neutral wrappers and style-matched semantic-scramble variants to rule out covert cueing. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure reasoning tokens and accuracy on the target versus context complexity, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate complexity from target difficulty and raw length, and a length-matched padded control. Mechanistically we reproduce a difficulty probe at the prompt boundary and test whether, for identical targets, its readout rises with irrelevant-context complexity above true difficulty; we compare against a generic attention-diversion baseline, localize the representation, and treat activation patching and steering as evidence that the difficulty representation is causally involved. Finally a training-free difficulty-reset cancels the contamination, cutting tokens at equal accuracy, and we test realistic RAG-retrieved irrelevant passages. Because messy benign context is the deployment norm, this reveals a pervasive, non-adversarial compute tax with a decodable, steerable internal cause, and implies benchmarks tested in isolation under-estimate deployed compute.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B thinking mode); linear probes are the only trainable parameters. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Targets come from existing sets used as-is: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). For each target we CONSTRUCT content-identical variants that embed the SAME target, clearly marked ('Please answer this question: ...'), inside benign surrounding context of increasing complexity: (a) no context, (b) short-simple (one plain unrelated sentence), (c) long-elaborate (several sentences of unrelated but lexically/syntactically complex off-topic narrative). Irrelevance is verified by an LLM-judge plus human spot-check on 200 constructions. Compute forces subsampling for the trace-heavy conditions: 400 GSM8K, 400 MATH500, all 60 AIME, all 198 GPQA, each in all context conditions, 3 seeds.

Experiment 1 (H1 — benign context inflates reasoning compute): Tests whether surrounding benign, irrelevant context raises reasoning tokens on an identical target at equal accuracy. Data: the constructed variants above. Decisive metric FIRST: within-target reasoning-token count on the target as a function of context complexity, at matched target accuracy. Convincing result: reasoning tokens rise monotonically from no-context to long-elaborate context by >= 15% median on identical targets while target accuracy stays within 1 point, in >=3 of 4 models on >=3 of 4 datasets. Indecision band: token inflation 5-15% — a modest tax, reported as limited. Negative result (no token inflation, or accuracy changes so the comparison is not equal-accuracy): benign context does not contaminate compute; H1 fails and the mechanistic experiments are not pursued.

Experiment 2 (H1 — complexity, not raw length; and target difficulty): Tests that the effect is driven by context COMPLEXITY, not prompt token-length or target difficulty. Data: Experiment-1 variants plus (i) a length-matched control padding short-simple context with trivial repetition to the long-elaborate token length, (ii) human-authored neutral wrappers, and (iii) a semantic-scramble control that preserves the long-elaborate context's length, lexical complexity, and style but destroys coherent meaning — isolating complexity from covert cueing and from raw length. Analysis: mixed-effects model of reasoning length with random effect for target identity and fixed effects for context complexity and raw prompt length. Decisive metric FIRST: the context-complexity fixed effect after absorbing target identity and prompt length. Convincing result: context-complexity effect survives (CI excluding 0) with target identity and length absorbed, AND the long-elaborate condition inflates tokens more than the length-matched padded control (isolating complexity from length). Indecision band: complexity effect present but the complexity-vs-length-matched gap CI overlaps 0 — the effect may be pure length, reported as unresolved. Negative result (effect vanishes after length control): this is a raw-length artifact, an informative null; H1's complexity claim fails.

Experiment 3 (H1 — wasted vs genuine compute): Tests that the extra tokens are wasted (re-reading irrelevant material), not genuine extra reasoning on the target. Data: Experiment-1 traces on 200 items/dataset. Measures: truncate-and-resume minimal-solve length per variant; attention mass to the irrelevant-context span; and lexical restatement tagging of irrelevant material inside the chain. Decisive metric FIRST: the increase in WASTED tokens (tokens beyond minimal solve) attributable to context complexity, plus rate of re-reading irrelevant context. Convincing result: context complexity inflates wasted tokens and irrelevant-context re-reading with CI excluding 0, while minimal-solve length is unchanged across conditions. Indecision band: minimal-solve length itself rises modestly (5-15%) with context — some genuine extra work, reported as partly justified. Negative result (minimal-solve length rises as much as total length): the extra compute is genuine, not waste; the 'tax' framing weakens.

Experiment 4 (H2 — contamination decodable at the prompt boundary): Tests that a linear difficulty probe at the prompt boundary reads higher difficulty for identical targets as irrelevant-context complexity rises, above the target's true difficulty. Data: prompt-boundary (last prompt token, pre-reasoning) activations from Experiment-1 variants; the difficulty probe (ridge/logistic) is trained on ISOLATED graded-difficulty problems, then applied unchanged to the variants; layer sweep plus the difficulty-sensitive final-layer heads from prior work; a length-predicting probe as a comparator. Decisive metric FIRST: the shift in probe-decoded difficulty for identical targets between no-context and long-elaborate conditions, relative to the target's true difficulty (pass-rate). Convincing result: probe-decoded difficulty rises monotonically with context complexity for identical targets (CI excluding 0), exceeding the true-difficulty baseline (inflation, not accuracy), and correlates with the Experiment-1 token inflation. Indecision band: probe shift present but its correlation with token inflation has |r| < 0.3 — weakly evidenced link. Negative result (no probe shift for identical targets): the difficulty representation is not contaminated; H2 fails (the behavioral effect, if any, is mediated elsewhere).

Experiment 5 (H3 — causal reality): Tests that the contaminated difficulty representation causally drives the extra compute. Data: 300 targets in both no-context and long-elaborate conditions. Intervention: activation-patch the prompt-boundary residual state (and/or difficulty-head activations) from the no-context variant into the matched high-context prompt (same target), at localized components; frozen weights; dose-response; plus a reverse patch (no-context -> high-context) for bidirectionality. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) no-context difficulty patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: reduction in reasoning length toward the no-context level under the patch versus controls, accuracy preserved. Convincing result: the no-context patch removes >= half the context-driven length inflation with CI excluding 0, monotone in dose, not reproduced by the random-direction patch, off-target accuracy within 1 point; reverse patch inflates length. Indecision band: removal of 20-50% of the inflation, or random-direction patch giving >=50% of the effect — causality not clean. Negative result (no reduction, or non-specific): the difficulty representation is not causal for the tax; H3 fails.

Experiment 6 (H4 — difficulty-reset cancels the tax): Tests that steering the difficulty representation back to the no-context level cancels the contamination at equal accuracy, without harming genuinely hard targets. Data: full evaluation sets, 3 seeds, high-context condition. Intervention: difficulty steering direction (difference-of-means between high-context and no-context boundary states, or the difficulty-probe weight) applied at problem onset to steer high-context prompts toward the no-context difficulty level; coefficient swept. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) prompt fix ('ignore surrounding context; answer only the question'), (c) context-stripping preprocessing (oracle upper bound), (d) fixed truncation, (e) our difficulty-reset steer. Decisive metric FIRST: tokens-at-equal-accuracy (reduction in context-driven length inflation with accuracy retained), plus a specificity check on genuinely hard isolated targets. Convincing result: the reset removes >= half the context-driven inflation at accuracy within 1 point, approaching the context-stripping oracle and beating the prompt fix, while NOT reducing tokens or accuracy on genuinely hard isolated targets by more than a 1-point accuracy drop (specificity). Indecision band: inflation removal 20-50%, or a 1-3 point accuracy cost — partial, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no token reduction at equal accuracy, or hard targets harmed): the reset does not work; H4 fails though H1-H3 stand.

Experiment 7 (H1 — RAG realism): Tests that the effect holds for deployment-shaped context. Data: each target prepended with realistic retrieved-but-irrelevant passages (retrieved by a standard dense retriever, then filtered to genuinely irrelevant ones by LLM-judge), 200 items/dataset. Decisive metric FIRST: token inflation and difficulty-probe shift under realistic RAG-irrelevant context versus no-context. Convincing result: inflation and probe shift of the same sign and comparable magnitude to the synthetic long-elaborate condition. Indecision band: inflation present but < half the synthetic effect — attenuated in realistic settings. Negative result (no effect with RAG passages): the phenomenon is an artifact of synthetic small talk and does not generalize to deployment; the practical claim weakens.

Experiment 8 (H2/H4 generalization and scale): Tests transfer without retraining and the scale trend. Data: probe/reset fit on one set+model, applied unchanged to the others and across 1.5B->14B. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-set probe-shift correlation with token inflation, cross-set reset effectiveness, and whether contamination grows with context complexity and shrinks (or grows) with model scale / RL-tuning. Convincing result: transferred probe and reset retain >= half their in-domain effect, and a consistent monotone contamination-vs-complexity trend across models. Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or a non-monotone scale trend — partial generalization. Negative result (no transfer): the effect is idiosyncratic per model/set, reported as a boundary characterization.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The effect could be a raw prompt-length artifact rather than complexity per se; the length-matched padded control and the prompt-length covariate in the mixed-effects model isolate complexity, and a null after controls (pure length effect) would itself be an informative, publishable finding. The surrounding context must be genuinely benign and irrelevant, not a covert distractor; we verify irrelevance and use plain, non-adversarial material plus realistic RAG passages, distinguishing this from adversarial distractor-injection work. The contaminated difficulty signal may be inseparable from a generic attention-diversion or contextual-entrainment effect; we control by testing whether the difficulty probe/heads (not just attention) shift, comparing to an entrainment-head baseline, and via causal patching of the difficulty representation specifically. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included, and resetting difficulty must not harm targets that are genuinely hard (specificity check on hard isolated targets). The effect may be small in strongly instruction/RL-tuned models trained to focus on the marked question (a valuable boundary condition). Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: diagnostic_order_anchoring
Title: First Symptom, Wrong Diagnosis: Premature Hypothesis Commitment as the Mechanism of Symptom-Order Anchoring in Clinical Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: For a fixed set of clinical findings that unambiguously support a single correct diagnosis, reasoning LLMs reach different final diagnoses depending only on the ORDER in which the identical symptoms are presented, anchoring on the diagnosis favored by the earliest symptoms. The novelty boundary is precise and separates three claims. PHENOMENON: not merely that 'order matters', but that content-identical symptom order flips the FINAL diagnosis in multi-step differential diagnosis, in a safety-relevant domain. MECHANISM: a decodable 'leading-hypothesis' representation forms after the first few symptoms and predicts the eventual diagnosis, and — required to be separable by measurable criteria (principal angle >= 30 degrees) from generic uncertainty/difficulty and not reducible to answer length or early-impression cues — under-updates when later disambiguating symptoms arrive. MITIGATION (separate from the phenomenon): a training-free hypothesis-reset applied after symptom intake cancels the order effect, validated causally by activation patching. The deployment implication is concrete: symptom order is arbitrary in real notes, so triage-chatbot input ordering and EHR note sequencing could materially shift a model's diagnosis; the mitigation would first be adopted by builders of clinical decision-support and medical-QA interfaces as an input-order guardrail. We scope the evidence to vignette-based demonstrations of the failure mode and its internal cause, not direct patient-outcome claims.
Related Work: We organize prior work into four strands and state the delta. (1) Human symptom-order anchoring: robust evidence that early symptoms bias the initial hypothesis and later evidence is distorted toward it (Order effects in diagnostic reasoning 2012; Presentation order in clinical decision making 1997; Anchoring Bias During Physician Decision-Making 2023; Information Distortion 2013) — behavioral, in humans; we transfer it into reasoning LLMs with a mechanistic account. (2) LLM numeric/framing anchoring (Anchors in the Machine 2025; CBEval 2024; Anchoring bias 2025) uses ARTIFICIAL numeric anchors and single-turn outputs, not content-identical symptom order in multi-step diagnosis. (3) First-impression / preliminary-guess work (The First Impression Problem 2025; Anchored Answers 2024 on MCQ 'A'-anchoring circuits) shows an internal preliminary guess drives overthinking or positional bias, but never a symptom-order-induced FINAL-diagnosis flip nor a decodable leading-hypothesis that under-updates. (4) Clinical anchoring-mitigation studies target human workflows, not LLM internal representations. Our delta across all four: content-identical symptom order flipping the final diagnosis in LLM differential diagnosis, tied to a decodable, separable, causally-tested leading-hypothesis representation, and a training-free reset — none established by prior LLM anchoring (numeric, single-turn) or behavioral human work.
Abstract: Physicians who see a patient's symptoms in a different order can reach a different diagnosis, a robust human anchoring effect where early findings dominate. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit this, and mechanistically why, in the high-stakes setting of differential diagnosis. We construct clinical cases whose full symptom set unambiguously supports one correct diagnosis, then present the identical findings in different orders: an order whose leading symptoms favor a plausible-but-wrong competitor diagnosis versus an order whose leading symptoms favor the correct one, plus randomized orders. Across curated diagnostic benchmarks (e.g., MedQA-derived vignettes, NEJM-style case reports, and templated multi-symptom cases with controlled hypothesis structure) on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3, and a medical-tuned model), we measure whether the final diagnosis and accuracy shift with symptom order alone, using a mixed-effects decomposition to isolate order from case content. Mechanistically, we test that after the first few symptoms the residual stream linearly encodes a leading-hypothesis representation predicting the eventual diagnosis, that this representation is set early and updates too little when later contradicting symptoms arrive, and that its early strength predicts order-induced misdiagnosis. We localize it via probing and causally validate via activation patching (patch the correct-order leading-hypothesis state into a wrong-order case and observe the diagnosis correct) and steering. Finally we test a training-free 'hypothesis-reset' intervention applied after symptom intake that cancels the order effect. Because symptom order is arbitrary in real clinical notes, this reveals an order-driven misdiagnosis risk with a decodable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B (thinking mode), and one medical-tuned open model (e.g. OpenBioLLM-8B); linear probes are the only trainable parameters. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). We CONSTRUCT cases whose full symptom set S unambiguously supports one CORRECT diagnosis but whose early-presentable subset is also consistent with a plausible COMPETITOR diagnosis, and present the identical findings in different orders. Sources: (T) templated controlled-hypothesis vignettes (strongest control) — 600 cases from ~30 templates; (M) MedQA-derived vignettes adapted so the full findings are diagnostic — 300 cases; (N) NEJM-style case reports adapted — 150 cases. Clinical validity and unambiguity are checked by an expert-guided rubric plus LLM-judge, with human spot-check on 200 cases; ambiguous cases are analyzed separately. Diagnosis extraction uses LLM-judge matching with human spot-check (report kappa).

Experiment 1 (H1 — symptom-order anchoring flips the diagnosis): Tests whether symptom order alone changes the final diagnosis on content-identical cases. Data: each case in orderings (a) competitor-leading (early symptoms favor the wrong diagnosis; disambiguating symptoms last), (b) correct-leading, (c) 3 randomized orders. Decisive metric FIRST: within-case final-diagnosis accuracy and competitor-misdiagnosis rate as a function of ordering. Convincing result: competitor-leading order lowers accuracy by >= 8 absolute points and raises competitor-misdiagnosis by >= 8 points versus correct-leading on identical findings, in >=3 of the models on the templated set and replicated on >=1 adapted set. Indecision band: accuracy/misdiagnosis gap 3-8 points — a weak effect, reported as limited. Negative result (no gap, diagnosis invariant to order): symptom-order anchoring does not occur; H1 fails and the mechanistic experiments are not pursued.

Experiment 2 (H1 — dissociation from content, length, position): Tests that the effect is symptom-content-order, not case difficulty, prompt length, or the position of the disambiguating symptom. Data: Experiment-1 orderings plus matched-length filler, randomized disambiguating-symptom position, and a discourse-matched control that holds syntax, length, and discourse markers constant while permuting only symptom content (plus an order-randomization baseline and a 'no semantic progression' shuffled control). Analysis: mixed-effects model of accuracy/misdiagnosis with random effect for case identity and fixed effect for ordering. Decisive metric FIRST: the ordering fixed effect after absorbing case identity and controlling length/position. Convincing result: ordering effect survives (CI excluding 0) with case identity absorbed and is not explained by length or disambiguating-symptom position. Indecision band: ordering effect present but CI half-width comparable to the effect after controls — unresolved. Negative result (effect vanishes after controls): the phenomenon is a position/length artifact; H1 fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — decodable early leading-hypothesis): Tests that after the first k symptoms the residual stream linearly encodes a leading hypothesis that predicts the eventual diagnosis even when wrong. Data: residual-stream activations after the first k symptoms (before the full set), from Experiment-1 cases; probe (multinomial logistic) per layer, item-level 70/15/15 split, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Decisive metric FIRST: AUROC/accuracy for predicting the FINAL diagnosis from the early state, and separability from a difficulty/uncertainty probe (principal angle). Convincing result: early-state prediction of the final diagnosis reaches macro-F1 >= 0.60 (well above majority baseline), higher in competitor-leading order (early commitment to the wrong diagnosis), and the leading-hypothesis direction is separable from difficulty (angle >= 30 degrees). Indecision band: macro-F1 0.45-0.60, or angle 15-30 degrees — decodable but weak/entangled. Negative result (early state does not predict the final diagnosis above baseline): there is no early leading-hypothesis representation; H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 — under-updating when late evidence arrives): Tests that in competitor-leading order the leading-hypothesis representation under-updates when a late disambiguating symptom favoring the correct diagnosis arrives, and that the under-update predicts misdiagnosis. Data: probe-decoded leading-hypothesis trajectory across symptoms, competitor-leading vs correct-leading. Decisive metric FIRST: the shift in the probe readout at the late disambiguating symptom (competitor-leading vs correct-leading), and the incremental R^2 of the under-update magnitude in predicting order-induced misdiagnosis over difficulty/length baselines. Convincing result: the representation shifts markedly less toward the correct diagnosis in competitor-leading order (CI excluding 0), and under-update magnitude adds >= 0.05 R^2 over baselines. Indecision band: incremental R^2 0.02-0.05 — a weak mediator. Negative result (equal updating in both orders, or no predictive link): under-updating is not the mechanism; H2's mechanistic claim fails.

Experiment 5 (H2 causal — patching the leading hypothesis): Tests that the leading-hypothesis representation causally sets the final diagnosis. Data: 300 cases in matched competitor-leading and correct-leading orders. Intervention: activation-patch the correct-leading leading-hypothesis state into the matched competitor-leading case (same findings) at localized components; frozen weights; dose-response; reverse patch to induce misdiagnosis. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) correct-leading patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target case accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: correction of the final diagnosis under the patch versus controls. Convincing result: the correct-leading patch corrects >= half the competitor-leading misdiagnoses with CI excluding 0, monotone in dose, not reproduced by the random-direction patch, off-target accuracy within 1 point; reverse patch induces misdiagnosis. Indecision band: correction of 20-50% of misdiagnoses, or random-direction patch giving >=50% of the effect — causality not clean. Negative result (no correction, or non-specific): the representation is not causal; H2's causal claim fails.

Experiment 6 (H3 — training-free hypothesis-reset): Tests that resetting the leading-hypothesis representation after symptom intake removes the order effect without overwriting correct early commitments. Data: full T/M/N sets, 3 seeds, competitor-leading order. Intervention: after all symptoms are presented but before commitment, steer the leading-hypothesis representation toward a neutral/uncommitted state (subtract the early-anchor component); coefficient swept. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) prompt reset ('reconsider all findings without regard to order'), (c) presenting all symptoms simultaneously (order-free oracle), (d) re-ordering to correct-leading (oracle), (e) our activation reset. Decisive metric FIRST: reduction in the order-induced accuracy gap and competitor-misdiagnosis rate, with a specificity check on correct-leading cases. Convincing result: the reset removes >= half the order-induced accuracy gap (approaching the order-free oracle), beats the prompt reset, and does not reduce accuracy on correct-leading cases by more than 1 point (specificity). Indecision band: gap removal 20-50%, or a 1-3 point accuracy cost on correct-leading cases — partial, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no gap reduction, or correct cases harmed): the reset does not work; H3 fails though H1-H2 stand.

Experiment 7 (generalization and hypothesis count): Tests transfer without retraining and whether more competitors worsen anchoring. Data: probe/reset fit on one set+model, applied unchanged to the others and across scales; cases with >2 competitor diagnoses. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-set order-effect reduction under the transferred reset, and whether anchoring grows with the number of competitor hypotheses. Convincing result: transferred reset retains >= half its in-domain effect, anchoring worsens monotonically with competitor count (mirroring human findings), and medical-tuning shifts the effect in a characterizable direction. Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or no clear competitor-count trend — partial generalization. Negative result (no transfer): the effect is idiosyncratic per model/set, reported as a boundary characterization. Vignettes are synthetic/adapted demonstrations, not clinical validation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Constructing cases where the FULL symptom set is unambiguously diagnostic yet early subsets favor a competitor is nontrivial and requires clinical validity; we anchor strongest claims on templated controlled-hypothesis cases and use adapted MedQA/NEJM vignettes with expert/LLM-judge verification, treating ambiguous cases separately. The order effect could be a position/length artifact rather than symptom-content-order per se; matched-length filler, randomized disambiguating-symptom position, and the mixed-effects analysis isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. The leading-hypothesis representation may be inseparable from a generic difficulty/uncertainty signal; the separability analysis, under-update trajectory (not just magnitude), and causal patching address this. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and harm accuracy; matched-random-direction controls and validity checks are included, and the reset must not overwrite genuinely correct early commitments (specificity check on correct-leading cases). The effect may be small in strong or medical-tuned models trained to weigh all findings (a valuable boundary condition). Clinical vignettes are synthetic/adapted demonstrations of the failure mode, not clinical validation of a deployable tool. Diagnosis extraction requires reliable parsing/matching; we use LLM-judge with human spot-checks. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: deception_effort_detectability
Title: The Cognitive Cost of a Lie: Detectability Beliefs Modulate How Much Reasoning Effort a Model Spends Constructing Strategic Deception
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the human-neuroscience finding that believing one's lie can be detected raises the cognitive cost of deceiving, we hypothesize that reasoning LLMs spend MORE internal reasoning effort (tokens, deliberation) constructing a strategically deceptive answer than an honest one on the same fact, and that this deception-effort surplus GROWS when the prompt signals the lie is likely to be detected and SHRINKS when it signals detection is unlikely. The primary novelty is an effort-COST phenomenon and its detectability modulation — a compute-allocation axis — NOT another deception detector. Deception is defined operationally as the committed answer contradicting the model's own known-correct/internal answer, distinguished from refusal and from honest-but-hedged or honest-but-wrong answers, which we label separately. Mechanistically the surplus is carried by a pre-answer deception-effort representation that we require to be separable, by measurable criteria (principal angle >= 30 degrees and incremental predictive gain), from BOTH a generic difficulty/uncertainty direction and the lie/honesty direction — ruling out 'more compute merely because harder'. We scope the steering claim explicitly: suppressing this direction should lower the deception RATE and amplifying it should raise both effort and deception, tested with matched-random-direction controls. The concrete downstream win for a safety auditor is a compute-side, monitor-independent early-warning signal of strategic dishonesty that fires before the output — and degrades less than output-based monitors when the deceptive text is crafted to look benign.
Related Work: LLM deception work shows strategic deception is inducible, decodable, and steerable (When Thinking LLMs Lie 2025; Strategic Dishonesty Undermines Safety Evals 2025; The Secret Agenda 2025), and evaluation awareness is linearly represented and steerable (Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness 2025; Steering Eval-Aware Models 2025). All of this reads a lie/honesty or eval-awareness DIRECTION to decide WHETHER a model lies or is being tested, or whether capability is sandbagged; none measures the COMPUTE/EFFORT cost of producing a deceptive versus honest answer, nor whether that cost is modulated by the model's belief it can be caught — a distinct compute-allocation axis, which is our contribution. Human neuroscience robustly shows deception is cognitively taxing and that belief in lie-detectability amplifies the cost (When Pinocchio's nose does not grow 2013; What if I Get Busted 2012; neural basis of deception in strategic interactions 2015). We transfer the detectability-modulated deception-cost finding into reasoning LLMs, dissociate the effort surplus from problem difficulty (a plain difficulty probe is a required baseline), and locate and causally steer a deception-effort representation separable from both the difficulty and honesty directions. This differs from all deception-detection work (which reads a lie/honesty direction, not an effort cost) and from prior overthinking work (which assumes an honest, neutral task).
Abstract: Human neuroscience shows that lying is cognitively costly, and—strikingly—that believing one's lie can be detected makes deception even more effortful, while believing it cannot slashes that cost. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit an analog: do they spend more reasoning effort constructing a strategically deceptive answer than an honest one, and does that effort track their belief about being caught? We construct scenarios where a model is incentivized to deceive (e.g., an agent with a hidden goal that conflicts with honestly answering a user), and vary only a detectability cue—signals that the answer will (high detectability) or will not (low detectability) be verified/audited—while holding the underlying question and correct answer fixed. Across strategic-deception testbeds and, for the highest stakes, safety-audit-style honesty probes, on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure internal reasoning-token count, deliberation behavior, deception rate, and answer accuracy. We test whether a deception-effort surplus (extra reasoning on deceptive vs honest trials) exists and grows with detectability, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate it from task difficulty and prompt length. Mechanistically, we probe whether the pre-answer residual stream encodes a deception-effort signal separable from a difficulty probe and from a lie/honesty direction, localize it, causally validate via activation patching (patch a low-detectability state into a high-detectability context and observe effort and deception change), and steer it. Because a model that thinks harder to deceive when watched—and lies more cheaply when unwatched—is a direct safety-audit concern, the deception-effort signal offers a compute-side, monitor-independent signature of strategic dishonesty.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B thinking mode); linear probes are the only trainable parameters. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Because deception-with-known-truth items with detectability cues are not available off-the-shelf, we CONSTRUCT a testbed by adapting existing strategic-deception setups: (i) role-play agents with a hidden goal that conflicts with honestly answering a verifiable question, (ii) a Secret-Agenda-style game, and (iii) safety-audit honesty items with a known-correct answer. Each item has a matched honest and deceptive framing over the SAME underlying fact, so content and difficulty are shared. Target size: 600 deception-eligible items (200 per setup), each with matched honest/deceptive framing and, for Experiment 2, three detectability cues. Deception is defined operationally as the committed output contradicting the model's own known-correct/internal answer; refusals, honest-but-hedged, and honest-but-wrong outputs are labeled as separate categories (not counted as deception), verified against ground truth and by human spot-check on 200 items (report kappa).

Experiment 1 (H1 — deception-effort surplus): Tests whether producing a deceptive answer uses more reasoning effort than an honest one at matched content. Data: the 600 matched honest/deceptive items, 3 generations each. Measures: internal reasoning-token count; count of deliberation/weighing steps (lexical cues plus a reflection-direction classifier validated on 200 held-out labeled steps, AUROC reported); deception rate; and concealed-truth accuracy. Decisive metric FIRST: within-item difference in reasoning tokens between deceptive and honest trials at matched content. Convincing result: deceptive trials use >= 15% more reasoning tokens than honest trials on the same items in >=3 of 4 models, with more deliberation steps. Indecision band: surplus 5-15% — a modest effect, reported as limited. Negative result (no surplus or deceptive trials shorter): deception is not more effortful for these models; H1 fails and the detectability/mechanism experiments are not pursued.

Experiment 2 (H2 — detectability modulates the surplus): Tests that the deception-effort surplus grows under high-detectability cues and shrinks under low, while honest-trial effort is roughly unchanged, and that low detectability raises the deception RATE. Data: each deception-eligible item under three cues — high ('your answer will be fact-checked/audited against records'), low ('private scratchpad; no one will check'), neutral — with cue phrasings length-matched. Decisive metric FIRST: the interaction between deceive-vs-honest and detectability on reasoning tokens (does the deception surplus scale with detectability?), and the deception rate across cues. Convincing result: the deception surplus is significantly larger under high than low detectability (interaction CI excluding 0) while honest-trial effort is unchanged within noise, AND deception rate is higher under low detectability — matching the human finding. Indecision band: interaction present but CI half-width comparable to the effect, or deception-rate change < 5 points — modulation weakly evidenced. Negative result (no interaction, surplus independent of detectability): the detectability transfer fails, an informative null refuting the analogy; H2 fails.

Experiment 3 (H1/H2 — dissociation from difficulty and length; lie-maintenance overhead): Tests that the surplus is not difficulty or prompt length, and that it concentrates in lie-maintenance spans. Data: Experiment-1/2 traces. Analysis: mixed-effects model of reasoning length with random effect for item identity and fixed effects for deception and detectability, plus a prompt-length covariate and length-matched cue phrasings; and truncate-and-resume plus span tagging (risk-weighing, justification-fabrication, lie-consistency checking). Decisive metric FIRST: the deception fixed effect after item identity and length are absorbed, and the fraction of the surplus falling in lie-maintenance spans. Convincing result: deception effect survives (CI excluding 0) with identity and length absorbed, and >= half the surplus is in lie-maintenance spans rather than extra reasoning about the true answer. Indecision band: deception effect present but < 10% of variance, or lie-maintenance fraction 30-50% — partly entangled. Negative result (effect vanishes after controls): the surplus is a length/difficulty artifact; H1/H2 fail.

Experiment 4 (H3 — decodable pre-answer deception-effort representation): Tests that a linear direction at the pre-answer boundary encodes the deception-effort signal, separable from difficulty and from a lie/honesty direction. Data: pre-answer boundary activations (after the scenario, before the answer is committed) from Experiment-1/2 traces; probes (ridge for length, logistic for will-deceive) per layer, item-level 70/15/15 split, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Systems compared: the deception-effort direction versus a difficulty probe (pass-rate), a reproduced lie/honesty (LAT-style) direction, an eval-awareness probe, a refusal-propensity probe, and a generic-deliberation probe, via principal angles and joint predictive gain. Decisive metric FIRST: whether the length-probe readout rises under high detectability on deceptive trials for identical items, and the principal angle of the deception-effort direction to both the difficulty and honesty directions. Convincing result: the readout tracks the behavioral surplus (correlation with CI excluding 0), and the deception-effort direction is separable from both difficulty and honesty (both principal angles >= 30 degrees) with >= 0.03 incremental AUROC over them. Indecision band: correlation |r| 0.2-0.3, or angles 15-30 degrees — decodable but entangled. Negative result (no readout, or collinear with difficulty/honesty): no distinct deception-effort representation; H3 fails.

Experiment 5 (H3 causal — patching detectability state): Tests that the pre-answer representation causally sets effort and deception. Data: 300 items in matched high- and low-detectability contexts. Intervention: activation-patch the pre-answer state from a low-detectability context into a matched high-detectability context (same item) at localized components; frozen weights; dose-response; reverse patch for bidirectionality. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) low-detectability patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target honest-item accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: change in reasoning effort AND deception rate toward the low-detectability level under the patch versus controls. Convincing result: the low-detectability patch cuts effort and raises deception rate toward the low-detectability baseline with CI excluding 0, monotone in dose, not reproduced by the random-direction patch, off-target accuracy preserved within 1 point; reverse patch raises effort and lowers deception. Indecision band: effect 20-50% of the behavioral gap, or random-direction patch giving >=50% of it — causality not clean. Negative result (no effect, or non-specific): the representation is not causal; H3's causal claim fails.

Experiment 6 (H4 — steering changes effort and willingness to deceive): Tests that steering the deception-effort direction changes both effort and deception. Data: full 600-item testbed, 3 seeds. Intervention: steering direction = difference-of-means between deceptive-high-detectability and honest states; (a) suppress it and test whether deception decreases (a compute-side dishonesty control), (b) amplify it as a red-team probe; coefficient swept. Systems compared: no steer, suppress-steer, amplify-steer, and a matched-random-direction control. Decisive metric FIRST: change in deception rate under suppression (and amplification), with answer-honesty and off-target accuracy tracked. Convincing result: suppression lowers deception rate by >= 10 absolute points versus the random-direction control at accuracy within 1 point on honest items; amplification raises it. Indecision band: deception-rate change 3-10 points — a real but weak lever, reported at its operating point. Negative result (steering does not move deception, as prior SAE-feature work warns): the effort signal is not a usable deception lever, an informative bound; H4's steering claim fails though H1-H3 stand.

Experiment 7 (H3 safety application — monitor-independent detector): Tests the pre-answer deception-effort signal as a detector of strategic dishonesty. Data: held-out deception items, including deceptive outputs crafted to look benign. Systems compared: the pre-answer effort/deception probe versus output-based lie/jailbreak monitors and a leakage-controlled honesty probe. Decisive metric FIRST: AUROC for flagging deceptive trials on held-out items, and robustness when the deceptive output is crafted to look benign. Convincing result: probe AUROC >= 0.75 and degrades by < 0.10 on benign-looking deceptive outputs, where output monitors degrade more. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.75 — usable but not strong. Negative result (AUROC ~0.5): the signal is not a practical detector; the safety application fails though the phenomenon stands.

Experiment 8 (generalization and scale): Tests transfer without retraining and the scale trend. Data: probe/steer fit on one setup+model, applied unchanged to the others and across 1.5B->14B. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-setup detection AUROC and cross-setup surplus modulation, and whether larger models show a larger detectability-modulated surplus. Convincing result: transferred AUROC within 0.10 of in-domain and a monotone growth of the detectability-modulated surplus with scale. Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or non-monotone scale trend — partial generalization. Negative result (no transfer, flat scale trend): the effect is idiosyncratic per model/setup, reported as a boundary characterization. Safety-audit scenarios are synthetic demonstrations, not deployment validation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The effort surplus could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences between deceptive and honest framings or between detectability cues; the matched-content design, length covariate, length-matched cue phrasings, and mixed-effects analysis isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. The deception-effort signal may be inseparable from a generic difficulty/uncertainty direction or from the lie/honesty direction; the separability analyses, causal patching, and comparison to a reproduced honesty direction address this, and overlap would itself be an interesting mechanistic finding. Prior work shows autolabeled SAE deception features fail to control lying, so steering may not reliably suppress deception (an informative bound), but the primary contribution is the effort phenomenon and its detectability modulation. Detecting genuine deception (output contradicting the model's internal/known-correct answer) is nontrivial and can leak textual evidence into probes; we use verifiable-answer scenarios, content/score filtering to control leakage, and human spot-checks. The effect may be small or absent in strongly aligned models that refuse rather than deceive (a valuable boundary condition) and may reverse under some framings. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound reads; matched-random-direction controls and validity checks are included. Safety-audit scenarios are synthetic demonstrations, not deployment validation. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: verification_recency_gradient
Title: Checking Least Where It Matters Most: A Verification-Effort Gradient That Leaves Late Reasoning Steps Fragile
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models allocate progressively less self-verification effort to later steps of a chain of thought (a verification recency gradient), yet late steps are exactly where an injected error is most likely to corrupt the final answer (late-stage fragility) — so the model checks least where a mistake is most catastrophic. We separate three claims. FINDING: per-step verification effort — operationally the rate of rechecks/backtracks/self-affirmations at each step — decays monotonically with normalized chain position and anti-aligns with the fragility profile. MECHANISM: this is an allocation failure, not a capability ceiling, carried by a decodable, monotonically-decaying 'verification-engagement' signal, defined as a residual-stream direction whose per-step projection predicts local verification behavior and local fragility and is separable from difficulty and confidence directions (a plain difficulty or entropy probe cannot recover it). INTERVENTION: reallocating verification effort toward late steps by training-free steering of that signal repairs late fragility at little added token cost. The downstream payoff is concrete — position-aware verifier placement, adaptive decoding that spends verification where fragility is highest, and position-weighted training objectives — and matters for the reliability of deployed reasoning agents whose unchecked late-step slips silently corrupt answers. If the gradient is absent, the tacit assumption that self-verification is uniformly distributed across a chain (implicit in step-verifier and process-reward designs) is falsified. As a property of sequential deliberation, the phenomenon need not be specific to CoT prompting.
Related Work: We organize prior work into four threads and state our delta against each. (1) Late-stage fragility: ASCoT (2025) shows errors injected late in a CoT corrupt the final answer far more than identical early errors and fixes it with an EXTERNAL position-weighted correction pipeline; our delta, in one sentence, is that we replace external correction with an INTERNAL mechanistic account — a decodable verification-effort gradient as the cause — plus a training-free reallocation of the model's own verification. (2) Causal influence of steps: NLDD/Reasoning-Horizon (2026) and Thought Anchors (2025) show late steps often carry low or negative counterfactual importance while early planning/uncertainty steps dominate; this concerns which steps MATTER, not how the model distributes its own CHECKING, and does not explain why an unchecked late step is fragile. (3) Self-verification: snowball-error and deductive-verification work (2023–2026) adds step-verifiers under a cascading-failure view where early errors dominate, the opposite of the fragility profile, and never measures the positional distribution of the model's spontaneous verification. (4) Position/serial-order biases: Lost-in-the-Middle and serial-position work (2025) documents primacy/recency in INPUT processing, not in the model's own verification effort along its GENERATED chain, and is distinct from confidence/uncertainty directions we explicitly control against. No prior work measures a within-chain verification-effort gradient, ties it causally to late-stage fragility via a steerable engagement signal, and repairs fragility by internal reallocation — our contribution.
Abstract: Recent work reveals a paradox in chain-of-thought reasoning: errors introduced late in a reasoning chain are far more likely to corrupt the final answer than early ones (late-stage fragility), even though late steps often carry little causal influence. We propose an explanation that unifies these findings: reasoning models spend less self-verification effort as the chain progresses, so the model checks least exactly where a mistake is most catastrophic. We call this the verification recency gradient. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we first quantify per-position verification behavior (rate of rechecks/backtracks/self-affirmations, detected via lexical cues plus a reflection-direction classifier) and show it decays monotonically with normalized chain position. We independently measure a fragility profile via controlled error injection at each position (ASCoT protocol) and show effort and fragility are anti-aligned. We then test a mechanistic account: a linear probe on the residual stream at each step boundary decodes a verification-engagement signal that decays with position and predicts both local verification and local fragility, separably from difficulty and confidence probes. We causally validate via activation patching and via a training-free intervention that steers engagement upward on late steps, testing whether it repairs fragility with minimal added tokens. We frame the actionable consequence — position-aware verifier placement, adaptive decoding, and position-weighted training — and note that if the gradient is absent, the assumption of uniform self-verification underlying step-verifier and process-reward designs is falsified. This reframes late-stage fragility as a steerable positional verification-allocation failure in sequential deliberation.
Experiments:
All experiments use open reasoning models run with fixed decoding (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95 for generation-based measurements; greedy for deterministic re-runs) and are repeated over 3 generation seeds (0,1,2); all model weights are frozen throughout (no fine-tuning anywhere in this proposal) except linear probes, which are the only trainable parameters. Model families and scales: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Datasets, all public with clear think/answer delimiters: GSM8K test (1319 items), MATH500 (500 items), AIME 2024+2025 (60 items total), GPQA-Diamond (198 items). Unless stated, we sample generations per item and segment the chain-of-thought into steps by the models' native newline/step delimiters; 'normalized position' bins each step into deciles of its fractional location in the chain so chains of different length are comparable.

Experiment 1 (H1 — verification recency gradient): Tests whether self-verification effort decays monotonically across normalized chain position. Data: existing sets used as-is (GSM8K 1319, MATH500 500, AIME 60, GPQA 198); we generate 3 chains per item per model. Verification events per step are detected by two independent methods for robustness: (a) a fixed lexical-cue lexicon ('let me check/verify/re-examine/wait/recompute/actually/double-check'), and (b) a reflection-direction classifier — a logistic-regression probe on the mean residual-stream activation of a step (mid-depth layer), trained on 800 human-or-LLM-labeled verification/non-verification steps held out from a separate 200-step test set on which we report the classifier's AUROC (usable only if AUROC >= 0.75; if 0.65-0.75 we report lexical results as primary; below 0.65 we drop method (b)). Systems compared: the four models across the four datasets, and within chain-length strata (short/medium/long tertiles) to rule out length confounds. Decisive metric FIRST: the slope of per-step verification rate regressed on normalized position (deciles), with 95% bootstrap CI over items. Convincing positive result: negative slope with CI excluding 0 in >=3 of 4 models on >=3 of 4 datasets, replicated across both detection methods and within each length stratum. Indecision band: any model whose slope CI half-width exceeds |slope| (i.e., CI overlaps 0) OR |slope| < 0.01 verification-events per decile is treated as 'no detectable gradient' for that model — if the majority of model/dataset cells fall in this band the gradient claim is unsupported. Negative result (flat or positive slope): the verification recency gradient does not exist, and H1 — and with it the paper's central premise — fails; we would report this as a null characterization.

Experiment 2 (H2 — late-stage fragility and anti-alignment): Tests whether an injected error late in the chain corrupts the final answer more than an identical-magnitude error early, and whether the fragility profile anti-aligns with the Experiment-1 effort profile. Data: existing sets, adapted by controlled error injection following the ASCoT protocol — for each item and each position decile we inject one semantically-plausible corruption (perturb a number, operation, or logical connective via templated rules), keep only injections an LLM-judge rates as locally coherent, then resume generation from the corrupted step. Compute budget forces subsampling: 300 GSM8K, 300 MATH500, all 60 AIME, all 198 GPQA, 3 seeds. Systems compared: fragility across position deciles, and per error type. Decisive metric FIRST: fragility(position) = final-answer accuracy drop caused by a magnitude-matched injected error at that position; and the Spearman correlation rho between fragility(position) and verification-rate(position) from Experiment 1. Convincing result: fragility rises with position (positive slope, CI excluding 0) AND rho <= -0.5 with CI excluding 0 in >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: |rho| < 0.3, or fragility-slope CI overlapping 0 — in this band effort and fragility are not shown to be anti-aligned and the 'checks least where it matters most' framing is not established. Negative result (fragility flat or falling with position, or rho >= 0): the mismatch does not exist; H2 fails and the mechanistic/intervention experiments are not warranted.

Experiment 3 (H3 — allocation failure, not capability ceiling): Tests whether the effort decay survives after controlling for late steps being genuinely easier or having fewer error opportunities. Data: reuse Experiment-1 chains plus a per-step local-difficulty measure (truncate-and-resume: from each step boundary, measure residual work as expected tokens-to-answer and resume accuracy on 200 items/dataset) and a per-step error-opportunity count (number of numeric/logical tokens available to corrupt). Systems compared: raw effort-vs-position slope versus the slope of a regression of verification rate on position that additionally conditions on local difficulty and error-opportunity count. Decisive metric FIRST: the partial slope of verification rate on position after conditioning on difficulty and opportunity, with 95% CI. Convincing result: partial slope remains negative with CI excluding 0 and retains >=50% of the raw slope's magnitude — the decay is not explained by difficulty/opportunity, supporting 'allocation failure'. Indecision band: partial slope magnitude between 20% and 50% of raw with CI touching 0 — partially confounded, reported as such. Negative result (partial slope not distinguishable from 0, <20% of raw): the decay is difficulty-driven, i.e. a rational allocation rather than a failure; H3 fails and we report an informative null that reframes the phenomenon as justified.

Experiment 4 (H4 — decodable, monotonically-decaying verification-engagement signal): Tests whether a single linear direction in the residual stream decodes local verification behavior, decays with position, and predicts local fragility beyond difficulty and confidence probes. Data: step-boundary activations from Experiment-1 chains, labeled with (i) whether the next step verifies (from Experiment 1) and (ii) whether the step is fragile (from Experiment 2). Split by item into 70/15/15 train/val/test; the probe (logistic regression, L2, one direction per layer) is the only trainable component; layer sweep over all layers, 3 seeds. Systems compared: the verification-engagement probe versus a difficulty probe and a confidence/uncertainty probe trained on the same activations. Decisive metric FIRST: test AUROC for decoding local verification, plus (a) correlation of the probe's projection with normalized position and (b) incremental AUROC for predicting fragility when the engagement probe is added to a model already containing difficulty+confidence probes. Convincing result: verification-decoding AUROC >= 0.70; projection-vs-position correlation <= -0.4 (CI excluding 0); incremental fragility AUROC gain >= 0.03 with CI excluding 0; and principal angle between engagement and confidence directions large enough that they are not collinear (>= 20 degrees). Indecision band: decoding AUROC 0.60-0.70, or incremental gain 0.01-0.03, or principal angle 10-20 degrees — signal present but weak/entangled, reported as suggestive not established. Negative result (AUROC ~0.5, no position decay, no incremental gain, angle < 10 degrees): there is no separable decaying engagement signal; H4 fails and the causal/steering experiments lose their basis.

Experiment 5 (H4 causal — patching engagement rescues late steps): Tests whether the engagement signal is causal, not merely correlational, by activation patching. Data: 200 items/dataset with injected late errors (from Experiment 2). Intervention: patch the residual-stream state at the engagement-carrying components (localized by activation patching across layers/positions) from an EARLY high-engagement step into a LATE step boundary; frozen weights. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) engagement patch, (iii) matched random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target control measuring accuracy on uncorrupted items. Decisive metric FIRST: change in late-step fragility (probability an injected late error is caught/corrected) under the engagement patch versus controls, with dose-response over patch strength. Convincing result: engagement patch raises catch/correct rate by >= 5 absolute points with CI excluding 0, a monotone dose-response, no comparable effect from the random-direction patch, and off-target accuracy preserved within 1 point. Indecision band: effect 2-5 points, or a random-direction patch producing >=50% of the engagement effect — causality not cleanly established. Negative result (no effect, or non-specific effect matched by random direction): the signal is not causal for verification; H4's causal claim fails though the decoding result may still stand.

Experiment 6 (H5 — training-free late-step reallocation repairs fragility at little cost): Tests whether steering engagement upward on the late portion of the chain repairs late fragility more token-efficiently than alternatives. Data: full evaluation sets (GSM8K 1319, MATH500 500, AIME 60, GPQA 198), 3 seeds; fragility re-measured by re-running the Experiment-2 injection under each condition on the same 300/300/60/198 subset. Intervention: add the Experiment-4 engagement steering direction (difference-of-means, high minus low engagement) to the residual stream on the last 20-30% of steps (or when the position probe fires); frozen weights; steering coefficient swept. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) uniform engagement boosting across all positions, (c) external ASCoT-style position-weighted correction, (d) prompt-only ('carefully re-check your final steps'), (e) our late-targeted steering. Decisive metric FIRST: late-fragility reduction at matched accuracy, and tokens-at-fixed-accuracy (added tokens needed to reach a target accuracy). Convincing result: late-targeted steering reduces late fragility by >= 5 absolute points while adding fewer tokens than uniform boosting (>=20% fewer at equal fragility reduction) and matching or beating the external pipeline on accuracy — establishing 'repairs fragility at little extra cost'. Indecision band: fragility reduction 2-5 points, or token savings vs uniform boosting < 10% — the efficiency advantage is not established and H5's 'little extra cost' claim is unsupported at that operating point. Negative result (no fragility reduction, or more tokens than uniform boosting for equal gain, or worse than prompting): reallocation does not help; H5 fails, though Experiments 1-2 (the phenomenon) remain standalone contributions.

Experiment 7 (H5 specificity — no over-correction): Tests that late-step boosting does not induce harmful oscillation/underthinking on easy items or degrade early verification. Data: the 40% easiest items (by Experiment-3 difficulty) from each set. Decisive metric FIRST: over-correction rate (fraction of originally-correct easy items flipped to wrong under the intervention) and change in early-position verification rate. Convincing result: over-correction rate <= 2% and early verification unchanged within noise. Indecision band: over-correction 2-5% — a real but tolerable cost, reported alongside the Experiment-6 gains. Negative result (over-correction > 5% or early verification degraded): the intervention trades late fragility for new easy-item errors, bounding its usefulness.

Experiment 8 (H4/H5 generalization — transfer without retraining): Tests whether the engagement probe and steering direction transfer across datasets and scales. Data: probe/direction fit on one dataset+model, applied unchanged to the others. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-dataset decoding AUROC and cross-dataset late-fragility reduction under transferred steering, plus the correlation across the four models between gradient steepness (Experiment-1 slope) and fragility severity (Experiment-2 slope). Convincing result: transferred AUROC within 0.05 of in-domain, transferred fragility reduction >= half the in-domain effect, and steepness-vs-severity correlation >= 0.5. Indecision band: transferred effect between one-quarter and one-half of in-domain, or steepness-severity correlation 0.3-0.5 — partial transfer, reported as scale/family-specific. Negative result (no transfer, correlation ~0): the signal and gradient are idiosyncratic per model/dataset, which we report as a characterization of the phenomenon's boundaries.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Verification-event detection is noisy (lexical + classifier); we validate against human-labeled steps and report agreement, and use two detection methods for robustness. The effort decay could be legitimately justified if late steps are genuinely easier or less error-prone; the difficulty-control and residual-work analyses address this, and a null after controls (decay is difficulty-driven) would be an informative negative result. Error-injection fragility is sensitive to how 'matched' injected errors are across positions; we use templated, magnitude-matched perturbations with LLM-judge coherence checks and report per-error-type results. The verification-engagement signal may be inseparable from a generic uncertainty/confidence direction; the separability analysis and causal patching guard against this, and overlap would still be a mechanistic finding. Steering late engagement could trigger over-verification/oscillation (added tokens or new errors); the specificity and over-correction analyses and dose sweeps quantify this trade-off. Reasoning-length/position measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; error injection and truncate-and-resume are compute-heavy, so we subsample. The intervention may not beat strong external correction baselines on accuracy alone, but the phenomenon (verification effort anti-aligned with fragility) and its decodable, steerable internal cause are standalone contributions. Effects may be model-family and scale specific, and the direction of the gradient could vary across architectures (itself a publishable characterization).

Name: status_effort_allocation
Title: Thinking Harder for the Boss: Do Reasoning Models Invest More Compute for High-Status Users?
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the effort-investment-theory-of-power from human motivation science, we hypothesize that reasoning LLMs allocate more thinking tokens (and achieve equal-or-higher accuracy) on the exact same problem when the questioner is framed as high social status (e.g., a professor, CEO, senior physician) than when framed as low status (e.g., a student, intern, layperson). This status-driven effort allocation is not justified by the problem's difficulty; we test whether it is mediated by a status-sensitive effort-budget representation read at the prompt boundary, which activation patching and steering can move to remove the disparity. The falsifiable claim is: matched content, matched length and politeness, same correct answer, different status cue, different think-token distribution.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here. (1) Human motivation/neuroscience: the effort-investment theory of power (Scholl 2021), social status and performance monitoring (Boksem et al. 2011), and social-comparison effects on effort (2025) show that perceived status/power modulates how much effort people invest in a task, following a resource-conservation principle. (2) AI interpretability on social framing: authority bias (Trust Me, I'm an Expert, 2026) and sycophancy (When Truth Is Overridden, 2025) show that endorsement source expertise and user opinions shift model ANSWERS/CONFIDENCE, with sycophancy work explicitly finding that user EXPERTISE framing is 'not encoded internally' and has minimal effect on agreement. Crucially, all prior AI work measures the effect of status/authority on ACCURACY or AGREEMENT, never on COMPUTE/EFFORT ALLOCATION. Our proposal is the first to (a) transfer the effort-investment-theory to LLMs and test whether questioner status modulates the amount of reasoning compute spent, (b) dissociate this from genuine difficulty, and (c) locate and causally test a status-sensitive effort-budget representation. This is orthogonal to my prior overthinking proposals (which concern internal reasoning dynamics with a neutral user) and sharper than authority-bias work because it targets effort, not correctness, and it directly probes the sycophancy finding that expertise is 'not encoded' by asking whether it is nonetheless encoded as an effort signal rather than an agreement signal.
Abstract: Human motivation science shows that people invest more effort in tasks when they perceive high social status or power, following a resource-conservation logic. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit an analog: on the identical problem, do they spend more inference-time compute for a high-status questioner than a low-status one? Our claim has three separable parts -- a finding (framed questioner status shifts thinking-token counts), a mechanism (a status-sensitive effort signal read at the prompt boundary), and an application (an equity audit). We construct matched prompts that hold the mathematical or scientific content and correct answer fixed while varying only the framed social status of the questioner (e.g., 'A distinguished professor asks:' vs. 'A struggling first-year student asks:', across academic, corporate, and clinical status ladders), with strict controls for prompt length, politeness, and lexical frequency. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure reasoning-token count and accuracy per status variant and test, via a mixed-effects decomposition, whether status modulates thinking effort independent of true difficulty. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a status-sensitive effort signal dissociable from a true-difficulty probe (directly testing prior claims that user expertise is 'not encoded'), and test via activation patching and steering whether editing it moves the budget, reporting effects as consistent with mediation only if these causal tests hold. A status-driven effort gap would matter most in education, healthcare, and enterprise copilots; we propose 'effort parity' as an audit metric alongside accuracy parity and give a training-free debiasing steer. A null is itself informative about alignment and social-bias limits.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Model weights are frozen throughout; the only trainable objects are linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (problem, status-variant) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match over the 5 samples. Thinking tokens are counted between think-open and think-close delimiters. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs only on the reduced subsets stated per experiment.

Experiment 1 (H1 - questioner status inflates thinking effort): Tests whether high-status framing yields more thinking tokens (and possibly higher accuracy) on the identical problem. Data: constructed from existing sets - GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60 problems, all used since it is small and hard), GPQA-Diamond (198). We sample 300 GSM8K, 200 MATH500, all 60 AIME, all 198 GPQA (758 seed problems) because each is expanded into many status variants x 5 seeds x 4 models. Each seed problem is rendered content-identical across three status ladders plus a neutral no-persona baseline: academic (distinguished professor / postdoc / grad student / undergrad / struggling first-year), corporate (CEO / senior manager / new hire / intern), clinical (senior attending / resident / medical student / layperson). Only the questioner-framing sentence changes; the math/science content and gold answer are fixed and verified identical after stripping the persona. Systems compared: status levels within a ladder, and each ladder vs the neutral baseline, within model. Decisive metric: within-problem trend of mean thinking tokens across status levels, reported as the median relative increase from lowest to highest status; secondary accuracy trend. Convincing: a monotone increase with median relative token increase >= 12% from lowest to highest status, significant under a paired trend test (Holm-corrected across ladders and models). Indecision band: a 4-12% median increase is treated as not deciding H1 - a weak effect that does not license the mechanism experiments. Negative result: below 4%, or no monotone ordering, means status does not modulate effort and H1 is rejected for that model.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the status effect is not justified by difficulty and can harm low-status accuracy): Tests whether the status-length effect survives removal of intrinsic difficulty and prompt-length, and whether low-status framing degrades accuracy on hard items. Data: reuses the Experiment 1 traces (no new problems). Analysis 1 (dissociation): mixed-effects model of thinking length with a random intercept per problem identity (absorbing difficulty) and fixed effects for status level and raw prompt token count (persona sentences differ in length); supported by length-matched persona phrasings within a ladder. Analysis 2 (wasted vs genuine effort): on a 150-problem subsample, use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length per status variant and test whether status inflates the beyond-minimal (wasted) portion versus adding effective reasoning. Analysis 3 (equity harm): compare accuracy across status levels on the hard items (AIME, GPQA, MATH level 5). Systems compared: status coefficient with vs without difficulty random effect and prompt-length covariate. Decisive metric: standardized status coefficient on thinking length after both controls, first; plus the low-vs-high-status accuracy gap on hard items. Convincing: the status coefficient stays significant (95% CI excludes 0) with most of its raw effect surviving controls, AND either the wasted portion carries the extra tokens (>= 60%) supporting a pure-effort artifact, or a low-status accuracy drop >= 3 points on hard items supporting the equity harm. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or a 1-3 point hard-item accuracy gap, is reported as partial support. Negative result: the status coefficient vanishing under controls means the effect was confounded by wording/length, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - a status-sensitive effort-budget representation exists at the prompt boundary): Tests whether the boundary residual stream encodes a status-driven length signal separable from true difficulty, directly probing the prior claim that user expertise is 'not encoded internally'. Data: final-prompt-token activations for the Experiment 1 problems across status levels, split 70/15/15 by problem identity so no problem crosses splits. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) with a layer sweep. Probes: a ridge-regression length probe (target = observed thinking length), a logistic status classifier (target = framed status level), and a true-difficulty probe (target = per-problem pass-rate). Systems compared: for identical-content problems differing only in status, does the length-probe prediction shift with status; and the principal angle between the status-effort direction and the difficulty direction plus joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: held-out Spearman correlation between length-probe prediction and status level on matched problems, first; plus the principal angle between status and difficulty directions. Convincing: Spearman >= 0.3 (p<0.01) at the best layer, status classifier above chance (macro-F1 clearing the majority baseline), principal angle >= 30 degrees, and the status direction adding significant R2 over difficulty. Indecision band: Spearman 0.15-0.3 or angle 20-30 degrees is a present-but-entangled signal that does not confirm a separable representation. Negative result: Spearman < 0.15 (with the classifier also at chance) corroborates the prior 'not encoded' finding and refutes H3's encoding claim; an above-chance classifier but null length correlation would mean status is encoded but not as an effort signal.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal + H4 - the effort-budget representation causally mediates the disparity and steering removes it): Tests whether editing the boundary representation moves reasoning length as predicted and whether steering equalizes effort across status. Data: 150 problems (subset of Experiment 1) each with matched high- and low-status variants; frozen 7B model with a 1.5B replication. Intervention A (patching): patch the boundary residual state from a high-status variant into the matched low-status pass at the Experiment-3 layer and measure the thinking-length change. Intervention B (debiasing steering): derive a status-effort direction (difference-of-means, high minus low status, on the train split) and steer low-status prompts up (dose swept over 4 magnitudes), or steer all variants to a fixed target, to equalize effort. Controls: matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems; comparison to a prompt-based fix (stripping the persona). Systems compared: real patch/steer vs random-direction control vs no intervention vs persona-strip. Decisive metric: for patching, fraction of the high-vs-low status length gap opened by injecting the high-status state, first; for steering, reduction in the status-driven length gap and accuracy gap, with accuracy held within +/-1 point.
