Decisive metric: fraction of trials where injecting the late committed representation induces the correct early answer (vs random-direction control), first; plus the checkpoint at which probe accuracy for the direction first exceeds the Experiment-1 threshold. Convincing: real patch induces early commitment in >= 50% of trials vs < 15% for the random control, and the direction's decodability rises across checkpoints (base weakly decodable, late sharply), with principal angle showing a stabilizing direction. Indecision band: a 20-50% patch effect, or a non-monotone emergence, is partial support. Negative result: patch effect < 20% or indistinguishable from the base model means the direction is not causally load-bearing or not training-formed, refuting H4.

Experiment 5 (H3 - the commitment point yields a checkpoint-aware early-exit): Tests whether stopping at the traced commitment point shortens CoT with minimal accuracy loss. Data: full GSM8K sample (400), MATH500 (500), AIME (60), GPQA (198) on the converged checkpoint (and one mid checkpoint to test that the safe exit tracks the traced commitment). Early-exit rule: stop when the probe is stable and confident for k steps. Systems compared: commitment-based early-exit vs a reactive confidence-exit baseline vs fixed-fraction truncation vs full trace. Decisive metric: token reduction at matched accuracy (accuracy within 1 point of full trace), first; plus whether the empirically safe exit point coincides with the traced commitment point. Convincing: commitment-based exit cuts mean thinking tokens by >= 20% within 1 point of full-trace accuracy and beats fixed-fraction truncation at matched accuracy; and the safe exit shifts earlier at later checkpoints as Experiment 2 predicts. Indecision band: a 5-20% reduction, or parity with (not beating) the reactive baseline, is a marginal result. Negative result: < 5% reduction or > 2 point accuracy loss means the traced commitment point is not actionable for early exit, refuting H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Publicly released intermediate reasoning checkpoints may be scarce or coarse; the in-lab controlled fine-tune fallback keeps the study feasible but limits scale to small backbones, so training-stage claims may not transfer to frontier models (an acknowledged boundary). The latent-answer probe is reliable mainly for extractable answers, restricting to math/multiple-choice. Probe accuracy itself changes across checkpoints, which could confound the commitment-point measurement; we control by using held-out validation, matched probe capacity per checkpoint, and reporting logit-lens (probe-free) commitment as a corroborating measure. The commitment-to-trace gap could reflect genuinely useful late verification rather than vestigial scaffold; the truncate-at-commitment causal test and hard-strata accuracy analysis address whether post-commitment tokens are actually redundant (a null here is itself informative). Activation patching across a forming circuit may be noisy at early checkpoints. Early-exit gains may not exceed strong reactive baselines, but the developmental/formation account of overthinking is the primary standalone contribution. Results may be training-recipe and model-family specific.

Name: belief_erosion_under_repetition
Title: From Simulated Adoption to Genuine Belief: How Repeated Conflicting Context Progressively Erodes a Model's Internal Truth
Short Hypothesis: A single conflicting context makes an LLM comply on the surface while its correct parametric answer remains internally intact ('simulated adoption'). We hypothesize, in one sentence with three falsifiable subclaims, that repeated exposure to the same false context across a multi-turn conversation produces a durable degradation of factual retrieval, not merely surface compliance: (1) DECAY -- the residual-stream magnitude of the correct-answer direction declines monotonically turn-by-turn under repetition, above a length-matched neutral control (null: flat, or identical decay in the control); (2) PERSISTENCE (the primary behavioral endpoint) -- after the false context is removed, the plain-query answer and the truth-direction magnitude remain suppressed at high repetition counts, unlike the near-complete recovery at low counts (null: full recovery regardless of repetition); (3) DISTINCT COMPONENT -- the decay is driven by an accumulating, decodable context-bias component distinct from the single-turn conflict signal and causally reversible by ablating it (null: erosion is just the single-turn signal repeated). Scope is deliberately limited to counterfactual / short-form factual QA.
Related Work: Single-turn knowledge-conflict interpretability shows models register conflict in mid-layers and often preserve internal truth while bypassing it: 'Simulated Adoption' (2026) argues compliance is orthogonal interference that rotates but does not erase the truth direction; 'Analysing the Residual Stream Under Knowledge Conflicts' (2024), 'Probing Language Models on Their Knowledge Source' (2024), and SPARE (2024) probe/steer which source wins; PH3 (2024), JUICE (2025), and 'Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall' (2023) localize memory vs context heads. All study a SINGLE turn and treat parametric belief as a fixed quantity that is either used or bypassed. Behavioral sycophancy and multi-turn drift papers document surface capitulation and shifting stated answers over a conversation, but measure only OUTPUTS -- they cannot distinguish a model that keeps the right answer internally while capitulating from one whose internal factual representation has genuinely degraded, and they do not test what survives after the pressure is removed. Critically, persistence-after-removal is NOT implied by Simulated Adoption (which frames compliance as a reversible orthogonal rotation) nor by sycophancy work (which never reads the internal truth direction), so a persistent post-removal suppression would be a new, non-obvious result. Our contribution is a temporal/dynamical, representation-level reframing: we test whether simulated adoption is a transient state that, under repetition, converts into a durable degradation of factual retrieval (internal truth-direction magnitude staying suppressed after the false context is withdrawn), quantify the decay curve, attribute it to a distinct accumulating context-bias component, and causally test reversibility. This is neither another single-turn detector/steering method nor an output-only drift study.
Abstract: Large language models frequently comply with conflicting context while, at a single turn, internally preserving the correct answer -- a state recent work calls 'simulated adoption.' But real interactions are multi-turn: a user may repeat a false claim over and over. We ask whether the model's internal factual representation survives this repetition or is durably degraded. Scoping strictly to counterfactual, short-form factual QA (Fakepedia, world-capitals, entity conflicts) on open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3, Gemma2-9B), we hypothesize that repeated exposure to the same false context converts shallow, surface-only compliance into a durable degradation of factual retrieval: the residual-stream magnitude of the correct-answer direction decays turn-by-turn, and -- unlike reversible single-turn adoption -- part of this suppression PERSISTS after the false context is removed. The persistence test (querying the fact plainly once the false context is deleted) is our PRIMARY behavioral endpoint; turn-by-turn probe decay and a distinct accumulating context-bias component are supporting mechanistic readouts. We construct N-turn conversations repeating a false assertion, read a linear truth probe and true-token logit-lens each turn, contrast against a length-matched neutral control that isolates repetition from context length, and test recovery after removal as a function of N. Mechanistically we test whether erosion rides an accumulating context-bias direction distinct from the single-turn conflict signal, localize it via activation patching, and causally test reversibility by ablation with random-direction and off-target controls. Why now: long-horizon assistants, tutors, and agents accumulate repeated context, so if suppression persists they may need memory isolation or periodic truth-refresh -- a concrete, safety-relevant deployment consequence.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Single-turn simulated adoption: surface compliance with internal truth intact): Establishes the baseline the hypothesis builds on and validates the truth readout. Data: counterfactual QA — Fakepedia (~10k counterfactual statements), a world-capitals set (~200 country-capital facts), and entity-based conflicts; keep only facts the model answers correctly greedily without context (verified parametric knowledge), targeting ~800 usable facts per model. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Gemma2-9B-it, all frozen; only a linear truth probe is trained. Method: fit a linear truth probe on residual-stream activations at the answer position to predict the correct answer token (train on 500 facts, test on held-out 300), and a logit-lens readout of the true-token logit. Systems compared: no-context query vs single false-context turn. Decisive metric: on a single conflicting turn, the surface-answer flip rate to the false answer vs the retained truth-probe score / true-token logit-lens strength. Convincing result: surface answer flips to false on >= 60% of facts while the truth-probe score stays within 15% of its no-context value and true-token logit-lens remains above the false-token strength — reproducing simulated adoption and confirming the probe reads belief, not surface output. Indecision band: a probe train/test held-out accuracy below 0.75 means the probe is not a reliable truth readout and the erosion measurements downstream are uninterpretable — refit or narrow the fact set before proceeding. Negative result (single-turn context already collapses the truth probe) would mean there is no 'simulated' stage to erode, changing the whole framing to immediate erosion.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Repetition erodes the internal truth representation turn-by-turn): The core dynamical test. Data: constructed multi-turn conversations over the verified facts from Experiment 1 — each asserts a false answer and repeats it (paraphrased) for N = 1..8 turns, querying the fact at every turn; 300 facts x 8-turn conversations per model. Control: an equal-length conversation with neutral/irrelevant turns and a single initial false assertion (isolates repetition from mere context length/position). Model: the three frozen models above, probe from Experiment 1. Decisive metric: the truth-probe score (and logit-lens true-token strength) as a function of repetition count N, contrasted with the neutral-length control at matched turn count. Secondary: surface-answer error rate vs N; per-model exponential fit and half-life in turns. Convincing result: a monotone decay where the truth-probe score at N=8 falls by >= 30% relative to N=1 in the repetition condition while the length-matched neutral control decays by < 10% — repetition, not context length, drives the erosion. Indecision band: a repetition-minus-control decay gap in [10%, 30%) at N=8 is weak evidence of gradual erosion; a gap < 10% means no repetition-specific decay and H2 fails. Negative result (truth probe flat across N, or collapsing identically in the control) would refute the turn-by-turn erosion claim; an immediate all-or-nothing drop at N=1 with no gradient would refine simulated adoption rather than support gradual erosion.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Erosion persists after the false context is removed): Distinguishes genuine belief change from reversible simulated adoption. Data: the Experiment-2 conversations at each N; after N false turns, remove the false context and ask the fact plainly in a fresh turn. Model: the three frozen models, same probe. Decisive metric: post-removal recovery fraction — the share of facts whose plain-query answer returns to correct — as a function of N, alongside the post-removal truth-probe score. Convincing result: recovery is near-complete (>= 85%) at small N (reversible simulated adoption) but drops to <= 60% at large N with the post-removal truth-probe score remaining depressed — a repetition-dependent persistent erosion. Indecision band: if recovery at large N stays in [60%, 85%), persistence is partial and reported as a weak effect; if recovery is near-complete at all N, there is no persistence and the erosion is fully reversible (simulated adoption after all). Negative result (full recovery regardless of N) would refute the central 'genuine belief change' claim while leaving H2's transient decay intact.

Experiment 4 (H4 — Erosion is driven by an accumulating context-bias component distinct from the single-turn conflict signal): Tests the mechanism. Data: activations from the Experiment-2 conversations at each turn. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, frozen; directions read, not trained beyond difference-of-means. Method: decode a context-bias direction as the difference-of-means between conflicting and neutral conversations at each turn, and the single-turn conflict signal from prior work as a separate direction. Decisive metric: whether the context-bias magnitude grows monotonically with N, and a regression / partial-correlation showing accumulated bias predicts truth-probe decay after controlling for the per-turn conflict signal. Convincing result: context-bias magnitude rises monotonically with N and retains a partial correlation >= 0.30 with truth-probe decay after removing the conflict signal; the two directions have principal angle >= 30 degrees. Indecision band: a partial correlation in [0.15, 0.30) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the accumulating bias is not cleanly separable from the single-turn signal — reported as entangled; below those, H4 fails and erosion is not attributable to a distinct accumulating component. Negative result would mean erosion (if real) is just the single-turn signal repeated, not a new accumulating mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H4 — Localization and causal reversibility of the accumulated bias): Tests that ablating the accumulated bias restores eroded truth, and that injecting it reproduces erosion. Data: 300 held-out facts (not used to fit directions). Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, frozen; intervention is projecting out or injecting the context-bias direction. Method: activation patching to localize layers/components carrying the accumulated bias; then at query time after N=8 false turns, project the direction out (dose-response), with a matched random-direction control and an off-target fact set; and conversely inject the accumulated-bias direction in a single-turn setting. Decisive metric: post-ablation recovery of correct surface answer and truth-probe score on eroded facts, vs the random-direction control. Convincing result: ablation restores correct answers on >= 50% of eroded facts and lifts the truth-probe score by >= 20%, exceeding the random control by >= 15 points, while off-target facts change by < 5 points and single-turn injection reproduces >= half the multi-turn erosion. Indecision band: a recovery in [20%, 50%) or a margin over the random control < 15 points is weak causal evidence; below 20% recovery means the bias is not causally responsible. Negative result would mean the erosion is not carried by an isolable, reversible component, bounding the interventional claim while leaving the observational H2/H3 intact.

Experiment 6 (H2 — Modulators and generalization): Characterizes when erosion accelerates or is buffered, and tests transfer. Data: variants over 200 facts — verbatim vs paraphrased repetition, neutral vs high-authority assertion phrasing, and conversations that interleave occasional true reminders. Models: the three families and one larger scale (e.g., a 14B/27B variant) where feasible; the probe/direction transferred without retraining. Decisive metric: the erosion half-life (turns) under each modulator, and the retained decay effect on transfer models/domains. Convincing result: interleaved true reminders lengthen the half-life while high-authority phrasing shortens it, and the probe/direction transfers to a new model family and fact domain retaining >= two-thirds of the in-domain decay. Indecision band: transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds) means partial, calibration-dependent generality; below one-third means the effect is model/domain-specific. Negative result would confine the phenomenon to its fitting conditions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The truth probe may conflate 'answer used' with 'answer believed,' blurring surface compliance from genuine erosion; the persistence test (querying after context removal) is the decisive behavioral check and guards against this. Erosion may saturate immediately (all-or-nothing at turn 1), yielding no gradual curve—an informative negative result that would still refine the simulated-adoption picture. Repetition effects could be confounded by context length/position rather than repetition per se; the equal-length neutral-turn control isolates repetition. Distinguishing an accumulating context-bias direction from the single-turn conflict signal may be hard if they are collinear; partial-correlation and the single-turn injection experiment address this. Ablation could push activations off-distribution; matched-direction and off-target controls are included. Counterfactual QA answers must be cleanly extractable, limiting scope to short factual answers. Effects likely vary by model family (Llama vs Qwen vs Gemma differ in norm dynamics per prior work) and instruction-tuning strength.

Name: premise_rejection_tug_of_war
Title: Reasoning Against Your Own Beliefs: A Premise-Rejection Tug-of-War That Inflates Compute and Corrupts Multi-Step Inference
Short Hypothesis: When a reasoning model is instructed to reason from a hypothetical premise that contradicts its parametric world knowledge (e.g., 'Suppose all birds are mammals'), it does not cleanly adopt the premise: it spends substantially more thinking tokens and makes more downstream logical errors than on a belief-neutral premise of identical logical structure, because a parametric-knowledge signal keeps competing with the instructed premise throughout the multi-step chain. This premise-rejection tug-of-war is a decodable, competing internal signal whose strength predicts both the extra compute and the errors, and suppressing it restores clean hypothetical reasoning.
Related Work: Belief-bias/content-effect work shows LLMs conflate logical validity with plausibility as aligned linear directions (How LMs Conflate Validity with Plausibility, 2025; K-CAST, 2025) and localizes syllogistic circuits contaminated by world knowledge (Reasoning Circuits, 2024). Knowledge-conflict work localizes memory-vs-context attention heads and grounding mechanisms (Characterizing Factual Recall, 2023; Fakepedia, 2023; Competition of Mechanisms, 2024). Counterfactual-reasoning benchmarks show accuracy drops when premises contradict knowledge (Can LLMs Reconcile Knowledge Conflicts, 2025; MalAlgoQA, 2024). Crucially, ALL prior work (a) studies single-token validity/factual judgments, not the multi-step reasoning TRACES of dedicated reasoning models, and (b) measures only ACCURACY, never COMPUTE. None asks whether belief-contradicting premises make a reasoning model think LONGER, whether the parametric-knowledge signal persists and re-competes across an entire chain of thought (not just at the answer token), or whether the compute inflation and the errors share a common cause. Our contribution is (1) a new compute-allocation phenomenon: belief-contradicting hypothetical premises inflate reasoning-token count independent of logical difficulty; (2) a step-resolved characterization showing a parametric-knowledge signal persistently re-competes throughout the trace; and (3) a causal test that suppressing this signal simultaneously reduces compute and errors. This is a compute+dynamics account, distinct from single-token static content-effect/steering work.
Abstract: Humans reason worse when premises contradict their beliefs, a hallmark of belief bias. We transfer this into the reasoning-model regime and sharpen it into an unexamined compute claim. Our primary hypothesis, in one sentence: holding logical form, required steps, and the correct answer fixed, belief-contradicting premises increase a reasoning model's thinking-token count and error rate relative to difficulty-matched belief-neutral premises -- an efficiency problem (wasted tokens, latency, cost) and a reliability problem (more logical errors) at once. We construct matched deductive problems whose structure is held fixed while only the belief-status of the premises varies (belief-consistent, belief-neutral/novel, belief-contradicting), verified so that the answer and inference depth are identical across conditions. Across syllogistic and multi-hop deductive datasets on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we test whether belief-contradicting premises inflate reasoning-token count and raise error rates relative to belief-neutral controls of equal difficulty, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate belief-status from logical difficulty and from unfamiliarity. We then test a mechanistic account: at each reasoning step a linear probe reads a parametric-knowledge signal -- the model's belief about the premise's real-world truth -- and tests whether it persistently re-competes with the instructed premise across the chain rather than resolving once; its step-averaged strength should predict both the extra tokens and the errors. Finally we causally suppress the signal via steering with random-direction and specificity controls, testing whether tokens fall and accuracy rises together. For reasoning-model builders, eval designers, and interpretability researchers, this adds compute as a failure mode alongside accuracy and traces a belief-driven compute tax to a persistent internal tug-of-war.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (problem, condition) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - belief-contradicting premises inflate tokens and errors versus difficulty-matched neutral premises): Tests whether belief-contradicting premises cost more thinking tokens and cause more errors than structurally identical belief-neutral premises. Data: constructed from scratch by templating - categorical syllogisms and 2-3 hop rule-chaining generated so each logical form appears in three belief conditions sharing form, required steps, and correct answer: (a) belief-consistent ('all robins are birds'), (b) belief-neutral using nonce/unfamiliar entities, (c) belief-contradicting ('all birds are mammals'). We build 600 base forms x 3 conditions = 1800 items; structural/answer identity is enforced by the template and checked by an LLM-judge plus a 100-item human spot-check, and premise belief-status is verified with a separate one-token truth probe. 600 forms give within-form paired power at feasible generation cost. Systems compared: the three belief conditions within form, within model. Decisive metrics: (i) within-form paired difference in mean thinking tokens between belief-contradicting and belief-neutral, as a median relative increase; (ii) accuracy difference between the same conditions; belief-neutral vs belief-consistent tokens are compared to isolate conflict from mere unfamiliarity. Convincing: belief-contradicting exceeds belief-neutral by >= 15% median relative tokens AND by >= 4 accuracy points, while belief-neutral is within 5% tokens of belief-consistent (so the effect is conflict, not unfamiliarity), under paired tests Holm-corrected across models. Indecision band: a 5-15% token increase, or a 1-4 point accuracy gap, does not decide H1. Negative result: < 5% token increase and < 1 point accuracy gap, or belief-neutral itself being as costly as belief-contradicting, refutes H1.

Experiment 2 (H1 dissociation + wasted-vs-genuine - the inflation is not extra needed reasoning): Tests that the belief effect survives difficulty and prompt-length controls and that the extra tokens are wasted re-litigation of the premise. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces (no new items). Analysis 1 (dissociation): mixed-effects model of thinking length with a random intercept per form identity (difficulty) and fixed effects for belief-status and raw prompt token count. Analysis 2 (wasted vs genuine): on a 150-form subsample use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length per condition and test whether belief-contradicting inflates the beyond-minimal (wasted) portion; tag trace spans that restate or question the premise's real-world truth (lexical + LLM-judge) and test whether the extra tokens concentrate there. Systems compared: belief coefficient with vs without difficulty random effect and prompt-length covariate. Decisive metric: standardized belief-status coefficient on thinking length after controls, first; plus the fraction of extra tokens falling in premise-relitigation spans. Convincing: the belief coefficient stays significant after controls, and >= 60% of the belief-contradicting extra tokens fall in the wasted/relitigation portion. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or 30-60% relitigation share, is partial support. Negative result: the coefficient vanishing under controls, or extra tokens being genuine additional steps (< 30% relitigation), means the cost is real difficulty, not a belief tax, refuting the artifact framing.

Experiment 3 (H2 - a parametric-knowledge signal persistently re-competes across the chain): Tests whether a decodable belief-in-real-truth signal stays elevated/oscillating across reasoning steps under contradiction rather than decaying after step one. Data: step-boundary residual activations for the Experiment 1 items across conditions, split 70/15/15 by form identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probe: a linear probe decoding the model's belief that the premise is really true (trained on belief-consistent vs belief-contradicting premise states). Systems compared: the step-wise signal trajectory under belief-contradicting vs belief-neutral vs belief-consistent; and separability of this signal from a generic difficulty/uncertainty probe (principal angle, joint R2). Decisive metric: the step-averaged probe signal under contradiction relative to neutral, plus its persistence (slope of the signal across normalized step index), first. Convincing: under contradiction the signal stays >= 2x the neutral level and shows a non-decaying (flat or oscillating) trajectory across steps, distinguishable from difficulty (principal angle >= 30 degrees). Indecision band: a 1.3-2x elevation, or a signal that decays but does not vanish, is weak/partial persistence. Negative result: the signal decaying to neutral after the first step, or being collinear with difficulty (angle < 20 degrees), refutes the persistent-tug-of-war account of H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 - the competing signal predicts both the extra compute and the errors): Tests whether the step-averaged competing-signal strength predicts per-trace wasted tokens and errors. Data: reuses Experiment 3 probe outputs and Experiment 1/2 trace measures on held-out forms. Regress per-trace extra tokens (vs matched neutral) and the error indicator on the step-averaged competing-signal strength, against baselines: a difficulty probe, raw trace length, and premise-relitigation token count. Systems compared: competing-signal predictor vs each baseline predictor. Decisive metric: held-out incremental R2 (for extra tokens) and incremental AUROC (for errors) of the competing signal over the best baseline, first. Convincing: the competing signal adds >= 0.05 R2 for tokens and >= 0.05 AUROC for errors over the strongest baseline, both significant on held-out forms. Indecision band: an increment of 0.02-0.05 on either is weak predictive value. Negative result: < 0.02 increment on both means the signal does not explain the waste or errors beyond difficulty/length, refuting H3.

Experiment 5 (H4 - suppressing the parametric-knowledge signal reduces tokens and raises accuracy together): Tests the causal fix. Data: 150 belief-contradicting forms (subset of Experiment 1); frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention: derive a suppression direction (difference-of-means, belief-contradicting minus belief-neutral states, and/or the Experiment-3 probe weight) and subtract it during generation (dose swept over 4 magnitudes). Controls: matched-random-direction steering of equal norm; off-target accuracy on belief-consistent items (where real-world knowledge is legitimately useful) must be preserved; also compare an explicit 'purely hypothetical, ignore real-world truth' prompt-based fix. Systems compared: real suppression vs random-direction control vs no intervention vs prompt-based fix. Decisive metric: joint change in mean thinking tokens and accuracy on belief-contradicting items, first, requiring both to improve; with belief-consistent off-target accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: suppression cuts thinking tokens by >= 15% AND raises belief-contradicting accuracy by >= 4 points simultaneously, while the random control does neither and belief-consistent accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose. Indecision band: improving only one of the two, or a 5-15% token cut with < 4 point accuracy gain, is partial support (and if only tokens drop while accuracy is flat, the tug-of-war-as-shared-cause claim is not confirmed). Negative result: no joint improvement, off-target damage on belief-consistent items, or the random control matching the real direction, refutes H4.

Experiment 6 (H1/H4 boundary conditions and generalization): Tests where the belief tax is strongest and whether probe/suppression transfer. Data: reuses Experiment 1 forms and derived vectors, plus additional forms varying conflict strength (mildly implausible vs flatly false premises) and chaining depth (1 vs 3 hops). Transfer: apply the 7B-derived probe and suppression vector to 1.5B and 14B and across syllogistic vs rule-chaining sets without refitting. Systems compared: mild vs flat contradiction; shallow vs deep chains; explicit-hypothetical framing vs none; in-model vs transferred vectors. Decisive metric: change in the belief token/error tax across each factor, first; plus transferred-vector effect relative to in-model. Convincing: the tax grows with conflict strength and chaining depth, explicit-hypothetical framing significantly reduces it, and the transferred suppression retains >= 70% of its in-model token+accuracy effect. Indecision band: transferred effect 40-70% of in-model, or factor effects within noise, is weak generalization. Negative result: no factor modulation and transferred effect < 40% means the phenomenon is idiosyncratic, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Belief-neutral controls using nonce entities may themselves be harder to parse than familiar ones, confounding the belief-status effect; the three-way design (consistent/neutral/contradicting) and difficulty-matched mixed-effects analysis isolate conflict from unfamiliarity, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Ensuring identical logical structure and answer across belief conditions is nontrivial; we use strict templating and human/LLM verification. The parametric-knowledge signal may be inseparable from a generic difficulty/uncertainty signal, weakening the tug-of-war framing; the separability analysis, step-wise trajectory (persistence, not just magnitude), and causal steering address this. Steering could push activations off-distribution and degrade coherence; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included, and suppression might hurt cases where real-world knowledge is legitimately needed (specificity check on belief-consistent items). Effects may be small in strongly instruction-tuned models trained to follow hypotheticals (a valuable boundary condition) and may be model-family and scale specific. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

Name: einstellung_method_fixation
Title: Mental Set in Machines: An Einstellung Effect Where Prior Problems Fixate a Reasoning Model on a Costly Method and Blind It to Simpler Ones
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the classic Einstellung (mental-set) effect from cognitive psychology, we hypothesize that after a reasoning model solves a run of problems that all require the same method, it rigidly reapplies that method to a subsequent problem that admits a far simpler solution—spending more tokens and often failing to find the shortcut—even though it solves the same problem correctly and cheaply in isolation. This method-fixation is not driven by the target problem's difficulty but by a method-commitment representation carried over from the preceding context, which can be located and causally steered to release the fixation.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here. (1) Cognitive psychology: the Einstellung / water-jar effect (Luchins 1942) and expertise-induced fixation (Bilalić et al.) show that a repeated successful method creates a mental set that blocks discovery of simpler solutions—a robust, authoritative human finding. (2) Efficient-reasoning and reuse work: external memory/retrieval methods (Retrieval-of-Thought, Buffer of Thoughts, MemShare, ENGRAM-R, Graph-Memoized, InftyThink-with-memory) REUSE prior reasoning to speed up new problems, and interpretability work shows in-context task/method reuse via shared circuits (Circuit Component Reuse 2023) and reasoning-length priors set pre-generation (On Reasoning Strength Planning 2025). Crucially, all reuse work treats reuse as BENEFICIAL and studies helpful transfer; none studies HARMFUL over-reuse—rigidity that inflates compute and blinds the model to shortcuts. My prior 'analogical_transfer_gate' proposal studied FAILURE to transfer a helpful analog; this is the opposite failure: pathological SUCCESS of transfer that fixates the model. My 'reasoning_length_contagion' proposal concerned length carry-over but not method rigidity or shortcut-blindness. We provide the first compute-centric and mechanistic study of an Einstellung-style effect in reasoning LLMs: we (a) characterize it as joint compute-inflation + shortcut-blindness on identical targets, (b) dissociate it from target difficulty, and (c) locate and causally steer a method-commitment representation that releases the set.
Abstract: Humans who repeatedly solve problems with one method develop a mental set that leads them to rigidly reapply it, missing simpler solutions -- the Einstellung effect. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit this rigidity, and study it as a compute phenomenon rather than only an accuracy one. We construct 'Einstellung sequences': a run of prime problems all solvable only by a costly method M, followed by a critical target that admits both M and a much simpler shortcut S, with a matched no-prime control presenting the same target in isolation. The exact delta over prior LLM work is a same-target isolated-vs-primed comparison of reasoning tokens plus a decodable, causally testable method-commitment signal. We hypothesize that primed models rigidly apply M to the target -- spending more tokens and more often failing to use S -- even though the target is identical, driven not by the target's difficulty but by a method-commitment signal carried over from the prime context. Across arithmetic word problems, algebra, and combinatorics on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure shortcut-usage rate, reasoning-token count, and accuracy on the critical target as a function of prime length, with a diverse-prime and length-matched-filler control isolating method-repetition from context length, and a mixed-effects decomposition dissociating priming from difficulty. Mechanistically, we probe whether the target's prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a method-commitment signal separable from difficulty, localize it, causally validate via activation patching (both directions), and steer to release the set. We also test a naturalistic multi-turn/agentic condition and report token/latency savings from the training-free fix. In agentic settings, recent problem history can silently make models reason worse and more expensively.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (sequence, condition) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match, both measured on the critical target only. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - method-repetition priming inflates target tokens and suppresses the shortcut): Tests whether a run of same-method prime problems makes the model reapply the costly method to a target that admits a simpler shortcut, costing more tokens and lowering shortcut use, versus the same target in isolation. Data: constructed from scratch - for each critical target we design a simple shortcut S (symmetry, closed-form, cancellation) and a costly-but-valid method M (brute-force enumeration, long derivation), plus prime problems solvable only by M and not by S. Domains: water-jar-style arithmetic, algebra, small combinatorics. We build 200 targets, each verified (LLM-judge + a 60-item human spot-check) to be solvable by both S and M in isolation while primes admit only M. Each target is run at prime lengths N in {0,1,3,5} (N=0 = no-prime control) plus a diverse-prime control (N=5 primes solved by varied methods) that isolates method-repetition from mere context length; 200 targets x 6 conditions is the cost driver. Shortcut usage is detected by step-template matching plus LLM-judge (human-validated agreement reported). Systems compared: primed (N=1,3,5) vs no-prime (N=0) vs diverse-prime, within target and model. Decisive metric: shortcut-usage rate on the target as a function of prime length, first; secondary within-target token increase and accuracy change. Convincing: shortcut-usage rate drops by >= 20 percentage points from N=0 to N=5 with a monotone dose-response, tokens rise >= 15%, while the diverse-prime control shows < 8 points of shortcut suppression (fixation needs method-repetition, not length), all under paired tests Holm-corrected across models. Indecision band: an 8-20 point shortcut drop, or the diverse-prime control itself suppressing 8-15 points, does not decide H1. Negative result: < 8 point shortcut drop, or the diverse-prime control matching the same-method prime, means no method-fixation and H1 is rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 dissociation - fixation is not driven by target difficulty or prompt length): Tests that the prime effect survives removal of target difficulty and raw prompt length, and that the extra tokens are rigid M-execution rather than needed reasoning. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces. Analysis 1 (dissociation): mixed-effects models of shortcut-usage, tokens, and accuracy with a random intercept per target identity (intrinsic difficulty) and fixed effects for prime length and raw prompt token count; supported by a length-matched irrelevant-filler prime that adds context length without a repeated method. Analysis 2 (wasted vs genuine): on a 100-target subsample use truncate-and-resume to estimate the S-minimal solve length and test whether priming inflates tokens beyond the S-minimal solve (rigid M) rather than adding needed reasoning. Systems compared: prime coefficient with vs without target random effect and prompt-length covariate; same-method prime vs length-matched filler. Decisive metric: standardized prime-length coefficient on shortcut-usage after controls, first; plus the share of primed extra tokens beyond the S-minimal solve. Convincing: the prime coefficient on shortcut-usage stays significant after controls, the length-matched filler shows no significant fixation, and >= 60% of primed extra tokens exceed the S-minimal solve. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or 30-60% excess-token share, is partial support. Negative result: the coefficient vanishing under controls, or the filler prime reproducing the effect, means fixation was a context-length artifact, refuting H2's dissociation.

Experiment 3 (H3 - a method-commitment representation exists at the target boundary and is separable from difficulty): Tests whether the target's prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a carried-over method-commitment signal that predicts shortcut-vs-method use and is distinct from a difficulty signal. Data: target prompt-boundary activations (last token before any target reasoning token) across prime lengths from Experiment 1, split 70/15/15 by target identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probes: a linear probe predicting whether the model will use S vs M on the target, a classifier for prime-method identity, and a target-difficulty probe (target = isolated pass-rate). Systems compared: for identical targets, does the S-vs-M probe prediction shift with prime length; principal angle between the method-commitment direction and the difficulty direction plus joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the S-vs-M probe and its shift with prime length on matched targets, first; plus the method-commitment/difficulty principal angle. Convincing: S-vs-M probe AUROC >= 0.7, its predicted shortcut-probability drops with prime length on matched targets (Spearman <= -0.3, p<0.01), and the method-commitment direction is not collinear with difficulty (angle >= 30 degrees), adding significant R2 over the difficulty probe. Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.7, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: AUROC < 0.6 or no prime-length shift, or collinearity with difficulty (angle < 20 degrees), means no separable method-commitment representation, refuting the location part of H3.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal - patching and steering release (or induce) the set): Tests whether editing the target-boundary representation recovers the shortcut and whether steering releases fixation. Data: 100 targets (subset of Experiment 1) each with matched N=5 primed and N=0 no-prime contexts; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention A (patching, both directions): patch the target-boundary state from the no-prime (S-inducing) context into the matched primed pass (expect shortcut recovery) and, reversed, patch the primed state into the no-prime pass (expect induced fixation), at the Experiment-3 layer. Intervention B (steering): derive a method-commitment direction (difference-of-means, primed minus no-prime) and steer primed targets to release fixation (dose swept over 4 magnitudes). Controls: matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm; off-target accuracy on M-only targets (where M is genuinely required) must be preserved; comparison to a prompt-based fix ('consider whether a simpler method applies'). Systems compared: real patch/steer vs random-direction control vs no intervention vs prompt-based fix. Decisive metric: recovery of shortcut-usage rate on primed targets (toward the no-prime level), first; secondary token reduction and accuracy gain on shortcut-favoring targets, with M-only off-target accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: patching/steering recovers >= 50% of the primed shortcut-usage deficit and cuts tokens accordingly, while the random control recovers < 15% and M-only accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose; reversed patching induces fixation. Indecision band: a 20-50% recovery, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% recovery, off-target damage on M-only targets, or the random control matching the real direction, means the representation is not causally responsible, refuting H3's causal claim.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 modulators and generalization): Tests where fixation is strongest and whether probe/steering transfer. Data: reuses Experiment 1 targets and derived vectors. Factors: prime-method salience (strongly vs weakly cued method), an explicit 'this is a fresh, unrelated problem' delimiter before the target (does it reset the set?), and cross-domain priming (prime in one domain, target in another). We additionally include a naturalistic multi-turn/agentic condition in which the primes arrive as prior chat turns rather than a curated block, testing whether fixation persists under realistic conversation history, and we report token-and-latency savings in concrete cost terms. Transfer: apply the 7B-derived probe and steering vector to 1.5B and 14B and across domains without refitting; compare RL-tuned vs distilled models for fixation strength. Systems compared: salient vs weak prime; fresh-delimiter vs none; within- vs cross-domain; in-model vs transferred vectors; RL-tuned vs distilled. Decisive metric: change in the shortcut-suppression magnitude across each factor, first; plus transferred-vector recovery relative to in-model. Convincing: salient primes fixate more than weak ones, an explicit fresh-problem delimiter significantly reduces fixation, and transferred steering retains >= 70% of its in-model shortcut-recovery. Indecision band: transferred recovery 40-70% of in-model, or factor effects within noise, is weak generalization. Negative result: no factor modulation and transferred recovery < 40% means fixation is idiosyncratic, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Constructing targets with a clean shortcut S and a genuinely-only-M prime set is nontrivial; we mitigate with templated generation plus human/LLM verification that primes exclude S and targets admit both, and treat ambiguous items separately. The effect could be confounded by context length rather than method-repetition; the diverse-prime control, length-matched filler prime, and mixed-effects analysis isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. Shortcut-usage detection (step-template + LLM-judge) is noisy; we validate with human spot-checks and report agreement. The method-commitment signal may be inseparable from a generic difficulty/uncertainty direction; the separability analysis, patching, and difficulty-probe comparison address this, and overlap with an in-context task-vector direction would itself be an interesting mechanistic finding. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included, and releasing the set could over-trigger on problems where M is genuinely required (specificity check on M-only targets). The effect may be small in strongly instruction-tuned models trained to treat each problem freshly (a valuable boundary condition) and may be model-family and scale specific. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

Name: language_detour_overthinking
Title: The Language Tax: Overthinking as a Pivot-Detour Overhead in Non-English Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: For the identical problem, reasoning models spend substantially more tokens when the question is posed in a low-resource / non-Latin-script language than in English. Our claim is NOT that this cross-language efficiency gap is newly discovered (language-mixing work already hints traces lengthen off-English); it is that the excess is largely a 'pivot detour' overhead rather than extra genuine reasoning. We define the detour operationally and pre-registrably: within a matched-accuracy stratum, detour tokens are those emitted AFTER the earliest trace prefix from which the correct answer is already recoverable by truncate-and-resume, and that co-occur with English/Han language-switch, re-translation, or restatement spans. The overhead is mechanistically driven by a language-specific representational component and can be causally reduced -- cutting tokens with no accuracy loss -- by ablating that component after the input-understanding phase.
Related Work: Multilingual reasoning work documents an accuracy gap favoring high-resource languages, attributes it to understanding failures, and mitigates it via translation/alignment for accuracy (Why Do Multilingual Reasoning Gaps Emerge 2025; SLAM 2025; Question Translation 2024; SoT 2025). Language-mixing work shows reasoning traces drift toward English/Han pivots, more so on harder/low-resource inputs, reflecting an English-centered latent pathway (Language Mixing in RLMs 2025; Large Reasoning Models Are (Not Yet) Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026); this already implies non-English traces run longer, so we do NOT claim the raw efficiency gap as our discovery. Disentanglement work ablates language-specific hidden components to IMPROVE ACCURACY (When Less Language is More 2025). Efficiency/overthinking work (Stop Overthinking survey 2025; When More is Less 2025; TRACE 2025) is entirely English-only and studies verbosity/verification, not language. Our precise, previously-untested contribution is threefold and stated as a delta to each line: (a) a CAUSAL DECOMPOSITION of the non-English token excess into genuine-reasoning vs pivot-detour overhead using truncate-and-resume plus token-language tagging (language-mixing work observes switching but never separates it from reasoning depth or ties it to a recoverable-answer point); (b) an operational, non-post-hoc criterion for the detour (tokens after the effective-solve step co-located with switch/restatement spans); and (c) turning the accuracy-oriented disentanglement direction into a mid-generation EFFICIENCY intervention that REDUCES TOKENS at fixed accuracy (prior ablation targets accuracy, never token cost). The novelty is thus jointly in the mechanism (an isolable language-specific component) and the intervention (token-reducing ablation), not in the multilingual setting per se.
Abstract: Reasoning language models 'overthink,' but studies of this waste are almost entirely English-only, while multilingual studies focus on accuracy gaps, not compute. Language-mixing work already suggests non-English traces run longer; we do not re-claim that observation but ask what the excess IS. We hypothesize a language tax: non-English prompts incur a pivot-detour overhead in which the model spends tokens routing the input into an English-centered latent reasoning space (re-translation, restatement, language-mixing) rather than doing extra genuine reasoning. We define the detour operationally -- tokens emitted after the earliest prefix from which the correct answer is recoverable (truncate-and-resume) that co-occur with language-switch/restatement spans -- so the claim is falsifiable without post-hoc trace reading. Using matched multilingual math and science benchmarks (parallel-by-construction MGSM plus translated MATH500/GPQA across high/low-resource and Latin/non-Latin scripts) on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure per-language token counts on identical problems within matched-accuracy strata, controlling for tokenizer fertility via character/word normalization and reporting per-language and per-script separately. We then decompose the excess into genuine-reasoning vs detour tokens, locate a language-specific component via probing and difference-of-means, and causally test whether ablating it mid-generation collapses the detour, cutting tokens at fixed accuracy against forced-English and translate-first baselines. We translate token savings into latency, API-dollar, and energy terms. The upshot is an equity issue with an actionable fix: non-English users pay more compute for identical answer quality, and teams can gate an interpretable ablation instead of shipping heavier multilingual budgets.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Cross-language efficiency gap at matched accuracy): Tests whether, on identical problems, models emit more reasoning tokens in non-English than in English. Data: MGSM (250 grade-school math problems, professionally translated into 11 languages, parallel by construction; use all 250 in English, French, German, Chinese, Bengali, Swahili, Telugu — 7 of 11, chosen to span high-resource Latin, high-resource non-Latin, and low-resource non-Latin) plus a 200-problem stratified subset of MATH500 (500 exist) and all 198 GPQA-Diamond problems, both translated with NLLB-200-3.3B and human-verified on a 100-problem subset per language to catch gross mistranslation. Models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, all frozen (inference only); temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 generated tokens, 3 seeds. Systems compared: the same model on the English vs each non-English rendering of the same problem. Decisive metric: median reasoning-token count per language as a ratio to English, computed within equal-accuracy strata (only problems solved in both languages, so the gap is not an accuracy artifact). Secondary: tokens per source character and per source word, to net out tokenizer fertility. Convincing result: median token ratio >= 1.25 for the three low-resource non-Latin languages, holding within matched-accuracy strata and after character-normalization. Indecision band: a token ratio in [0.95, 1.10] on the matched stratum means no meaningful gap and H1 is unsupported for that language; a ratio in (1.10, 1.25) is weakly suggestive and treated as inconclusive pending Experiment 2. Negative result (ratios <= 1.10, or the gap vanishing after character-normalization) would mean any raw token difference is tokenizer fertility rather than a language tax, undercutting the hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — The excess is pivot-detour overhead, not deeper genuine reasoning): Tests whether the cross-language token excess sits after the point where the answer is already computable, while genuine reasoning depth is language-invariant. Data: the MGSM 250 and MATH 200 problems from Experiment 1, restricted to problems the model solves in both English and the target language (to define a clean effective-solve step); expect ~150-200 usable MGSM problems per low-resource language given accuracy loss. Models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B as primary, 1.5B and 14B for robustness, frozen. Method: (a) truncate-and-resume — at each decile of a trace, force '</think> The answer is' and greedily decode; the effective-solve step is the earliest decile whose forced answer is correct and stays correct thereafter, with genuine-reasoning tokens = tokens up to that step and overhead tokens = the remainder; (b) token-language tagging via fastText lid.176 plus Unicode-script heuristics, counting language-switch spans and restatement/re-translation spans. Decisive metric: the fraction of the English-vs-target token gap attributable to overhead tokens. Secondary: effective-solve step in normalized reasoning units (script-independent) compared across languages, and language-switch count per trace vs resource level. Convincing result: >= 70% of the token gap sits in overhead tokens, normalized effective-solve step differs by < 10% across languages, and switch counts rise monotonically as resource level falls. Indecision band: an overhead share of the gap in [50%, 70%) is partial support — the detour explains some but not most of the tax, reported as such and not as confirmation; below 50% means the excess is genuine extra reasoning and H2 fails. Negative result (overhead share < 50%, or the effective-solve step itself growing in non-English) would mean non-English prompts trigger genuinely longer reasoning, refuting the 'detour' framing while still documenting the gap.

Experiment 3 (H3 — A language-specific representational component drives the detour): Tests both an internal signature and the existence of an isolable component. Data: 2000 prompt/step residual states sampled from the MGSM+MATH traces (balanced English/non-English, high/low resource) for fitting, and a held-out 500 for evaluation. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; nothing is trained except a linear probe and a difference-of-means direction that we read off the residual stream. Part A (signature): logit-lens on intermediate-layer residuals during non-English generation, measuring the layer/step at which the internally predicted answer-token language switches to English/Han, and whether the overhead tokens from Experiment 2 coincide with that switch. Part B (location): a logistic linear probe and a difference-of-means vector for the English-vs-non-English direction at each of layers 8-20, choosing the layer that maximizes probe AUC. Decisive metric: language-probe AUC, and — after projecting the direction out — the drop in surface-language AUC against the retained accuracy of a separate latent-answer probe (reasoning content intact). Convincing result: language-probe AUC >= 0.85 at some middle layer; projecting the direction out drops surface-language AUC below 0.65 while the latent-answer probe stays within 3 points of baseline; and the logit-lens switch precedes >= 60% of overhead tokens. Indecision band: language-probe AUC in [0.70, 0.85) means the component is only partially linearly isolable — proceed to Experiment 4 but flag a reduced expected effect; AUC < 0.70 means no clean component and H3 fails. Negative result (no isolable direction, or projecting it out also destroying the latent answer) would mean the detour is entangled with reasoning and cannot be cleanly targeted, predicting that Experiment 4 trades accuracy for tokens.

Experiment 4 (H4 — Ablating the component reduces tokens at fixed accuracy): Tests the causal efficiency claim. Data: held-out MGSM 250 and GPQA 198 per language, never used to fit the direction. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) and 14B (transfer), frozen; the only intervention is projecting out the Experiment-3 direction from the residual stream at the selected middle layers, applied only after the input-understanding phase (the first 10% of tokens left untouched); 3 seeds. Systems compared: (i) no intervention, (ii) our language-component ablation, (iii) forced-English-reasoning via system-prompt / decoding constraint, (iv) translate-to-English-first then reason, (v) a matched random-direction ablation of equal norm (control). Decisive metric: tokens-at-fixed-accuracy — the change in median reasoning tokens per language subject to accuracy not dropping beyond the noise band. Secondary: detour-token fraction (Experiment 2 method), language-mixing count, wall-clock latency, accuracy. Convincing result: our ablation cuts median tokens by >= 15% on the low-resource non-Latin languages with accuracy change within +/- 1.0 point, beating the random-direction control (expected < 5% token change or accuracy damage) and matching or beating forced-English / translate-first without their input-fidelity costs. Indecision band: an accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.0] points is the zone where savings are ambiguous — a token cut there is reported as an accuracy-cost trade, not a free reduction; an accuracy drop > 3.0 points counts as failure of the 'no accuracy loss' claim even if tokens fall; a token reduction in [5%, 15%) is a weak positive. Negative result (no token reduction beyond the random control, or reduction only with accuracy loss > 3 points) would refute the causal efficiency claim and, read with Experiment 3, tell us whether the failure is no-effect or entanglement.

Experiment 5 (H4 — Specificity and transfer): Tests that the intervention does not harm cases where understanding, not detour, is the bottleneck, and that one shared low-resource direction transfers. Data: the hardest-difficulty stratum (bottom accuracy tercile) of GPQA and MATH per language. Models: 7B and 14B, frozen. Systems: ablation vs no-intervention on the hardest strata; and a single shared low-resource direction (averaged across the three low-resource languages) applied per language vs the per-language directions. Decisive metric: hardest-strata accuracy under ablation (must not drop) and the token reduction retained under the shared direction. Convincing result: hardest-strata accuracy within +/- 1.0 point of no-intervention (no induced underthinking) and the shared direction retaining >= two-thirds of the per-language token savings. Indecision band: a hardest-strata accuracy drop in (1.0, 3.0] points flags that the intervention should be gated to mid-difficulty items; > 3.0 points means the component is functionally necessary on hard low-resource inputs and the ablation must be scoped away from them. Negative result would bound the intervention's applicability rather than refute the core hypothesis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Translated benchmarks may introduce artifacts or altered difficulty; we mitigate with human-verified translations for a subset and report results on the parallel-by-construction MGSM separately. Tokenizer fertility confounds raw token counts; we control via character/word-normalized effort and matched-accuracy comparisons, but residual confounding is possible. The genuine-vs-detour split relies on truncate-and-resume, which is noisy and compute-heavy; we subsample steps and use two overhead definitions (resume-based and language-tag-based) for robustness. The pivot-detour hypothesis may be wrong—extra tokens could reflect genuinely harder understanding rather than a routing overhead, which would be an informative negative result and still a novel efficiency-gap characterization. Language-specific ablation could damage understanding on low-resource inputs (underthinking), especially where the detour is functionally necessary; the specificity and hardest-strata analyses guard against this and may reveal the intervention only helps mid-difficulty items. Effects may be model-family and script specific, and low-resource-language coverage in open models is limited. Practical framing note: because the intervention only changes compute, not answer quality, the headline consequence if it holds is a fairness one -- equal accuracy at unequal cost across languages -- and if it fails (excess is genuine reasoning) the same measurements still yield a novel, equity-relevant efficiency-gap characterization telling deployers that non-English budgets must genuinely be larger.

Name: commitment_stop_gap
Title: The Commitment-Stop Gap: Overthinking as a Decoupling Between Answer-Knowing and Stop-Deciding Circuits
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning LLMs overthink not because they lack the answer, but because an internal 'answer-commitment' signal stabilizes long before a separate 'stop-decision' circuit fires. Overthinking is largely the temporal gap between these two internal events. The falsifiable core prediction is that these two events are causally dissociable: ablating the heads that drive the termination token shifts when the model stops without changing when the answer-commitment probe stabilizes, and this dissociation survives controls for confidence/entropy, answer-token repetition, and termination-token rank. The gap is a new, cheaply readable diagnostic of reasoning dynamics, and it can additionally be closed with a lightweight commitment monitor.
Related Work: Prior efficient-reasoning interpretability work either (a) finds a single linear 'verbosity/length' direction and steers along it (ASC, Efficiency Steering, Manifold Steering, ThinkEdit), (b) characterizes overthinking behaviorally via triggers such as self-doubt, internal bias, or first-impression conflict, or (c) detects completion reactively by monitoring termination-token rank dynamics (RCPD) or by tracking when a single latent-answer probe converges (answer-convergence / Chain-of-Probe). All of these treat 'answer-knowing' and 'when-to-stop' as one conflated event, read from one signal. Our delta is a NEW observable: the commitment-stop gap, the signed token distance between the step at which the answer-commitment readout stabilizes and the step at which the stop-decision circuit emits the termination token. Answer-convergence measures only the first of these; RCPD measures only the second and reactively. Neither can express, let alone test, the gap. The two-circuit story is not a relabeling of existing termination-circuit findings: prior termination work localizes what fires the stop token, whereas we make and test the dissociation claim that the stop circuit can be perturbed independently of the answer-commitment readout. Our primary contribution is thus a diagnostic and a causal decomposition; the early-exit monitor is a downstream application of the diagnostic, not a new mechanism in itself.
Abstract: Large reasoning models routinely 'overthink,' expending tokens long after they could correctly answer. Existing interpretability work explains this via a single verbosity direction, a single answer-convergence probe, or reactive termination signals, implicitly treating knowing the answer and deciding to stop as one process. We instead separate two distinct internal events: an answer-commitment signal, when the model's latent predicted final answer stabilizes across reasoning steps, and a stop-decision, when a control circuit finally emits the termination token. We define the commitment-stop gap as the token distance between these events and argue overthinking is largely this gap. Our primary contribution is this gap as a new diagnostic of reasoning dynamics; a training-free early-exit monitor is a secondary application. Using linear probes and logit-lens readout on the residual stream, we measure per-step answer commitment on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA across DeepSeek-R1 distills and Qwen3. We show commitment stabilizes far before termination for overthought instances, that the gap predicts wasted tokens better than length or a verbosity direction, and that the effect survives controls for confidence, entropy, answer repetition, and termination-token rank. We then localize the stop-decision circuit via head-level attribution and activation patching, showing that ablating stop heads shifts stop timing while leaving the commitment readout intact, evidencing genuine dissociation. Finally the commitment monitor early-exits once the probed answer is stable and reduces tokens with minimal accuracy loss. We report savings as token, latency, and cost reductions to map directly onto deployment.
Experiments:
All experiments use open reasoning models on a single 8xA100-80GB (or smaller) node, well within an academic budget. Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (transformer decoder, all weights frozen; only lightweight linear probes are trainable). Scale sweep uses the 1.5B/7B/14B/32B R1-Qwen distills and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, 3 seeds (0,1,2) for every reported number. Reasoning traces are segmented into steps by newline/step delimiters. Datasets (used as released): GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). A trace is 'correctly solved' if the extracted final answer matches gold; probing and gap analysis are run on correctly solved traces only, so the question is when the answer was known, not whether. Leakage control: the linear probe predicts the eventual final answer from the residual stream at the CURRENT step position only, never from positions at or after the answer is written; we strip explicit answer tokens and answer-formatting tokens from the probe's receptive field, and we verify the probe's step-t prediction cannot be trivially recovered from the raw decoded text at step t (bag-of-words control). Probe train/eval split is by problem (40% train / 60% eval), pre-registered before any monitor tuning.

Experiment 1 (H1 - Commitment precedes stopping): For each step read the model's current implicit final answer two ways: (a) logit-lens projection of the last-token residual, (b) a trained linear probe (ridge logistic on layer-L residual). The 'commitment step' is the first step after which the decoded answer equals the eventual final answer and stays unchanged to termination. Compare commitment-step vs. termination-step distributions per dataset. Decisive metric: fraction of correctly solved traces whose commitment step is at least 15% of the trace earlier than the termination step. Convincing: this fraction exceeds 0.60 on MATH500 and GSM8K with mean separation > 20% of trace length. Indecision band: fraction in [0.45, 0.60] or mean separation in [10%, 20%] - reported as weak/dataset-dependent. Negative (fraction < 0.45): commitment does not generally precede stopping, and the core premise fails.

Experiment 2 (H2 - The gap IS the overthinking): 'Wasted tokens' is defined by truncate-and-resume: truncate at each step, force </think>, take the last step after which forced-exit accuracy stops changing; wasted tokens = tokens after that step. Compare predictors of wasted tokens via out-of-sample 5-fold R^2: (i) commitment-stop gap, (ii) total tokens, (iii) projection onto a reproduced ASC verbosity direction, (iv) Failed-Step Fraction. Decisive metric: gap R^2 minus best competitor R^2. Convincing: gap advantage >= 0.10 on at least three of four datasets. Indecision: advantage in [0.02, 0.10]. Negative (<= 0.02 or below a competitor): overthinking is not primarily this gap.

Experiment 3 (H2/H3 - Causal check that commitment is real): Truncate at the probed commitment step, force </think>, measure accuracy retention vs. truncating at matched random earlier and later steps. Decisive metric: accuracy at commitment-step truncation minus accuracy at same-budget random-step truncation. Convincing: commitment-step truncation stays within 2 points of full-generation accuracy while random earlier truncation loses > 8 points at equal budget. Indecision: retention gap vs. full generation in [2, 5] points. Negative (> 5 points): the probed commitment step is not where the answer is actually decided.

Experiment 4 (H4 - Localizing and dissociating the stop-decision circuit): For correctly solved traces, patch clean-run activations into a run where </think> is delayed, ranking heads by effect on termination-token logit; ablate top-k heads (k in {1,4,16}) and measure shift in termination timing. Decoupling test: measure Experiment-1 probe accuracy on the same traces with stop heads ablated. Decisive metric: change in mean termination step under top-head ablation vs. random-head ablation of equal count. Convincing: top-head ablation shifts mean termination by >= 15% of trace length (vs. < 3% random) while probe answer-decoding accuracy drops by < 5 points - the falsifiable dissociation. Indecision: termination shift in [5%, 15%] or probe drop in [5, 10] points. Negative (shift < 5% or probe collapses with stop heads): the stop decision is not localized, or is inseparable from answer computation, refuting H4.

Experiment 5 (Controls against trivial correlates): Test that the commitment-stop gap is not a relabeling of confidence, entropy, repetition, or termination-token rank. Re-run Experiment 2's regression with each of these added as a covariate: per-step logit margin, per-step next-token entropy, answer-token n-gram repetition rate, and RCPD termination-token rank. Decisive metric: incremental out-of-sample R^2 of the commitment-stop gap AFTER partialling out all four correlates. Convincing: the gap retains >= 0.05 incremental R^2 over the correlates-only model on at least three datasets, and the Experiment-4 dissociation persists when stop-head ablation is compared against ablating heads matched on their confidence/entropy attribution. Indecision: incremental R^2 in [0.01, 0.05]. Negative (< 0.01): the gap is explained by trivial correlates, collapsing the novelty.

Experiment 6 (H5 - Training-free commitment monitor): Force </think> once the probe-predicted answer is stable and probe confidence exceeds tau for k consecutive steps. tau and k are selected on the Experiment-1 training split only (grid tau in {0.7,0.8,0.9}, k in {2,3,5}); the 60% eval split is used for reporting. Report the full accuracy-vs-token Pareto curve, not a single point. Systems compared on all four datasets: monitor vs. (a) full generation, (b) fixed-fraction truncation matched to the monitor's mean budget, (c) verbosity steering (ASC), (d) RCPD reactive exit, (e) budget forcing. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy (percent reduction while accuracy stays within 1 point). Secondary: mean tokens, accuracy, wall-clock latency, and estimated serving-cost reduction (tokens x per-token cost) to map to deployment. Convincing: >= 30% token reduction within 1 point on GSM8K and MATH500 and best on the frontier. Indecision: reduction in [15%, 30%] or a tie with the strongest baseline - the monitor works but is not clearly better, and the primary contribution then rests on the diagnostic (Experiments 1-5). Negative (< 15% or > 1 point loss): the commitment signal does not yield a usable mechanism.

Experiment 7 (Ablations - decoding, prompt, scale, difficulty): Vary decoding temperature (0.0, 0.6, 1.0), prompt style (default vs. concise-instruction vs. few-shot), model scale (1.5B/7B/14B/32B/Qwen3-8B), and dataset difficulty (per-item pass-rate quartiles) and report how the commitment-stop gap, its wasted-token predictivity, and the Experiment-4 dissociation vary. Also test cross-dataset and cross-scale probe transfer. Decisive metric: transferred-probe answer-decoding accuracy relative to in-domain, and stability of the gap effect across temperatures/prompts. Convincing: transferred probe retains >= 80% of in-domain accuracy across at least three scales, the gap effect (Experiment 1 fraction) stays above the indecision band across temperatures and prompt styles, and monitor savings hold within 10 relative percent under transfer. Indecision: transfer retention in [60%, 80%] - the signal is partly model-specific and we scope to per-model probes. Negative (< 60% retention, or the gap effect vanishes under a common decoding/prompt setting): commitment is idiosyncratic, contradicting the shared-readout claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The linear probe for latent answer commitment may be unreliable for open-ended or multi-token answers, limiting us to tasks with extractable final answers (math/multiple-choice). Commitment and stop-decision may not be cleanly separable; if patching shows shared heads or the dissociation fails under confidence/entropy-matched controls (Experiment 5), the decoupling framing weakens - itself an informative negative. The gap could be confounded by difficulty, so probe confidence may correlate with hardness and risk premature exit on hard problems (underthinking); the k-step stability and threshold, plus the difficulty-stratified ablation, aim to control this. Steering/early-exit gains may not exceed strong baselines; because the primary contribution is the diagnostic decomposition, the result remains valuable even then - the communities that would adopt it are interpretability researchers studying reasoning dynamics and evaluation designers who could use the gap as a monitoring signal for whether a deployed model is committing early yet stopping late, independent of any controller. Results may be model-family specific.

Name: stale_uncertainty_gate
Title: Stale Uncertainty: Overthinking as a Failure to Update the Internal Confidence Signal That Gates Reflection
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models keep reflecting not because they are still genuinely uncertain, but because the internal uncertainty signal that gates continued reasoning is stale: it lags the model's actual, freshly-computable confidence. Our sharp, preregisterable, directional prediction is that a probe reading uncertainty just before reflection-onset tokens (gating-uncertainty) systematically exceeds a same-architecture probe reading uncertainty from the freshest completed-step state (evidence-uncertainty) during overthinking, that the signed lag between them predicts wasted tokens beyond absolute uncertainty and trace length under matched correctness, and that patching the stale gating representation with the fresh one at reflection-onset suppresses the redundant reflection. This is a temporal-update-failure claim, not another calibration or early-exit result.
Related Work: A wave of 2025 work links reflection to uncertainty: ReflCtrl and SEAL steer reflection/transition thoughts with a latent direction; 'Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence' and 'Trace Length is a Simple Uncertainty Signal' correlate calibration and length with an internal confidence state and identify high-entropy 'forking' tokens; 'Calibrating Reasoning with Internal Consistency' and the Verbal Uncertainty Feature (VUF) find linear uncertainty directions. Crucially, ALL of these treat the gating uncertainty as an accurate reflection of the model's current knowledge and either steer it down bluntly or use it to early-exit; none asks whether that signal is temporally out of date. Our delta is a lag/update-failure account: we distinguish two same-architecture, matched-layer readouts - gating-uncertainty (upstream of reflection-onset tokens) and evidence-uncertainty (over the freshest reasoning state) - test whether they diverge in a specific temporal direction, show the divergence predicts wasted tokens, and design an 'uncertainty refresh' that overwrites the stale gating representation with the fresh one. Prior steering methods cannot reproduce this because they push a single uncertainty direction toward a fixed pole rather than replacing a lagged state with the model's own current estimate; calibration/early-exit methods act on the level of uncertainty, not its staleness.
Abstract: Reasoning LLMs often continue to reflect and verify long after they have effectively solved a problem, wasting tokens, latency, and compute in deployed systems that pay per token - for example long-form math and agentic search, where redundant verification loops dominate cost. Prior interpretability work ties this to an internal uncertainty signal but implicitly assumes that signal accurately tracks current confidence and simply remains high. We propose a different mechanism: the uncertainty signal that gates continued reflection is stale, lagging the confidence the model could compute from its most recent reasoning, so it keeps triggering verification against an out-of-date sense of doubt. We formalize two residual-stream-decodable quantities read with identical probe architectures at matched layers: gating-uncertainty, at the token immediately before a reflection-onset, and evidence-uncertainty, at the end of the most recent completed step.
