Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on DeepSeek-R1 distills (1.5B-14B) and Qwen3, we test whether gating-uncertainty systematically lags evidence-uncertainty during overthinking via cross-correlation and the identified forking tokens, and whether the lag predicts wasted tokens better than absolute uncertainty or length. We preempt the main alternative - reflection as deliberate exploration - by contrasting tasks where further reflection helps versus does not. We localize where the gating signal is read via activation patching, and introduce a training-free 'uncertainty refresh' that patches the stale gating representation with the fresh evidence representation at reflection-onset. We report token, latency, and per-query cost savings against ReflCtrl/SEAL steering and length/consistency early-exit, with a minimal-viable fallback of the lag diagnostic alone.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear uncertainty probes are trainable. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into steps; reflection-onset tokens marked by lexical cues (wait / let me check / but) plus a reflection-direction classifier reproduced from ReflCtrl. Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). Signal definitions (pre-registered): gating-uncertainty is read from the residual at the exact token position immediately preceding a reflection-onset token; evidence-uncertainty from the residual at the last token of the most recent completed step; BOTH use the identical probe architecture and the SAME layer, to remove read-position/architecture confounds.

Experiment 1 (H1 - Two separable uncertainty readouts): Train two identical-architecture linear probes to predict eventual answer correctness from the residual stream at the two positions. Split 40/60 by problem. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of each probe for eventual correctness; separability via correlation between the two probe outputs at matched positions. Convincing: both AUROC >= 0.70 and output correlation r < 0.8. Indecision: either AUROC in [0.6, 0.7] or correlation in [0.8, 0.9]. Negative (AUROC < 0.6 or correlation > 0.9): the readouts are not separable/useful, undercutting the framing.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Gating lags evidence, with read-position controls): For each reflection episode compare gating- to evidence-uncertainty and estimate the lag as the offset k for which evidence-uncertainty at step t-k best matches gating-uncertainty at step t (cross-correlation). Controls: a matched-layer control (both probes at several layers), and a shuffled-time baseline (randomly permuting step order) that should destroy any true lag. Decisive metric: mean signed difference (gating minus evidence) at onsets during overthought traces and the modal best-fit lag k, with the shuffled-time baseline as the null. Convincing: gating exceeds evidence at onsets (paired p < 0.01, d > 0.5) with modal lag k >= 1 step, higher onset firing in high-lag windows, and no such effect under shuffled-time. Indecision: 0.2 < d < 0.5, or k = 0 with a small positive difference. Negative (d < 0.2, gating <= evidence, or effect survives shuffling): no directional staleness, refuting H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Lag predicts wasted tokens): 'Wasted tokens' = tokens after the last accuracy-changing step (truncate-and-resume). Compare out-of-sample 5-fold R^2 of predictors: (i) per-trace mean lag, (ii) absolute gating-uncertainty, (iii) trace length, (iv) internal-consistency score. Under matched correctness. Decisive metric: lag R^2 minus best competitor R^2. Convincing: lag beats the best competitor by >= 0.10 on at least three datasets. Indecision: advantage in [0.02, 0.10]. Negative (<= 0.02): the lag does not specifically explain waste.

Experiment 4 (Exploration alternative - direct test): Preempt the deliberate-exploration interpretation. Partition items into those where additional reflection empirically raises accuracy (reflection-helps) vs. does not (reflection-wasteful), using truncate-and-resume. Test whether the lag still predicts wasted tokens specifically on reflection-wasteful items while being smaller on reflection-helps items. Decisive metric: difference in mean lag between reflection-wasteful and reflection-helps items, and lag's wasted-token R^2 within each partition. Convincing: lag is significantly larger on reflection-wasteful items and predicts waste there but not on reflection-helps items - consistent with staleness, not useful exploration. Indecision: a weak but directionally-correct separation. Negative (lag equal across partitions): the signal reflects generic reflection, not stale gating, weakening the mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H2 - Localizing where the gating signal is read): Activation patching to find layers/heads where gating-uncertainty feeds the reflection-onset decision; ablate and measure change in reflection frequency and lag. Decisive metric: change in reflection-onset rate under top-component vs. equal-count random ablation. Convincing: top-component ablation changes reflection rate by >= 10 points (vs. < 3 random) with accuracy within 3 points. Indecision: [3, 10] points. Negative (< 3 points or accuracy collapse): not localized/intervenable.

Experiment 6 (H3 - Uncertainty-refresh breaks the loop): At reflection-onset, patch the residual components carrying gating-uncertainty with the fresh evidence-uncertainty representation, then continue. Report the full accuracy-vs-token Pareto curve. Systems compared on all four datasets: refresh vs. (a) no intervention, (b) fixed truncation matched to refresh budget, (c) ReflCtrl/SEAL steering, (d) trace-length early-exit, (e) internal-consistency early-exit. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy. Secondary: reflection-count reduction, mean tokens, wall-clock latency, per-query cost. Convincing: >= 20% token reduction within 1 point on GSM8K and MATH500 with reflection count cut >= 40%, on or above every baseline frontier. Indecision: reduction in [10%, 20%] or a frontier-tie - the lag diagnosis (Experiments 1-5) is then the standalone contribution (the minimal viable result). Negative (< 10% or > 1 point loss): refresh does not yield usable savings.

Experiment 7 (H3 - Preserving genuine reflection): On the hardest quartile and on corrective-reflection cases, gate refresh by an evidence-uncertainty threshold and measure accuracy. Decisive metric: accuracy change on hard/corrective items with vs. without refresh at the deployed threshold. Convincing: drop < 1 point while easy-item savings hold. Indecision: 1-3 point drop. Negative (> 3 point drop): refresh harms genuine reflection, bounding H3.

Experiment 8 (Probe-noise, calibration, and generality): Report each probe's calibration and inter-run stability (seed variance), and transfer both probes and the refresh trigger across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain, and refresh token-savings retention. Convincing: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales and savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision: retention in [60%, 80%]. Negative (< 60% retention): the lag signal is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The distinction between gating and evidence uncertainty relies on read-position choices; we remove the confound with matched-layer, identical-architecture probes and a shuffled-time null, but if the two probes are not separable the lag framing weakens (an informative negative). Confidence probes are noisy for open-ended answers, so we focus on math/multiple-choice with extractable answers. The stale-uncertainty hypothesis may be wrong - reflection could be deliberate exploration - which Experiment 4 tests directly; a null there still yields a publishable characterization. The refresh patch alters internal state and may introduce overconfidence and underthinking on hard items; the evidence-uncertainty threshold guards against this. Intervention gains may not exceed strong steering baselines; because the lag diagnostic is the primary deliverable and its adopters are reasoning-model builders serving at scale (not only interpretability researchers), the result remains valuable, with the diagnostic alone as the minimal-viable outcome. Results may be model-family specific and vary non-monotonically with scale.

Name: recompute_loop_forgetting
Title: Recompute Loops: Overthinking as Retrieval Failure of the Model's Own Scratchpad
Short Hypothesis: A meaningful fraction of wasted reasoning tokens are spent re-deriving intermediate results the model already computed earlier in the same chain-of-thought. We define a 'recompute loop' operationally as a value-producing statement whose result is semantically equivalent to one already established earlier in the trace AND that re-derives rather than merely references it, excluding legitimate self-verification (re-derivation that changes or checks the earlier value) and paraphrased restatement (no new derivation). We hypothesize recompute loops arise because the model fails to retrieve its own prior conclusion from context - a working-memory/retrieval failure - detectable at the recomputation onset via degraded attention to the earlier result, and causally suppressible by injecting that result's representation. The primary contribution is the mechanistic characterization (recompute loops as retrieval failure); the onset-triggered memory-injection intervention is a secondary application.
Related Work: Existing efficiency work treats redundancy as scattered attention or verbosity: Think Clearly (2025) prunes low-attention tokens reactively; TTS (2025) labels steps decorative vs. load-bearing post-hoc; NLDD (2026) shows a reasoning horizon; When More is Less (2025) targets a global optimal length. Retrieval/reuse methods operate ACROSS problems or via external memory: Reuse-Don't-Recompute and Memory-of-Thought cache and re-inject solutions from PRIOR problems; Thought-Retriever retrieves from an external store. Working-memory interpretability (LLMs Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory, 2025; Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity, 2024; Strong Memory Weak Control, 2025) documents self-contradiction and drift but proposes no efficiency mechanism. The one-line deltas: Think Clearly/TTS remove tokens by attention/importance regardless of why they are redundant; Reuse-Don't-Recompute/Memory-of-Thought/Thought-Retriever reuse content across problems via external memory; we instead identify a specific WITHIN-TRACE redundancy - recomputation of an already-derived intermediate - and attribute it to a retrieval failure of the model's own scratchpad, intervening at onset with an internal memory injection. We narrow our novelty claim accordingly: not the first to identify redundancy, but the first to characterize within-trace recomputation as a retrieval-failure phenomenon and to intervene at its onset.
Abstract: Reasoning models 'overthink,' but the structure of the wasted computation is poorly understood. We identify a concrete pattern we call recompute loops: within a single chain of thought, the model re-derives an intermediate quantity (an equation, a partial sum, a constraint, a candidate answer) it already established earlier in the same trace, without checking or changing it. We hypothesize recompute loops are a symptom of the model failing to retrieve its own prior conclusion from context - a working-memory/retrieval failure - rather than generic verbosity, and we treat the mechanistic characterization as the primary contribution. First, we build an automatic detector for recomputed results by matching semantically-equivalent value-producing statements across a trace, with explicit exclusion rules for self-verification and paraphrase, and quantify their token cost across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on DeepSeek-R1 distills (1.5B-14B) and Qwen3. Second, we test the retrieval-failure hypothesis with a causal chain: at recomputation onset we measure attention back to the original derivation, probe whether the earlier result is still linearly recoverable, patch in that result's representation, and ablate the intervention timing. Third, we turn the diagnosis into a training-free onset-triggered memory injection that reminds the model of the already-derived result so it continues instead of re-deriving. We evaluate token savings at equal accuracy against reactive pruning, verbosity steering, and length-aware baselines, report the savings as tokens, wall-clock latency, and serving cost, and separate the user-facing benefit (faster, cheaper answers) from the research benefit (a named, quantifiable waste category linked to working-memory limits). We analyze failure cases where recomputation is corrective.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only a cheap onset probe is trainable. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into steps by newline/step delimiters. Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). Operational labels (pre-registered): a value-producing statement is a RECOMPUTE if its computed value is semantically equivalent to an earlier statement's value AND it re-executes the derivation; it is EXCLUDED if it verifies/changes the earlier value (self-correction) or merely restates it without derivation (paraphrase). Positive example: earlier 'so x=12', later '3*4=12' re-derived in a fresh sub-derivation. Negative examples: 'let me double-check: 3*4=12, yes' (verification), 'recall x=12' (paraphrase). Annotation guidelines and these rules are fixed before scoring.

Experiment 1 (H1 - Recompute loops exist and are costly): Detector parses value-producing statements and flags recomputes via an LLM-judge under the operational rules. Detector validity: two annotators label a 300-statement sample against the guidelines; report precision/recall and inter-annotator agreement (kappa). Decisive metric: fraction of thinking tokens attributable to recompute loops per dataset. Convincing: recompute loops account for >= 15% of thinking tokens on average at detector precision >= 0.8 and annotator kappa > 0.6. Indecision: token fraction in [7%, 15%] or precision in [0.65, 0.8]. Negative (< 7% of tokens or precision < 0.65): not a material or reliably measurable source of waste.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Distinct from generic waste, verification, and paraphrase): Show recompute loops are a distinct category. Correlate recompute-token fraction with total tokens and with 'wasted tokens' (tokens after the last accuracy-changing step, truncate-and-resume); compute overlap with TTS decorative labels; and report the share of flagged events that survive the verification/paraphrase exclusion rules. Decisive metric: share of recompute tokens on steps labeled load-bearing (non-decorative). Convincing: > 40% of recompute tokens sit on non-decorative steps AND < 15% of initially-flagged events are reclassified as verification/paraphrase under audit. Indecision: 25-40% non-decorative. Negative (< 25% non-decorative): largely a subset of decorative waste.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Retrieval-failure signature): At each recompute onset measure attention mass to the tokens of the original derivation vs. matched control positions where the same result is referenced/reused without recomputation. Decisive metric: paired difference in attention-to-original (recompute onsets vs. reuse controls). Convincing: recompute onsets show significantly lower attention (p < 0.01, Cohen's d > 0.5), localized to few heads. Indecision: 0.2 < d < 0.5. Negative (d < 0.2): no degraded self-attention, refuting the retrieval-failure mechanism (an informative negative).

Experiment 4 (H2 - Causal chain: probe, patch, timing): Strengthen the causal argument in three linked tests. (a) Probing: at onset, test whether the earlier result is still linearly recoverable from the residual (recoverability should be degraded vs. reuse controls). (b) Patching: patch in the residual-stream representation of the original result and measure the drop in probability of continuing the recomputation, vs. a norm-matched random patch. (c) Timing ablation: apply the patch at onset, one step before, and one step after, to show the effect is specific to onset. Decisive metric: recompute-continuation probability drop under true patch vs. random patch, and its dependence on timing. Convincing: true-result patch reduces recompute-continuation by >= 20 points (vs. < 5 random), maximized at onset. Indecision: reduction in [8, 20] points. Negative (< 8 points): injecting the earlier result does not causally suppress recomputation.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Memory injection: savings, cost, and detector ablation): Run the detector online via a cheap residual-stream onset probe (trained on Experiment-1 labels, 40/60 split by problem); on predicted onset, inject a terse reminder of the prior result and continue. Ablation: also run (i) injection WITHOUT the mechanistic detector (inject at fixed intervals) and (ii) the detector WITHOUT injection (just flag), to isolate what each component contributes. Systems compared on all four datasets: memory injection vs. (a) no intervention, (b) fixed truncation matched to injection mean budget, (c) Think Clearly reactive pruning, (d) verbosity/CREST-style steering, (e) length-aware filtering. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy (percent reduction while accuracy within 1 point). Secondary: recompute-loop count reduction, mean tokens, wall-clock latency, and estimated serving-cost reduction per query. Convincing: >= 15% token reduction within 1 point on GSM8K and MATH500 with recompute count cut >= 50%, matching or beating every baseline on the frontier, and the detector-guided variant beating the fixed-interval variant. Indecision: reduction in [7%, 15%] or a frontier-tie - the diagnosis (Experiments 1-4) is then the standalone contribution. Negative (< 7% or > 1 point loss): no usable savings.

Experiment 6 (H3 - Preserving corrective re-derivation, null-friendly analysis): Label a sample of onsets as corrective vs. blind, measure accuracy impact of suppressing each class, and additionally characterize WHEN recomputation does NOT occur (what predicts a model correctly reusing its result) to test the retrieval-failure account from the null side. Decisive metric: accuracy change on corrective-containing items with injection vs. withheld, plus a predictor analysis of no-recompute cases. Convincing: with the corrective-aware trigger, accuracy on corrective items drops < 1 point while blind-recompute savings are retained, and attention-to-original predicts no-recompute cases. Indecision: 1-3 point drop. Negative (> 3 point drop): blind and corrective recomputation cannot be cheaply separated, bounding H3 to easy items.

Experiment 7 (H1/H2 - Generality across data and scale): Transfer detector and onset probe across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining, with a problem-level split to avoid overfitting to GSM8K/MATH-style traces. Decisive metric: transferred onset-probe AUROC relative to in-domain, and recompute-token-fraction stability across scales. Convincing: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales and prevalence stays within a factor of 2. Indecision: retention in [60%, 80%]. Negative (< 60% retention or prevalence varying by > 3x): the phenomenon is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Detecting semantically-equivalent recomputations is nontrivial and may be noisy; we mitigate with parsing, an LLM-judge under explicit exclusion rules, and human validation, but false positives could over-trigger. Some recomputation is beneficial (self-correction, verification), so the trigger must separate blind from corrective re-derivation, which may be hard on the hardest items. The retrieval-failure hypothesis may be wrong - recomputation might be a deliberate learned strategy - which would be an informative negative that still yields a named waste category. Memory injection alters context and could introduce distribution shift or new errors. Intervention gains may not exceed strong reactive-pruning baselines; in that case the standalone contribution is the structured diagnosis, whose adopters are reasoning-model deployers wanting cheaper inference and interpretability researchers studying working memory - a distinction we keep explicit between user-facing and research benefit. Results may be model-family specific and biphasic across scales.

Name: corrective_check_foresight
Title: Worth Checking? A Prospective Internal Signal That Distinguishes Corrective from Confirmatory Self-Verification
Short Hypothesis: The sharp delta from prior work: existing efficiency probes predict, reactively, whether the CURRENT answer is already correct; we predict, prospectively and PER CHECK, the value of a specific impending verification step at the moment it begins -- whether an actual latent error exists to be caught, i.e. whether this check will be CORRECTIVE (changes the answer, ideally wrong->right) or merely CONFIRMATORY (re-confirms an already-correct answer and wastes tokens). We hypothesize the residual stream at check onset linearly encodes this 'value-of-verification' signal, that it is distinct from a plain answer-correctness or uncertainty signal, and that gating verification on it -- skip predicted-confirmatory checks, allow predicted-corrective ones -- suppresses waste while PRESERVING the rare corrective checks that blunt suppression destroys, cutting tokens at fixed accuracy and, crucially, without the hard-item accuracy loss suppression incurs. The unit of prediction is the individual check instance, not the per-answer state; 'corrective' vs 'confirmatory' is defined by comparing the model's extracted answer immediately before and after the check.
Related Work: A large recent cluster addresses redundant self-verification: probes that read whether the current answer is correct and early-exit (Reasoning Models Know When They're Right 2025; Temporal Predictors 2025; Gnosis 2025); reflection-direction steering tied to uncertainty (ReflCtrl 2025); wholesale suppression of self-affirmation/confirmatory rechecks (Efficient Reasoning via Suppression of Self-Affirmation 2025; Self-Verification Dilemma 2026 via offline experience retrieval); semantic-convergence early exit (PUMA 2026); and RL-based step-potential termination (SPAE 2026, ASRR 2025, Structured Reasoning 2026). Cast as a one-line 'what they predict / what they cannot': correctness/early-exit probes predict whether the answer is CURRENTLY right (not whether a given check will fix it); uncertainty/reflection steering predicts global confidence (not a specific check's utility); offline-experience and self-affirmation suppression decide to skip checks in bulk (not which individual check is corrective); semantic-convergence exit predicts redundancy of continued reasoning (not the counterfactual utility of the next check). All conflate 'the answer is currently right' with 'this check is not worth doing' -- yet the rare corrective checks occur precisely when the answer is WRONG, so blunt suppression kills them and costs hard-item accuracy. Our contribution is a different, prospective, per-check quantity: whether a latent error exists to be caught by the impending check, read at onset before the check is generated, aimed at preserving genuine self-correction that all suppression methods endanger. To our knowledge no prior work predicts a check's corrective-vs-confirmatory outcome from pre-check internal state.
Abstract: Reasoning models spend a large fraction of tokens on self-verification, yet analyses show the overwhelming majority of these rechecks are confirmatory -- they re-confirm an already-correct result and change nothing -- while a rare, precious few are corrective, catching a genuine error. Existing efficiency methods suppress verification wholesale or exit when the current answer looks correct, but this endangers exactly the corrective checks that occur when the answer is wrong, risking accuracy loss on hard problems. We ask a sharper, per-check question: does the model already know, at the moment it BEGINS a verification step, whether there is an actual error to catch -- whether this specific check will be corrective or merely confirmatory -- before performing it? We hypothesize the residual stream at check onset linearly encodes this value-of-verification signal, distinct from a plain answer-correctness or uncertainty signal. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we label each recheck corrective or confirmatory by comparing extracted pre- and post-check answers (human-audited, with inter-annotator agreement reported), train a lightweight onset probe with correctness/uncertainty controls, and causally validate by steering and by gating: skip predicted-confirmatory checks, allow predicted-corrective ones. The target is deployment-time inference: we aim to match wholesale suppression's token savings while retaining >=80% corrective-check recall and hard-strata accuracy within 1 point -- lower latency and cost without sacrificing hard-question success. We report token savings at fixed accuracy, corrective-check recall, and hard-item accuracy against correctness early-exit, reflection steering, and confirmatory suppression, reframing efficient verification as predicting a check's utility.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Rechecks are detectable and overwhelmingly confirmatory): Establishes the labels and the stakes the rest depends on. Data: GSM8K (1000-problem sample of 1319 test), MATH500 (500), AIME 2022-2024 (90), GPQA-Diamond (198); all restricted to extractable numeric/multiple-choice answers so an answer change is unambiguous. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Method: segment each trace into steps, detect recheck onsets via lexical cues ('let me check / verify / wait / recompute') plus a reflection-direction classifier; for each recheck read the model's implicit answer just before and just after the check (logit-lens / answer probe and the emitted intermediate answer), labeling CORRECTIVE if the answer changed (especially wrong->right) and CONFIRMATORY otherwise. Decisive metric: the corrective:confirmatory ratio per dataset/model, plus a human spot-check of 200 labeled rechecks for label accuracy. Convincing result: corrective checks are < 20% of all rechecks (confirming they are rare and that blunt suppression has real stakes) and human-validated label accuracy >= 90%. Indecision band: label accuracy in [80%, 90%) means the labels are usable but noisy — report probe results with this noise floor; below 80% the labeling is unreliable and downstream probes are uninterpretable, requiring a cleaner answer-extraction rule first. Negative result (corrective checks are common, e.g., > 40%) would remove the efficiency motivation, since most checks would be worth keeping.

Experiment 2 (H2 — A prospective value-of-verification signal is decodable at check onset, distinct from answer-correctness): The core test. Data: ~5000 labeled rechecks from Experiment 1 for probe fitting and 1500 held-out (from disjoint problems), with class weighting for the corrective minority. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B for robustness, frozen; only linear probes trained. Method: at each recheck onset extract residual-stream activations BEFORE any check content is generated, and fit per-layer linear probes to predict corrective vs confirmatory. Systems compared: the value-of-verification probe vs (a) a plain answer-correctness probe read at the same position, (b) an uncertainty / reflection-direction score, (c) a prior-text bag-of-words classifier. Decisive metric: corrective-vs-confirmatory AUROC on held-out problems, reported with precision-recall on the corrective class given imbalance. Secondary: partial correlation and principal angle between the value-of-verification direction and the correctness direction. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.75 at some layer, a corrective-class precision-recall clearly above the base-rate line, a partial correlation with the corrective label >= 0.25 after removing the correctness probe, and principal angle >= 30 degrees from the correctness direction. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.75) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the signal is real but largely reducible to correctness — reported as an entangled utility correlate; AUROC < 0.65 or partial correlation < 0.10 means 'check utility' reduces to answer-correctness and H2 fails. Negative result would collapse the contribution into existing correctness-probe methods.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal validation: steering the signal shifts realized check outcomes): Tests that the direction causally governs whether a check corrects. Data: 400 held-out rechecks. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is adding/subtracting the value-of-verification direction at check onset, dose-response swept; 3 seeds. Systems compared: value-of-verification steering vs matched random-direction and correctness-direction controls. Decisive metric: the change in realized corrective rate (fraction of checks that actually change the answer) as a function of steering dose. Convincing result: a monotone dose-response in which positive steering raises and negative steering lowers the realized corrective rate by >= 10 percentage points, exceeding both controls by >= 8 points, plus activation-patching localization to a small set of layers. Indecision band: an effect in [4, 10) points or not separable from the random control by > 5 points is weak causal evidence, reported as such. Negative result (no outcome shift) would mean the decodable signal is not causally operative, weakening but not killing the gating application, which only needs prediction.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Correction-preserving gating cuts tokens at fixed accuracy while keeping corrective checks): The applied test of the efficiency claim. Data: full GSM8K sample, MATH500, AIME, GPQA held-out from probe fitting. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; training-free gate = at each recheck onset read the probe and skip the check when the predicted-confirmatory score is below threshold tau, else allow it; 3 seeds. Systems compared: no intervention, correctness-based early-exit, reflection steering, wholesale self-affirmation suppression, PUMA-style convergence exit, and our gate. Decisive metric: corrective-check recall (fraction of genuinely corrective checks allowed to run) at matched token savings, read jointly with hard-strata accuracy (AIME and the hardest MATH/GPQA tercile). Secondary: overall accuracy, mean tokens, tokens-at-fixed-accuracy. Convincing result: at token savings matching wholesale suppression (within 3% of its mean-token reduction), our gate retains corrective-check recall >= 0.80 and hard-strata accuracy within +/- 1.0 point of no-intervention, whereas wholesale suppression loses > 3 points on hard strata. Indecision band: corrective recall in [0.60, 0.80) at matched savings, or hard-strata accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.0] points, means the gate helps but does not cleanly beat suppression — reported as a modest improvement; recall < 0.60 or accuracy drop > 3 points means the gate fails its correction-preserving promise. Negative result (no better recall/accuracy than suppression at equal savings) would refute the practical claim while leaving the mechanistic H2 finding.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Threshold frontier, failure analysis, and generalization): Characterizes the trade-off and transfer. Data: the four datasets; failure cases mined from Experiment 4. Models: 7B and 14B, frozen. Method: sweep tau to trace the token-savings vs corrective-recall frontier; audit cases where the gate wrongly suppressed a corrective check (resulting accuracy loss) and wrongly allowed a confirmatory one (residual waste); transfer the probe and gate fit on one dataset/model to the others without retraining. Decisive metric: the tokens-vs-corrective-recall Pareto frontier and the retained gate performance on transfer targets. Convincing result: a frontier dominating the suppression baselines (higher corrective recall at equal tokens across a range of tau), and >= two-thirds of in-domain corrective recall retained on transfer. Indecision band: transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds) means partial, calibration-dependent transfer; below one-third means the probe is dataset/model-specific. Negative result would confine the method to its fitting conditions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The value-of-verification signal may be inseparable from a plain correctness signal (a corrective check is, almost by definition, one done when the answer is wrong); the separability, partial-correlation, and causal-steering analyses directly test this, and a null result would itself be an informative finding that 'check utility' reduces to answer-correctness. Labeling corrective vs confirmatory relies on detecting answer changes across a check, which is noisy for open-ended answers, so we restrict to math/multiple-choice with extractable answers and validate labels with human spot-checks. Corrective checks are rare, creating class imbalance that can inflate AUROC apparent performance; we report precision/recall and calibrated thresholds. Recheck-onset detection may be imperfect and miss implicit verification. Gating could still suppress a corrective check on a hard item (accuracy loss); the corrective-recall metric and hard-strata accuracy quantify this trade-off explicitly. Gains may not exceed strong suppression baselines on tokens alone - but the contribution is preserving accuracy/corrective recall at equal savings. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: analogical_transfer_gate
Title: Solved It Once, Solving It Again: An Internal Analogy Gate Governing Whether Reasoning Models Reuse a Worked Example or Re-Derive From Scratch
Short Hypothesis: Sharpened novelty: the first study of token-efficient SELF-REUSE of a just-seen worked example in reasoning LLMs. When shown a fully-worked solution to a structurally-identical problem immediately before the target, reasoning models frequently FAIL to transfer the method -- re-deriving from scratch and wasting large numbers of tokens -- and, mirroring human analogical transfer, this failure is modulated by surface vs. structural similarity, with a tempting-but-structurally-different distractor inducing HARMFUL reuse (an accuracy loss). Two separable impacts follow: an efficiency impact (wasted tokens on valid analogs) and a distinct safety/robustness impact (harmful reuse on invalid analogs, with prompt-design implications). Primary behavioral endpoint: transfer-failure rate on structural analogs. Primary mechanistic endpoint: at the token boundary where the target begins, a linearly-decodable analogy-gate signal predicts reuse vs. re-derivation with onset-peaked AUROC, is distinct from generic task-vectors/task-identity and from a scalar difficulty probe, and causally controls behavior under steering. Falsifier: onset representations predict only difficulty, or steering changes length without changing reuse behavior.
Related Work: Two previously-disconnected literatures. (1) Interpretability of in-context task reuse: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks (2023) and Function Induction (2025) show internal components/circuits are shared across tasks; Just-in-time and Distributed Task Representations (2025) show transferrable task vectors form sporadically at specific tokens; task-vector work extracts task IDENTITY from activations. Our analogy gate is distinct from these task vectors: a task vector encodes WHICH task/operation to perform (task identity), whereas the analogy gate encodes the model's DECISION of whether to reuse a specific just-seen worked solution versus re-derive it -- a binary transfer decision an identity probe does not capture. (2) Cognitive science on analogical transfer (Structure-Mapping Theory) shows humans reuse solutions to structurally-similar problems, gated by surface vs. structural similarity and by retrieval failure -- but prior analogy work tests SOLVING new analogies, not reuse of an immediately-preceding worked solution or its token savings; that delta is our setting. Crucially, no prior work asks the behavioral question we pose: does a reasoning model reuse its OWN just-seen worked solution on a new instance, or wastefully re-derive, and how much compute does this cost? Circuit-reuse work studies static shared components, not the dynamic in-context transfer decision; systems-level activation/KV caching reuses computation externally without asking whether the model recognizes the analogy. Our contribution is (a) quantifying in-context analogical-transfer failure as wasted reasoning tokens, (b) showing its surface-vs-structure modulation and distractor-induced harmful reuse, and (c) locating and causally steering an onset analogy gate distinct from task-identity probes. This differs from our prior proposals, which concern within-single-problem overthinking.
Abstract: Humans who have just solved a problem reuse the method when they meet a structurally identical one, thinking far less the second time. We ask whether reasoning language models do the same -- a question that decides, whenever worked examples are appended in assistants, code agents, or tutors, whether the model should compress or wastefully rethink. We present a reasoning model with a fully-worked solution, then a target that is structurally identical but differs in surface details, and measure whether it transfers the method (short reasoning) or re-derives from scratch (long, redundant reasoning). We hypothesize that models frequently fail to transfer, wasting tokens, and -- mirroring human analogy -- that transfer succeeds more with high surface similarity and fails when only deep structure is shared, while a surface-similar-but-structurally-different distractor induces harmful reuse. We treat these as separable impacts: an efficiency cost (wasted tokens on valid analogs) and a distinct safety cost (harmful reuse on invalid analogs). Across GSM8K, MATH500, and templated algorithmic word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we quantify a transfer-failure rate and its similarity modulation with difficulty-, length-, and lexical-overlap-matched controls. We then test a mechanistic account: at the target-onset boundary, the residual stream linearly encodes an analogy-gate signal predicting reuse vs. re-derivation, separable from task-identity and difficulty probes and peaking at onset. We localize it via activation patching, causally steer it with specificity controls, and build a training-free intervention that induces reuse when a valid analog is present, cutting tokens at equal accuracy. We reframe a slice of overthinking as steerable analogical-transfer failure.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Models fail to transfer, and the failure is modulated by surface vs structural similarity with distractor-induced harmful reuse): The behavioral test of the transfer-failure claim and its similarity modulation. Data: constructed analog sets. From 250 seed problems (GSM8K, MATH500, templated algorithmic word problems with well-defined methods) build, per seed, (a) a surface-similar structural analog (same method and cover story, different numbers), (b) a structure-only analog (same method, different domain/cover story), and (c) a surface-similar structurally-different distractor (similar wording, different method). Verify structural equivalence via solution-step-template matching plus an LLM-judge and a 150-item human spot-check, and verify difficulty parity across conditions by pass-rate matching. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Systems compared, per condition: [worked analog + target] vs [target alone] vs [irrelevant worked solution + target]. Decisive metric: transfer-failure rate (fraction of structural-analog trials with < 20% token reduction vs target-alone despite retained accuracy), reported separately for surface-similar and structure-only conditions. Secondary: mean token reduction and accuracy per condition; distractor-condition accuracy (harmful reuse). Convincing result: overall transfer-failure rate >= 40%; failure rate on structure-only analogs exceeds surface-similar by >= 15 percentage points (surface-vs-structure modulation); and the distractor lowers accuracy by >= 3 points vs target-alone (harmful reuse). Indecision band: an overall failure rate in [20%, 40%), or a surface-vs-structure gap in [5, 15) points, is weak support — failure and modulation are present but minor; below those thresholds means no meaningful failure or no similarity modulation and H1 is unsupported. Negative result (reliable transfer, or no surface-vs-structure difference, or no distractor harm) would refute the behavioral core.

Experiment 2 (H2 — A just-in-time analogy-gate signal at target onset predicts reuse vs re-derivation, separable from difficulty): Tests the decodable, temporally-local gate. Data: ~4000 [worked analog + target] boundary states from Experiment 1 labeled transfer vs re-derive, 1200 held-out from disjoint seeds. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B, frozen; only linear probes trained. Method: at the token boundary where the target begins fit per-layer linear probes to predict transfer vs re-derivation, and repeat at positions before and after onset to test temporal locality (just-in-time hypothesis). Systems compared: the analogy-gate probe vs (i) a difficulty probe on target pass-rate, (ii) a surface-overlap feature baseline, (iii) prior-text bag-of-words. Decisive metric: transfer-prediction AUROC on held-out seeds at target onset. Secondary: partial correlation after removing difficulty and surface overlap, principal angle from the difficulty direction, and the AUROC profile across token positions (locality). Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.75 at onset, partial correlation >= 0.25 after removing confounds, principal angle >= 30 degrees from difficulty, and AUROC peaking near onset (a >= 0.05 rise vs positions well before the target) supporting the just-in-time account. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.75) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means an entangled correlate; AUROC < 0.65 means no distinct gate and H2 fails. A flat AUROC-vs-position profile leaves the gate decodable but not specifically just-in-time (reported as such, not fatal to H2). Negative result would leave transfer failure without an internal decision variable.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Patching the analogy-recognition state causally switches reuse vs re-derivation): Tests causal carry. Data: 300 matched pairs sharing target and method but differing in analog type (surface-similar transfer-inducing vs structure-only re-derivation). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is activation patching of the target-boundary state at candidate layers from the transfer-inducing context into the re-derivation context and vice versa. Systems compared: real patch vs matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric: fraction of trials switching to reuse (token drop plus method-matched solution) under patching. Convincing result: patching flips >= 40% of re-derivation trials to reuse, exceeding the random control by >= 25 points, off-target accuracy unchanged (< 5 points). Indecision band: a flip rate in [20%, 40%) or margin over random < 25 points is weak; below 20% means the boundary state is not the causal gate. Negative result would leave the gate correlational.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Steering the gate flips behavior with specificity): The steering test. Data: held-out [surface-similar analog + target] and [distractor + target] trials. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; intervention is steering along the analogy-gate direction (difference-of-means of transfer vs re-derivation boundary states); dose-response swept; 3 seeds. Systems compared: steer-up (induce reuse) vs steer-down (control) vs no intervention vs matched random direction. Decisive metric: token reduction at retained accuracy on valid-analog trials under steer-up, read jointly with the specificity check that steering does not induce harmful reuse of the distractor. Convincing result: steer-up cuts median tokens by >= 20% at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point on valid-analog trials, beats the random control by >= 10 points of token change, and leaves distractor-trial accuracy within +/- 1.0 point. Indecision band: a token reduction in [5%, 20%), or a distractor-trial accuracy drop in (1.0, 3.0] points, is a weak/partly-harmful outcome; a distractor accuracy drop > 3 points fails specificity. Negative result (no reduction, or reduction only with harmful distractor reuse) would refute the controllable-gate claim.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 — Training-free efficiency application and generalization): Tests the applied payoff and transfer. Data: GSM8K/MATH500/algorithmic held-out trials with a valid worked analog in context (detected by template match); plus cross-domain analogs (a math method reused in a physics word problem). Models: 7B and 14B, frozen; apply gate steering to induce reuse when a valid analog is detected. Systems compared: gate steering vs no intervention vs prompting ('reuse the method above'). Decisive metric: tokens-at-equal-accuracy (median token reduction subject to accuracy within noise) over the valid-analog stream. Secondary: transfer of the probe and steering direction across datasets, scales, and to cross-domain analogs without retraining. Convincing result: gate steering saves >= 15% tokens at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point, matching or beating prompting, and retains >= two-thirds of its effect across datasets and on cross-domain analogs. Indecision band: token savings in [5%, 15%), or transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds), is a modest/partial outcome; below those means no practical edge or no transfer (rare cross-domain transfer at 1.5B being an informative scope result). Negative result would confine the contribution to the mechanistic findings.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The analogy gate may be inseparable from raw difficulty or surface-overlap features, weakening the mechanistic claim; the separability analysis, patching, and distractor-specificity tests directly address this, and a null would still yield a novel behavioral characterization of transfer failure. Constructing clean structural analogs that hold difficulty constant while varying surface similarity is nontrivial; we mitigate with template-based generation and human/LLM verification plus pass-rate matching. Transfer-success detection relies on token-count and method-match, which are noisy; we use both token-reduction and step-template matching and validate with human spot-checks. Inducing reuse could cause harmful transfer to structurally-different distractors (accuracy loss); the distractor condition and steering-specificity metric quantify this trade-off. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters. Effects and the strength of surface-vs-structure modulation may be model-family and scale specific, and cross-domain transfer may be rare in smaller models (itself an informative result).

Name: analogical_transfer_gate
Title: Solved It Once, Solving It Again: An Internal Analogy Gate That Determines Whether Reasoning Models Reuse a Worked Example or Re-Derive From Scratch
Short Hypothesis: Narrowly scoped setting: a fully-worked solution to a problem is placed in-context IMMEDIATELY BEFORE a target that is structurally identical but differs only in surface details (numbers, cover story, variable names). We hypothesize that reasoning models frequently FAIL to reuse the just-seen method -- re-deriving from scratch and wasting a large number of tokens -- and that, mirroring human analogical transfer, this failure is modulated by surface vs. structural similarity. The single falsifiable mechanistic claim: at the token boundary where the target begins (before any target reasoning token), the residual stream carries a linearly-decodable 'analogy-gate' signal that predicts reuse vs. re-derivation, that is distinct from a raw target-difficulty signal and from surface lexical overlap, and that causally controls the decision -- steering it flips the model between reuse and re-derivation. This is not generic in-context learning (the target is a new instance requiring the same method, not a demonstration to imitate token-for-token), not within-single-problem overthinking, and not static task-vector reuse; it is a dynamic, onset-specific decision to transfer or not. Falsifier: the onset representation predicts only difficulty, or steering changes length without changing reuse behavior.
Related Work: Three previously-disconnected lines, separated by what each addresses and the delta we add. (1) Behavioral analogical transfer in cognitive science (Structure-Mapping Theory; 'Transfer Between Analogies' 1995; 'A model of retrieval in problem solving' 1989; 'A theory of relation learning and cross-domain generalization' 2022) documents that humans reuse solutions to structurally-similar problems, gated by surface vs. structural similarity -- but says nothing about LLMs or token cost. (2) Mechanistic circuit/computation reuse and steering (Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks 2023; Shared Circuits for Sequence Continuation 2023; Extrapolation by Association 2025; task-vector extraction work) shows internal components are shared across tasks and task identity can be read from activations -- but studies STATIC shared components, not the dynamic in-context decision to transfer a just-seen worked solution, and offers no efficiency measurement. (3) Systems-level activation/KV caching (LLMCache, AttMemo, KVShare 2023-2025) reuses computation EXTERNALLY without asking whether the model itself recognizes the analogy. Our delta against all three: we pose the behavioral question none of them do -- does a reasoning model reuse its OWN just-seen worked solution on a new instance of the same problem, or wastefully re-derive, and how many tokens does that cost -- and then locate and causally steer an onset-specific analogy gate distinct from static task vectors and from a scalar difficulty probe. This differs from our prior proposals, which concern within-single-problem overthinking.
Abstract: Humans who have just solved a problem reuse the method when they encounter a structurally identical one, thinking far less the second time. We ask whether reasoning language models do the same in the specific, common setting where a worked example is appended immediately before a new instance -- as happens in assistants with few-shot exemplars, code agents, and tutoring systems. We present a reasoning model with a fully-worked solution, then a target that is structurally identical but differs in surface details, and measure whether it transfers the method (short, reuse-style reasoning) or re-derives from scratch (long, redundant reasoning). We hypothesize that models frequently fail to transfer, wasting tokens -- a concrete inference cost and latency penalty -- and that, mirroring human analogy, transfer succeeds more with high surface similarity and fails when only deep structure is shared. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and templated algorithmic word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we quantify a transfer-failure rate and its surface-vs-structure modulation with difficulty-, length-, and lexical-overlap-matched controls. We then test a falsifiable mechanistic account: at the token boundary where the target begins, the residual stream linearly encodes an analogy-gate signal predicting reuse vs. re-derivation, separable from difficulty and surface overlap. We localize it via activation patching, causally steer it to flip behavior with specificity controls (a tempting but structurally-different distractor must not induce harmful reuse), and turn it into a training-free intervention that induces reuse when a valid analog is present, cutting tokens at equal accuracy. The result reframes a slice of overthinking as steerable analogical-transfer failure with direct prompt-design and inference-routing implications.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Reasoning models frequently fail to transfer a just-seen worked solution to a structurally identical target): The behavioral test. Data: constructed analog pairs. Draw 250 seed problems from GSM8K, MATH500, and templated algorithmic word problems with well-defined solution methods; for each seed generate (a) a surface-similar structural analog (same method, similar cover story, different numbers), (b) a structure-only analog (same method, different cover story/domain), and (c) a surface-similar structurally-different distractor (similar wording, different method). Verify structural equivalence via solution-step-template matching plus an LLM-judge check and a 150-pair human spot-check. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Systems compared, per condition: [worked analog + target] vs [target alone] vs [irrelevant worked solution + target]. Decisive metric: transfer-failure rate — the fraction of structural-analog trials whose target reasoning-token count is not substantially reduced (< 20% below the target-alone baseline) despite retained accuracy. Secondary: mean token reduction and accuracy per condition (surface-similar vs structure-only vs distractor), and whether the distractor induces harmful reuse (accuracy drop). Convincing result: transfer-failure rate >= 40% overall with a real opportunity cost (surface-similar analogs cut tokens by >= 25% at retained accuracy when transfer does occur), establishing that models leave substantial savings on the table. Indecision band: a transfer-failure rate in [20%, 40%) means failure is real but modest; below 20% (models almost always transfer) means there is little phenomenon to explain and the mechanistic program is unmotivated. Negative result (models reliably transfer, near-zero failure) would refute the premise.

Experiment 2 (H2 — An analogy-gate signal at target onset linearly predicts transfer vs re-derivation, separable from difficulty): Tests the decodable gate. Data: ~4000 [worked analog + target] boundary states from Experiment 1 labeled transfer vs re-derive, 1200 held-out from disjoint seeds. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B, frozen; only linear probes trained. Method: at the token boundary where the target begins (after the worked example, before any target reasoning token) fit per-layer linear probes to predict transfer vs re-derivation. Systems compared: the analogy-gate probe vs (i) a difficulty probe trained on target pass-rate, (ii) a surface-similarity feature baseline, (iii) prior-text bag-of-words. Decisive metric: transfer-prediction AUROC on held-out seeds. Secondary: partial correlation with the transfer label after removing difficulty and surface overlap, and principal angle between the gate and difficulty directions. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.75 at some layer, partial correlation >= 0.25 after removing difficulty and surface overlap, and principal angle >= 30 degrees from the difficulty direction. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.75) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the gate is real but largely reducible to difficulty/surface features — reported as an entangled correlate; AUROC < 0.65 means no distinct gate and H2 fails. Negative result would leave transfer failure as a behavioral fact without an internal decision variable.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Patching the analogy-recognition state causally switches reuse vs re-derivation): Tests causal carry of the gate. Data: 300 matched pairs sharing the same target and method but differing in analog type (surface-similar transfer-inducing vs structure-only re-derivation). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is activation patching of the target-boundary state at candidate layers from the surface-similar context into the structure-only context and vice versa. Systems compared: real patch vs matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric: the fraction of trials that switch to reuse (token drop plus method-matched solution) under patching. Convincing result: patching flips >= 40% of re-derivation trials to reuse, exceeding the random-direction control by >= 25 points, with off-target accuracy unchanged (< 5 points). Indecision band: a flip rate in [20%, 40%) or margin over random < 25 points is weak causal evidence; below 20% means the boundary state is not the causal gate. Negative result would leave the gate correlational.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Steering the gate induces reuse when a valid analog is present, with specificity): The steering test. Data: held-out [surface-similar analog + target] and [distractor + target] trials. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; intervention is steering along the analogy-gate direction (difference-of-means of transfer vs re-derivation boundary states); dose-response swept; 3 seeds. Systems compared: steer-up (induce reuse) vs steer-down (control) vs no intervention vs matched random direction. Decisive metric: token reduction at retained accuracy on valid-analog trials under steer-up, read jointly with the specificity check that steering does NOT induce harmful reuse of the distractor (accuracy must not drop on distractor trials). Convincing result: steer-up cuts median tokens by >= 20% at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point on valid-analog trials, beats the random control by >= 10 points of token change, and leaves distractor-trial accuracy within +/- 1.0 point (no harmful transfer). Indecision band: a token reduction in [5%, 20%), or a distractor-trial accuracy drop in (1.0, 3.0] points, is a weak/partly-harmful outcome reported as such; a distractor accuracy drop > 3 points means steering forces indiscriminate reuse and fails specificity. Negative result (no token reduction, or reduction only with harmful distractor reuse) would refute the controllable-gate claim.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Training-free efficiency application and generalization): Tests the applied payoff and transfer. Data: GSM8K/MATH500/algorithmic held-out trials where a valid worked analog is in context (detected cheaply by template match); plus cross-domain analogs (a math method reused in a physics word problem). Models: 7B and 14B, frozen; apply gate steering to induce reuse when a valid analog is detected. Systems compared: gate steering vs no intervention vs simple prompting ('reuse the method above'). Decisive metric: tokens-at-equal-accuracy (median token reduction subject to accuracy within noise) over the valid-analog stream. Secondary: whether the probe and steering direction transfer across datasets, scales, and to cross-domain analogs without retraining. Convincing result: gate steering saves >= 15% tokens at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point, matching or beating the prompting baseline, and retains >= two-thirds of its effect across datasets and on cross-domain analogs. Indecision band: token savings in [5%, 15%), or transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds), is a modest/partial outcome; below those means no practical edge or no transfer (cross-domain transfer being rare, especially at 1.5B, is itself an informative scope result). Negative result would confine the contribution to the mechanistic findings.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The analogy gate may be inseparable from raw difficulty or surface-overlap features, weakening the mechanistic claim; the separability analysis, patching, and distractor-specificity tests directly address this, and a null would still yield a novel behavioral characterization of transfer failure. Constructing clean structural analogs that hold difficulty constant while varying surface similarity is nontrivial; we mitigate with template-based generation and human/LLM verification of structural equivalence. Transfer-success detection relies on token-count and method-match, which are noisy; we use both token-reduction and step-template matching and validate with human spot-checks. Inducing reuse could cause harmful transfer to structurally-different distractors (accuracy loss); the distractor condition and steering-specificity metric quantify this trade-off. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters. Effects and the strength of surface-vs-structure modulation may be model-family and scale specific, and cross-domain transfer may be rare in smaller models (itself an informative result).

Name: branch_worthiness_signal
Title: Does a Model Know When to Fork? An Internal Branch-Worthiness Signal for Per-Problem Parallel Compute Allocation
Short Hypothesis: A reasoning model's early hidden states, from a single greedy prefix, linearly encode a 'branch-worthiness' signal: whether the problem has multiple plausible competing solution paths that make parallel sampling (best-of-N / self-consistency) worthwhile, versus a single-basin problem where extra samples are wasted. We claim this signal is the entropy of the model's internal candidate-answer distribution living in middle layers, readable from a short prefix before any full trace. Our primary, pre-registered claim is CAUSAL-MECHANISTIC: steering this internal-entropy up or down changes the realized diversity of sampled answers, so the signal is the mechanistic origin of branch-worthiness, not merely a predictor of it - and this holds even if internal-entropy correlates with difficulty, because steering entropy while holding difficulty fixed still changes sampling utility.
Related Work: Test-time scaling work allocates parallel budget per-problem with black-box predictors: T2 (2026) estimates optimal parallelism from latent representations AFTER partial generation; OptScale/OSCA/SCALE/DORA (2024-2025) derive resource-allocation rules from uncertainty/reward proxies; First Finish Search (2025) returns the first-completing trace; Latent-Trajectory signals (Vilas et al. 2025) predict per-trace success from representation dynamics. All either predict per-trace quality post-hoc (needing the trace) or fit an opaque allocation predictor. Interpretability work (Distributional Reasoning in LLMs, 2024; How to Think Step-by-Step, 2024) shows middle layers hold a distribution over candidate answers via parallel pathways. The explicit delta: T2/OSCA/SCALE/DORA read an uncertainty or reward signal, usually after some generation, and cannot say WHY forking helps; our internal candidate-answer distribution entropy is (a) readable from a single short greedy prefix before any sampling, and (b) causally manipulable - steering it changes realized answer diversity, which their latent/uncertainty signals are never shown to do. This is a mechanistic account plus a causal test, not another allocation heuristic or per-trace success predictor.
Abstract: Parallel test-time scaling (best-of-N, self-consistency) improves reasoning accuracy but wastes compute: many problems are single-basin, where all samples converge to one answer and extra samples add nothing, while a minority are genuinely multi-path where parallel exploration pays off. Existing methods pick the sample count with opaque predictors and offer little mechanistic insight into what determines the value of forking. We hypothesize that a model's early hidden states encode a branch-worthiness signal rooted in the entropy of the internal candidate-answer distribution known to live in middle layers, and that this signal predicts - and causally governs - the marginal accuracy gain of parallel sampling before any sampling is done. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on DeepSeek-R1 distills (1.5B-14B) and Qwen3, we (1) measure per-problem parallel-sampling utility (accuracy gain from N=1 to N=k) as ground truth; (2) read the internal candidate-answer distribution from a short greedy prefix via logit-lens and probes and test whether its entropy predicts branch-worthiness better than prompt-length, difficulty probes, output-confidence, and a strongest-possible same-prefix same-probe-family baseline; (3) localize the carrying heads/layers via activation patching and causally test whether steering the entropy up/down changes realized answer diversity, including a negative control against trivial diversity inflation; and (4) build a training-free per-problem allocator that reads the signal from one prefix and sets N adaptively. We report cost-accuracy curves in samples, total tokens, and wall-clock against uniform-N, T2-style latent predictors, First Finish Search, and confidence allocation, with statistical uncertainty on all gains. The work reframes how many samples to draw as reading a mechanistically-grounded, causally-validated internal signal, staged from readout to localization to causal control to allocation.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear probes are trainable, interventions are activation edits. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B (smaller k for 14B to control cost). Sampling: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2; all gains reported with bootstrap 95% CIs. Analysis restricted to extractable-answer items (math / multiple-choice; we note the signal is not validated for open-ended generation). Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198); ground-truth utility (Experiment 1) on a 400-item stratified subsample of GSM8K/MATH500 plus all AIME/GPQA to bound N=16 cost. Experiments are staged: readout (2) and localization (4) first, then causal steering (5), then allocation (6).

Experiment 1 (H1 - Branch-worthiness ground truth exists and budget is wasted under uniform-N): For each problem draw N=16 independent full samples; parallel-utility = accuracy(self-consistency at N=16) minus accuracy(greedy N=1); answer-diversity = entropy of the final-answer distribution. Label single-basin (near-zero diversity, no utility) vs multi-path. Decisive metric: fraction of problems with parallel-utility <= 1 point (single-basin). Convincing: >= 40% single-basin with a non-degenerate multi-path minority (>= 15%). Indecision: single-basin fraction in [20%, 40%]. Negative (< 20% single-basin or < 5% multi-path): little to allocate over.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Short-prefix internal entropy predicts branch-worthiness): Generate only a short greedy prefix (lengths 32/64/128 tokens); at middle layers decode the internal candidate-answer distribution via (a) logit-lens and (b) a probe predicting the entropy of eventual sampled answers (internal-entropy). Split 40/60 by problem. Decisive metric: held-out Spearman and AUROC of short-prefix internal-entropy vs. ground-truth utility / single-basin label. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 for single-basin vs multi-path at prefix <= 128 tokens, Spearman > 0.4 vs utility. Indecision: AUROC in [0.62, 0.75]. Negative (< 0.62 at all prefix lengths): branch-worthiness is not readable early, refuting H1/H2.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Beating strong same-prefix and full-trace baselines, with difficulty controls): Predict parallel-utility from short-prefix internal-entropy vs. (i) prompt length, (ii) a pre-generation difficulty probe, (iii) verbal/output confidence after a full greedy trace, (iv) a T2-style black-box latent predictor, and crucially (v) a STRONGEST-POSSIBLE same-short-prefix baseline: a probe from the identical probe family trained on the same prefix residual to predict utility directly, plus early-logit-margin from the prefix. Report internal-entropy with difficulty, confidence, length, and early-logit-margin partialled out. Decisive metric: ranking AUROC/R^2 of internal-entropy minus the best no-full-trace baseline, and the gap to full-trace baselines. Convincing: short-prefix internal-entropy is within 0.03 AUROC of the best full-trace predictor while cheaper, beats every no-full-trace baseline (including the strong same-prefix probe) by >= 0.05 AUROC, and retains predictive power after partialling out difficulty. Indecision: within [0.03, 0.08] below the best full-trace predictor and only tied with difficulty - the causal test (Experiment 5) then becomes decisive for the mechanistic claim (the pre-registered fallback: even if entropy tracks difficulty, causal steering still supports the mechanism). Negative (worse than difficulty probe AND no causal effect): internal-entropy is just a difficulty proxy.

Experiment 4 (H2 - Localizing the candidate-answer distribution): Activation patching / head attribution to find middle layers/heads carrying the distribution; ablate and measure degradation of the entropy readout. Decisive metric: drop in Experiment-2 probe AUROC under top-component vs. equal-count random ablation. Convincing: top-component ablation drops AUROC by >= 0.1 (vs. < 0.03 random). Indecision: [0.03, 0.1]. Negative (< 0.03): not localized.

Experiment 5 (H2 - Causal: entropy reflects branch structure, with negative control): Steer the identified components to raise/lower internal-entropy on the prefix, then run N=16 sampling and measure realized answer-diversity, checking sample validity. Negative control: apply a norm-matched random-direction steer of equal magnitude to rule out trivial diversity inflation, and a difficulty-matched subset to show the effect is not mediated by difficulty. Decisive metric: change in realized answer-diversity when steering entropy up vs. down (paired), minus the random-direction control. Convincing: raising internal-entropy increases realized diversity and lowering it collapses samples (paired p < 0.01, monotone in magnitude), clearly above the random control, with < 5% degenerate samples. Indecision: significant but small effect (< 0.2 normalized entropy units) or > 10% degenerate samples. Negative (no effect above control or mostly degenerate): the signal is a spurious correlate.

Experiment 6 (H3 - Adaptive allocator: cost-accuracy in samples, tokens, and wall-clock): For each problem, generate one short prefix, read internal-entropy, set N via a monotone schedule (single-basin -> N=1; high entropy -> N=16); thresholds fit on the Experiment-2 training split. Systems compared on all four datasets: allocator vs. (a) uniform-N self-consistency, (b) First Finish Search, (c) confidence-based allocation, (d) T2-style predictor, under identical model/dataset settings. Decisive metric: compute at fixed accuracy - mean samples AND total tokens AND wall-clock to match uniform-N=16 accuracy within 1 point. Secondary: full Pareto cost-accuracy curve with CIs. Convincing: allocator matches uniform-N=16 accuracy within 1 point using >= 40% fewer samples and materially fewer total tokens/wall-clock, dominating or tying the best baseline. Indecision: 15-40% sample reduction or a T2-tie - the mechanistic grounding (Experiments 2-5) is then the standalone contribution. Negative (< 15% or > 1 point loss): no usable allocation savings.

Experiment 7 (H1 - Generality across data and scale): Transfer probe and allocator across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain and allocator sample-savings retention. Convincing: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales; savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision: [60%, 80%]. Negative (< 60%): branch-worthiness readout is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The internal candidate-answer distribution is cleanest for extractable-answer tasks, so we restrict to math/multiple-choice and do not claim open-ended generation. Short-prefix entropy may not capture branch structure that only emerges late, weakening prediction (an informative negative, mitigated by testing several prefix lengths). Internal-entropy may correlate with plain difficulty; the causal steering experiment (with a difficulty-matched subset) and the strong same-prefix baseline address this, and the pre-registered position is that causal control, not correlation, carries the mechanistic claim. Steering entropy could produce degenerate/off-distribution samples; a random-direction negative control and validity checks guard against trivial diversity inflation. The allocator's gains may not exceed strong latent-predictor baselines like T2; the mechanistic grounding remains a standalone contribution for serving, agentic reasoning, and offline eval settings that pay for parallel samples. Ground-truth utility with k up to 16 is compute-intensive; we subsample and use smaller k for larger models. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: strategy_affordance_mismatch
Title: Wrong Tool for the Job: Overthinking as a Strategy-Selection Mismatch Between the Problem's Afforded Solution Method and the One the Model Executes
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models pre-encode, before generating any reasoning token, a linearly-decodable multi-CLASS 'strategy affordance' signal indicating which class of solution method a problem invites, drawn from a small coarse taxonomy: DIRECT-RECALL/formula-application, MULTI-STEP-DERIVATION, CASE-ENUMERATION/search, and ELIMINATION (for MCQ). These classes are not reducible to a scalar hardness axis: two problems of equal difficulty (equal pass-rate) can afford different methods (a formula-application and a case-enumeration can be equally hard yet call for categorically different work). We claim a large slice of overthinking is a strategy MISMATCH -- the model executes a heavier strategy than the problem affords. The novelty is stated as a falsifiable COMPARATIVE hypothesis: a categorical affordance probe must (i) predict per-problem wasted tokens better than a scalar difficulty or success-likelihood probe, and (ii) yield a steering intervention that Pareto-dominates scalar length steering (more tokens saved at equal-or-better accuracy). If the affordance signal is inseparable from scalar difficulty or adds no predictive/interventional value beyond it, the account collapses into existing difficulty-budgeting and is refuted.
Related Work: Prior efficient-reasoning interpretability reads a SCALAR pre-generation signal and allocates a length/compute budget from it: LLMs Encode Their Failures (2026) and difficulty-perception probes predict model-specific difficulty for routing; Temporal Predictors of Outcome (2025) and Knowing Before Saying (2025) probe eventual correctness early; Tracing the Traces (2025) uses latent-trajectory signals to pick promising traces; FR-Ponder / Learning to Ponder (2025) learn instance-adaptive scalar compute; Efficiency Steering / ReflCtrl (2025) steer a single verbosity/reflection direction. The exact delta: every one of these treats the pre-generation signal as one-dimensional (how hard / how likely to succeed / how long) and controls a scalar knob (budget, length, reflection), so none can represent that two equally-hard problems afford categorically different methods, and none predicts or intervenes on the CLASS of strategy executed. A separate line (Behavior and Representation in LLMs for Combinatorial Optimization, 2025) shows hidden states support per-instance ALGORITHM selection, but for external solver choice, not the model's own reasoning, and offers no efficiency intervention. Directly inspired by cognitive neuroscience showing the brain decides WHETHER to engage costly forward planning via a fast planning-value proxy (ACC, 2021) and shifts between rule-based and memory-based processing via cost-benefit analysis (2025), we claim reasoning models carry a multi-class strategy-affordance representation, that overthinking is a MISMATCH between afforded and executed strategy (not a mis-set scalar budget), and that steering toward the afforded strategy is an interpretable efficiency fix -- a categorical account orthogonal to scalar difficulty/budget work and to our prior overthinking proposals (answer-commitment, verification, length priors).
Abstract: Reasoning language models overthink, and prior interpretability work explains this via a SCALAR internal signal (difficulty, success-likelihood, or a verbosity direction) that sets how MUCH to think. We propose a categorical account inspired by human cognitive control: before generating any reasoning token, a model encodes a strategy-affordance signal indicating WHICH kind of solution method a problem invites -- direct recall/formula-application, multi-step derivation, case-enumeration/search, or elimination. We hypothesize a large share of overthinking is a strategy mismatch: the model executes a heavier strategy than the problem affords (laboriously deriving what could be recalled, or enumerating what a formula solves in one line). Crucially, we frame novelty as a comparative, falsifiable claim -- the affordance probe must beat scalar difficulty/success probes at predicting wasted tokens and must yield steering that Pareto-dominates scalar length steering. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) label each problem's afforded and each trace's executed strategy via parsing plus LLM-judge with human validation; (2) train prompt-boundary probes to decode afforded strategy and test separability from difficulty on a difficulty-matched control set; (3) show a mismatch score predicts wasted tokens better than scalar baselines; (4) causally validate via activation patching; and (5) steer toward the afforded strategy at onset, targeting >=15% median token savings at accuracy within 1 point and beating scalar steering. The operational payoff is concrete -- cheaper, lower-latency inference and better compute routing for reasoning systems via inference-time strategy steering -- reframing a slice of overthinking as picking the wrong solution method.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Overthinking is substantially a strategy mismatch, not just a mis-set scalar budget): Establishes the phenomenon by labeling afforded vs executed strategy and measuring mismatch prevalence and its token cost. Data: GSM8K (1000-problem sample of 1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2022-2024 (90), GPQA-Diamond (198). Define a coarse, model-agnostic strategy taxonomy: DIRECT-RECALL/formula-application, MULTI-STEP-DERIVATION, CASE-ENUMERATION/search, and ELIMINATION (for MCQ). For each problem label the AFFORDED strategy = the cheapest strategy yielding the correct answer (from a model-produced minimal solution plus an independent LLM-judge, cross-checked against a reference minimal solution where available); for each generated trace label the EXECUTED strategy via pattern parsing plus LLM-judge. Validate on a 200-item human spot-check and report inter-rater agreement. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds.
