Decisive metric: the fraction of traces whose executed strategy is strictly heavier than afforded, and the token overhead of those traces relative to their afforded-strategy minimal-solve length (estimated by truncate-and-resume and by prompting the afforded strategy). Convincing result: >= 25% of traces are strictly-heavier mismatches carrying >= 30% median token overhead vs the afforded minimal solve, with human-validated label agreement (Cohen's kappa) >= 0.6 — mismatch is a large, real slice of waste. Indecision band: a mismatch prevalence in [10%, 25%), or label kappa in [0.4, 0.6), means mismatch is present but minor or the labels too noisy to rest strong claims on — reported as weak/exploratory; below 10% prevalence means overthinking is not meaningfully strategy mismatch and the account fails. Negative result (executed strategy almost always matches afforded) would refute the framing.

Experiment 2 (H2 — A multi-class strategy-affordance signal is decodable at the prompt boundary, separable from scalar difficulty): Tests the categorical pre-generation representation. Data: prompt-boundary activations for the Experiment-1 problems with afforded-strategy labels; 3000 for probe fitting, 800 held-out from disjoint problems. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B, frozen; only linear probes trained. Method: at the last prompt token (before any reasoning token) fit a multi-class linear probe per layer to predict the afforded strategy. Systems compared: the strategy probe vs (a) a scalar difficulty probe (pass-rate), (b) a success-likelihood probe, (c) surface features (length, TF-IDF). Decisive metric: held-out macro-F1 for afforded strategy, and the predictive gain of the strategy probe over difficulty in a joint model. Secondary: principal angle between strategy-class directions and the difficulty direction. Convincing result: macro-F1 >= 0.55 (against a >0.25 four-class chance baseline) at some middle layer, a significant predictive gain over difficulty, and principal angle >= 30 degrees from the difficulty direction — strategy affordance is a distinct, multi-dimensional signal. Indecision band: macro-F1 in [0.40, 0.55) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the affordance is only partly separable from difficulty — reported as an entangled categorical correlate; macro-F1 <= 0.40 or no gain over difficulty means the account collapses into scalar difficulty-budgeting and H1 fails. Negative result would remove the categorical basis of the whole hypothesis.

Experiment 3 (H3 — A mismatch score predicts wasted tokens better than scalar difficulty or success probes): The predictive test. Data: held-out Experiment-1 problems with per-problem wasted-token labels = tokens beyond the truncate-and-resume minimal-solve length. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen. Method: define a mismatch score from the probe-predicted afforded strategy vs the realized executed strategy; regress wasted tokens on the mismatch score and, separately, on each baseline (difficulty probe, success probe, raw trace length). Decisive metric: held-out R^2 for predicting wasted tokens from the mismatch score vs the best scalar baseline. Convincing result: the mismatch score's R^2 exceeds every scalar baseline's by >= 0.05 and is significant, showing waste is specifically strategy mismatch, not generic difficulty. Indecision band: an R^2 edge over the best baseline in [0.02, 0.05) is weak; <= 0.02 (or the difficulty probe matching the mismatch score) means mismatch adds no predictive value beyond scalar signals and H3 fails. Negative result would fold the contribution back into existing difficulty-budgeting.

Experiment 4 (H4 — Patching the affordance state causally switches the executed strategy): Tests the causal locus. Data: 300 constructed pairs sharing a target answer/method family but differing in afforded strategy (cheap-affording vs heavy-affording), built from templated problem variants; where clean pairs are unavailable they are excluded and reported. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is activation patching of the prompt-boundary state at candidate layers from a cheap-strategy-affording problem into a heavy-strategy context. Systems compared: real patch vs matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric: fraction of trials whose executed strategy switches toward the cheaper class (strategy relabel plus token drop) under patching. Convincing result: patching switches the strategy on >= 40% of trials, exceeding the random control by >= 25 points, with off-target accuracy unchanged (< 5 points). Indecision band: a switch rate in [20%, 40%) or margin over random < 25 points is weak causal support; below 20% means the boundary state does not causally carry the affordance. Negative result would leave the affordance correlational.

Experiment 5 (H4 — Steering toward the afforded strategy cuts tokens without hurting accuracy, beating scalar length steering): The applied test of the efficiency claim. Data: GSM8K/MATH500/AIME/GPQA held-out. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; intervention is steering along a strategy direction (difference-of-means between cheap- and heavy-strategy affordance activations) at problem onset, applied only when the probe predicts a cheap strategy is afforded; 3 seeds. Systems compared: no intervention, strategy steering, scalar length/verbosity steering, difficulty-budgeting (FR-Ponder-style), fixed truncation, and prompting ('use the simplest method'). Decisive metric: tokens-at-equal-accuracy (median token reduction subject to accuracy within noise), read against the strategy-switch rate. Secondary: accuracy overall and on hardest strata, wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: strategy steering cuts median tokens by >= 15% at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point and Pareto-dominates scalar length steering (more tokens saved at equal-or-better accuracy), driven by a measurable strategy-switch rate. Indecision band: a token reduction in [5%, 15%), or accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.0] points, is a weak/traded outcome; a reduction that fails to beat scalar length steering means the categorical target adds no practical value over blunt shortening (an informative reframing-only result); accuracy drop > 3 points fails the 'without hurting accuracy' claim. Negative result would refute the intervention claim while leaving the mechanistic H1-H3 findings.

Experiment 6 (H4 — Specificity, safety, and generalization): Tests that steering does not fire on genuinely heavy-afforded problems and that it transfers. Data: the hardest-strata (heavy-afforded) items from AIME and the bottom MATH/GPQA accuracy tercile, plus held-out sets across datasets. Models: 7B and 14B, frozen. Method: apply strategy steering gated by probe confidence and measure accuracy on truly heavy-afforded items as a function of confidence; transfer the probe and steering direction across datasets/scales without retraining. Decisive metric: accuracy on heavy-afforded items under gated steering (must not drop) and retained token savings on transfer targets. Convincing result: heavy-afforded accuracy within +/- 1.0 point of no-intervention (no induced underthinking) and >= two-thirds of the token savings retained across datasets/scales. Indecision band: a heavy-afforded accuracy drop in (1.0, 3.0] points flags that steering must be gated to higher confidence; > 3.0 points means the intervention harms hard problems and must be scoped away from them. Transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds) means partial, calibration-dependent generality; below one-third means it is model/dataset-specific. Negative result would bound applicability rather than refute the core account.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The strategy taxonomy may be fuzzy—some problems admit no single 'afforded' strategy, and labels from LLM-judge/parsing are noisy; we mitigate with a small, coarse class set, human validation, and reporting agreement, and treat ambiguous cases separately. The afforded-strategy signal may be inseparable from scalar difficulty (harder problems simply afford heavier strategies), which would collapse our account into existing difficulty-budgeting work—the separability analysis, joint-model predictive-gain test, and causal patching directly address this, and a null separability result is itself an informative finding. Constructing patching pairs that hold the answer/method fixed while flipping afforded strategy is nontrivial; we use templated problem variants and report where clean pairs are unavailable. Steering toward a cheaper strategy could cause underthinking on problems that truly need a heavy method (accuracy loss); the specificity/hardest-strata analysis and confidence gating quantify this trade-off. Minimal-solve-length estimation via truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy and noisy; we subsample. Intervention gains may not exceed strong scalar steering on tokens alone, but the mechanistic reframing (overthinking as strategy mismatch with a decodable, steerable affordance representation) is a standalone contribution. Effects are likely model-family and scale specific, and afforded-strategy structure may differ across domains.

Name: subgoal_schedule_myopia
Title: Solving the Wrong Subgoal First: Overthinking as a Dependency-Scheduling Failure in Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: A problem's subgoals form a dependency DAG whose prerequisites impose a partial order; reasoning models schedule subgoals myopically rather than dependency-respectingly, frequently attacking a subgoal before its prerequisites are established. This premature scheduling wastes tokens on flailing and re-derivation. The model already carries an internal, decodable 'prerequisite-readiness' signal at each subgoal-onset that it fails to consult, and steering generation toward dependency-respecting order cuts tokens without hurting accuracy.
Related Work: Probing work shows LLM hidden states encode reasoning-DAG geometry (From Chains to DAGs, 2026) and that models are largely myopic/incremental planners with weak global planning (No Global Plan in CoT, 2026; Internal Planning: Horizon and Branch Awareness, 2025; Detecting and Characterizing Planning, 2025). Efficiency work characterizes overthinking as an inverted-U length effect (When More is Less, 2025) or as decorative/redundant steps (Thought Anchors; TTS). A shortest-path study shows next-token predictors are biased toward systematically inefficient (backtracking) traces (2025). Crucially, none connect the problem's *dependency structure* to *compute waste*: no prior work identifies suboptimal subgoal *ordering* (attacking a subgoal before its prerequisites) as a distinct, quantifiable source of overthinking, nor tests whether a decodable prerequisite-readiness signal governs it, nor intervenes on scheduling to save compute. This differs from my prior proposals (which target stopping, verification, length priors, and framing effects) by targeting the *order* in which reasoning is performed. It also goes beyond DAG-probing (which is diagnostic and static) by tying the encoded DAG to a behavioral scheduling failure and a causal efficiency intervention. It is also distinct from external agent-planning and multi-call schedulers (which order tool/LLM calls across turns); our failure and intervention live entirely inside a single reasoning trace.
Abstract: Reasoning models overthink, but the role of ordering in that waste is unexamined. Many problems decompose into subgoals with prerequisite dependencies -- a directed acyclic graph whose topological orders are the valid schedules. We hypothesize that reasoning models schedule subgoals myopically: they frequently begin a subgoal before its prerequisites are established, then flail or re-derive, spending tokens a dependency-respecting order would avoid. This is a within-trace, single-generation scheduling failure -- distinct from external agent/multi-call planners -- defined crisply as a subgoal onset preceding the establishment of all its prerequisite nodes. We further hypothesize the model already encodes, at each subgoal onset, a prerequisite-readiness signal (are the inputs this subgoal needs already available in context?) that it does not act on. Using multi-step problems with recoverable dependency structure (GSM8K, MATH500, and templated multi-constraint word/logic problems where we annotate a ground-truth subgoal DAG) on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) segment traces into subgoals, align them to DAG nodes, and measure a scheduling-inversion rate and its token cost via truncate-and-resume and re-derivation detection; (2) show inversions predict wasted tokens beyond length or decorative-step baselines; (3) train a linear onset probe to decode prerequisite-readiness and test its separability from difficulty/confidence; (4) causally validate via activation patching; and (5) deploy a training-free scheduling steer that defers premature subgoals, cutting tokens at equal accuracy versus length-aware and reactive-pruning baselines, reported in concrete token/latency terms. We provide an annotated example trace and reframe a slice of overthinking as a dependency-scheduling failure with a decodable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per problem with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted. The subgoal DAG and trace-to-node alignment are shared infrastructure: templated multi-constraint word problems and small logic/scheduling puzzles have a DAG known by construction; for GSM8K and MATH500 we annotate the subgoal DAG by solution parsing plus LLM-judge, human-validated on a 100-item spot-check (inter-annotator/judge agreement reported). Traces are segmented into subgoals at step delimiters and each subgoal is aligned to a DAG node by semantic matching plus LLM-judge; a scheduling-inversion = a subgoal begun before all its prerequisite nodes were established earlier in the trace. We provide at least one fully annotated example trace (prerequisites, subgoal onsets, an inversion, and the ensuing re-derivation/recovery) to make the mechanism legible.

Experiment 1 (H1 - reasoning models commit scheduling inversions rather than respecting the dependency order): Tests whether models frequently begin subgoals before their prerequisites are established. Data: constructed and adapted - 300 templated multi-constraint word problems and 200 logic/scheduling puzzles built with known DAGs (varying width/depth), plus 400 GSM8K and 300 MATH500 problems with annotated DAGs; these counts give enough multi-subgoal traces while keeping per-trace segmentation/alignment affordable. Systems compared: the observed per-trace inversion rate against a random-scheduling null (the inversion rate expected if subgoals were ordered uniformly at random among the DAG's topological-order violations), across datasets and the four model sizes. Decisive metric: per-trace scheduling-inversion rate, first; reported against the random-scheduling null and against the ideal (zero-inversion) schedule. Convincing: the observed inversion rate is substantial (>= 15% of subgoal onsets are inversions) and significantly above zero, but below the random-null (models are partly, not fully, dependency-respecting), consistent across datasets. Indecision band: an inversion rate of 5-15% is a weak phenomenon reported as such and does not strongly motivate the intervention. Negative result: an inversion rate < 5% (models already schedule near-optimally) refutes H1 and removes the premise for the remaining experiments; an inversion rate at or above the random null would instead indicate alignment failure rather than a real scheduling signal and triggers an alignment audit.

Experiment 2 (H2 - inversions cause wasted tokens through flailing and re-derivation): Tests whether inversions predict wasted compute beyond length and decorative-step baselines. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces. For each inversion we measure downstream waste via (a) truncate-and-resume estimating the minimal-solve length under a forced dependency-respecting order (prerequisite subgoals prompted first) on a 200-problem subsample, (b) re-derivation detection (value-producing statements re-derived after a premature attempt), and (c) dead-end/backtrack detection. We then regress per-trace wasted tokens on inversion rate versus baselines: trace length, decorative-step fraction, and a difficulty probe. Systems compared: inversion-rate predictor vs each baseline predictor. Decisive metric: held-out incremental R2 of inversion rate for predicting wasted tokens over the strongest baseline, first; plus the mean wasted tokens attributable to a single inversion. Convincing: inversion rate adds >= 0.05 R2 over the best baseline (significant), and forcing a dependency-respecting order reduces minimal-solve length by >= 15% on the subsample. Indecision band: incremental R2 0.02-0.05, or a 5-15% forced-order reduction, is partial support. Negative result: incremental R2 < 0.02 and < 5% forced-order reduction means inversions do not cause measurable waste, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - a decodable prerequisite-readiness signal exists at subgoal onset and is separable from difficulty/confidence): Tests whether the residual stream at subgoal onset encodes whether the upcoming subgoal's prerequisites are satisfied, distinct from generic difficulty/confidence. Data: subgoal-onset activations (before the subgoal is generated) from Experiment 1 traces, labeled by DAG alignment as prerequisites-satisfied vs not, split 70/15/15 by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probes: a linear readiness probe (target = prerequisites satisfied), a difficulty probe (pass-rate), and a confidence probe. Systems compared: readiness probe vs difficulty/confidence probes; principal angles among their directions and joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the readiness probe, first; plus its principal angle to the difficulty and confidence directions. Convincing: readiness AUROC >= 0.7 at the best layer, the readiness direction not collinear with difficulty or confidence (angle >= 30 degrees to each), adding significant R2 over both - establishing that readiness is decodable even at onsets the model then treats as inversions (an unconsulted signal). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.7, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: AUROC < 0.6, or collinearity with difficulty/confidence (angle < 20 degrees), means there is no distinct readiness signal, refuting H3.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal - patching readiness redirects the model to a ready subgoal): Tests whether the readiness representation causally governs which subgoal is attacked. Data: 150 premature-onset contexts (subset of Experiment 1) where a dependency-ready subgoal is also available; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention: patch a high-readiness state (from a context where a ready subgoal is available) into the premature-onset context at the Experiment-3 layer and test whether the model switches to a dependency-ready subgoal (inversion avoided, tokens dropped). Controls: matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems preserved. Systems compared: real readiness patch vs random-direction control vs no intervention. Decisive metric: fraction of premature onsets redirected to a dependency-ready subgoal under patching, first; secondary token reduction, with accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: real patching redirects >= 50% of premature onsets and reduces tokens while the random control redirects < 15% and accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose. Indecision band: a 20-50% redirection, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% redirection or the random control matching the real direction means readiness is correlational not causal, refuting H3's causal reading.

Experiment 5 (H4 - a scheduling steer cuts tokens at equal accuracy): Tests the training-free intervention. Data: full templated set (300), puzzles (200), GSM8K sample (400), MATH500 sample (300) on the 7B model (with 1.5B and 14B-subsample replications). Online, at each subgoal onset the readiness probe is read; when it predicts low readiness (an impending inversion), a steer is applied - steering along the readiness direction, or injecting a terse 'first establish prerequisites' cue - to defer the premature subgoal. Systems compared: scheduling steer vs no intervention vs length-aware filtering vs reactive pruning vs decorative-step skipping vs fixed truncation. Decisive metric: token reduction at matched accuracy (accuracy within 1 point of no-intervention), first; secondary inversion-rate reduction and wall-clock speedup, on overall and hardest strata. Convincing: the scheduling steer cuts mean thinking tokens by >= 15% within 1 point of baseline accuracy and beats the length-aware and reactive-pruning baselines at matched accuracy, with a measurable inversion-rate drop. Indecision band: a 5-15% token reduction, or parity with (not beating) the strongest baseline, is a marginal result. Negative result: < 5% reduction or > 2 point accuracy loss means scheduling steering is not an efficiency win, refuting H4.

Experiment 6 (H4 specificity and generalization - beneficial-exploration guard and transfer): Tests that suppressing inversions does not remove genuinely useful exploration, and whether probe/steer transfer. Data: reuses Experiment 5 runs plus a hand-labeled subset where an apparent inversion is beneficial exploration (the model probes a subgoal to discover its prerequisites). Transfer: apply the 7B-derived readiness probe and steer to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting; correlate inversion rate with DAG width/depth. Systems compared: steer with vs without the beneficial-exploration guard threshold; in-model vs transferred probe/steer; low- vs high-width/depth DAGs. Decisive metric: accuracy on beneficial-exploration items under the guarded steer, first; plus transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-model and the inversion-rate/DAG-complexity correlation. Convincing: the guarded steer preserves beneficial-exploration accuracy within 1 point of no-intervention while still cutting tokens elsewhere, transferred probe retains >= 70% of in-model AUROC, and inversion rate rises with DAG width/depth. Indecision band: transferred AUROC 40-70% of in-model, or a beneficial-exploration accuracy loss of 1-3 points, is weak/partial. Negative result: the guard failing to protect beneficial exploration (> 3 point loss) or transferred AUROC < 40% means the intervention is unsafe or idiosyncratic, bounding H4's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Annotating a ground-truth subgoal DAG for open math is noisy; we anchor the strongest claims on templated problems and puzzles with known structure, using GSM8K/MATH500 as corroboration with human-validated annotations. Aligning generated subgoals to DAG nodes is imperfect; we use semantic matching + LLM-judge with agreement reporting. Some scheduling 'inversions' may be legitimate exploration (probing a subgoal to learn its prerequisites), so suppressing them could hurt accuracy; the failure analysis and steer thresholds explicitly guard this, and finding that inversions are largely beneficial would be an informative negative result. The readiness signal may be inseparable from generic difficulty/confidence, weakening the mechanistic framing; the separability analysis and causal patching address this. Steering could push activations off-distribution and introduce errors; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Intervention gains may not exceed strong length-aware or pruning baselines, but the scheduling-failure diagnosis (a named, quantifiable, dependency-structured source of overthinking) is a standalone contribution. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

Name: expected_value_of_control
Title: Worth the Thought: Do Reward and Efficacy Framings Modulate How Hard Reasoning Models Think, via an Internal Value Signal?
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the Expected-Value-of-Control theory from cognitive neuroscience, we hypothesize that reasoning LLMs allocate more thinking compute (tokens, verification) to the identical problem when the prompt frames the answer as high-reward or as one where effort is highly efficacious, and LESS when a high opportunity cost of time is signalled, even though difficulty and the correct answer are unchanged. We test whether this reward/efficacy/opportunity-cost modulation is carried by an internal value representation (a hypothesized proxy, possibly the reported LLM value neurons) read at the prompt boundary that patching, steering, and ablation can move independent of difficulty. We prioritize the reward and efficacy axes and treat opportunity cost as exploratory.
Related Work: Cognitive neuroscience robustly shows humans allocate cognitive effort by weighing expected reward, efficacy (how much effort changes outcome), and the opportunity cost of time / average reward rate: Expected-Value-of-Control theory (Shenhav; 'When effort matters' 2020 shows reward and efficacy separately modulate control allocation), and reward-rate/opportunity-cost studies (2022, 2025) show MORE reward at stake or higher efficacy raises effort while high average reward rate LOWERS it. In LLMs, a 'Sparse Reward Subsystem' (2026) identifies value neurons encoding state value critical to reasoning, and Latent Thinking Optimization (2025) shows latent thoughts encode reward signals. Efficient-reasoning interpretability (LLMs Encode Their Failures 2026; FR-Ponder 2025; When More is Less 2025; Efficiency Steering 2025) reads a scalar DIFFICULTY/length signal to allocate compute, always under a fixed, neutral framing, and treats compute as difficulty-driven. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether framing the problem's REWARD, EFFICACY, or OPPORTUNITY COST changes how much a reasoning model thinks on identical problems, dissociates this from genuine difficulty, or ties it to a value representation. To our knowledge no prior LLM work decomposes effort allocation along all three EVC axes: we (a) transfer Expected-Value-of-Control to reasoning LLMs as a compute-allocation phenomenon driven by reward/efficacy/opportunity-cost framing, (b) dissociate it from difficulty, and (c) test whether a hypothesized value signal (plausibly the value neurons of the Sparse Reward Subsystem) mediates it via patching, steering, and ablation. This is orthogonal to all my prior overthinking proposals (which assume neutral prompts) and sharper than difficulty-budgeting work because it manipulates motivational value, not difficulty.
Abstract: Cognitive neuroscience shows humans decide how much mental effort to invest by weighing three motivational quantities: the reward at stake, the efficacy of effort (how much it changes the outcome), and the opportunity cost of time. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit an analog of this Expected-Value-of-Control computation. Our delta over generic incentive-sensitivity ('artificial effort') work is a multi-axis decomposition -- reward vs efficacy vs opportunity cost -- not a single incentive knob. We construct matched prompts holding a math or science problem's content and correct answer fixed while varying only motivational framing: high vs low reward, high vs low efficacy, and high vs low opportunity cost, with an irrelevant-framing placebo and length-matched phrasings so effects cannot reduce to wording or prompt length. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure reasoning tokens, verification, and accuracy, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate framing from difficulty; we prioritize reward and efficacy and treat opportunity cost as exploratory. We predict high reward and high efficacy increase thinking while high opportunity cost decreases it. Mechanistically, we test one falsifiable hypothesis: a prompt-boundary value/effort direction predicts reasoning length beyond a difficulty probe and shifts sign-correctly with framing. We treat it as a hypothesized proxy -- possibly overlapping reported value neurons -- and validate it causally via patching, steering, and ablation with random-direction controls, separating 'changes tokens' from 'changes correctness'. The primary payoff is for eval-validity and test-time-compute control: motivational framing is a hidden confounder in benchmark comparability, and the value direction offers a training-free knob.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (problem, framing) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. To keep the framing matrix affordable we prioritize the reward and efficacy axes and subsample problems per cell (below). Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - reward, efficacy, and opportunity-cost framing modulate thinking effort in the predicted directions): Tests whether high reward and high efficacy raise thinking tokens/verification and high opportunity cost lowers them, on identical problems. Data: constructed from existing sets - GSM8K test (1319; sample 200), MATH500 (500; sample 200), AIME 2024+2025 (60; all), GPQA-Diamond (198; all); 658 seed problems, expanded across three framing axes each at high/low plus a neutral baseline (7 cells per problem) x 5 seeds x 4 models. Axes: REWARD ('a lot rides on getting this right' vs 'this is just a throwaway question'), EFFICACY ('careful step-by-step reasoning strongly determines correctness here' vs 'the answer is largely luck no matter how hard you think'), OPPORTUNITY COST ('you have a long queue of other urgent problems' vs 'there is nothing else to do; take all the time you need'). Content and gold answer are verified identical after stripping the framing sentence. Verification depth = self-check/recheck step count via lexical cues plus a reflection-direction classifier. Systems compared: each axis's high vs low vs neutral, within problem and model. Decisive metric: within-problem paired token difference per axis (high minus low), as a median relative change, first; secondary verification change and accuracy (to confirm extra effort is not merely error-correction). Convincing: high reward and high efficacy each raise tokens by >= 10% median relative, and high opportunity cost lowers tokens by >= 10%, all in the predicted sign under paired Wilcoxon tests (Holm-corrected across axes and models). Indecision band: a 4-10% effect on an axis, or a mixed sign across models, does not decide H1 for that axis. Negative result: < 4% on an axis, or a sign opposite to the human-EVC prediction, refutes H1 for that axis (an opposite sign is still a reportable characterization but rejects the hypothesis as written).

Experiment 2 (H1 dissociation - the framing effect requires motivational content and is not difficulty or length): Tests that framing effects survive difficulty and prompt-length controls and require motivational content. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces plus an irrelevant-framing placebo cell (a neutral comment about the weather) matched in length. Analysis: mixed-effects models of thinking length (and accuracy) with a random intercept per problem identity (difficulty) and fixed effects for each framing axis and raw prompt token count; supported by length-matched phrasings and the placebo. On a 150-problem subsample, truncate-and-resume estimates minimal-solve length to test whether high-reward/high-efficacy framing inflates the beyond-minimal (wasted) portion rather than adding needed reasoning. Systems compared: framing coefficients with vs without difficulty random effect and prompt-length covariate; motivational framings vs the irrelevant placebo. Decisive metric: standardized framing-axis coefficients on thinking length after controls, first; plus the placebo coefficient (expected ~0). Convincing: reward and efficacy coefficients remain significant after controls with the placebo coefficient not significant, and >= 60% of the reward/efficacy extra tokens fall in the wasted portion. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or a placebo effect of similar-but-smaller magnitude, is partial support. Negative result: framing coefficients vanishing under controls, or the placebo reproducing the effect, means the modulation was a length/lexical artifact, refuting the dissociation part of H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - a value/effort representation at the prompt boundary carries the framing effect and is separable from difficulty): Tests whether the boundary residual stream encodes a value signal that predicts reasoning length beyond a difficulty probe and shifts with framing. Data: final-prompt-token activations for the Experiment 1 problems across framing cells, split 70/15/15 by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probes: (i) a ridge length probe (target = observed thinking length), (ii) a value probe fit by regressing activations on the framing-induced value level, and (iii) a true-difficulty probe (target = pass-rate); we additionally screen for individual high-weight units as candidate 'value neurons'. Systems compared: for identical problems, does the length-probe prediction rise with reward/efficacy and fall with opportunity cost; principal angle between the value/effort direction and the difficulty direction plus joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: incremental R2 of the value direction for predicting reasoning length over the difficulty probe on held-out problems, first; plus the sign-correct monotone shift of the length-probe prediction across framing levels and the value/difficulty principal angle. Convincing: the value direction adds >= 0.05 R2 over difficulty (significant), the length-probe prediction moves in the predicted sign across all three axes, and the value direction is not collinear with difficulty (angle >= 30 degrees). Indecision band: incremental R2 0.02-0.05, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: incremental R2 < 0.02, no sign-correct shift, or collinearity with difficulty (angle < 20 degrees), means the framing effect is not carried by a distinct value representation, refuting H2's location claim.

Experiment 4 (H2 causal + H3 - patching/steering/ablating the value representation moves reasoning length independent of difficulty): Tests whether editing the value representation changes reasoning length as predicted. Data: 150 problems (subset of Experiment 1) each with matched high- and low-value variants per axis; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention A (patching): patch the boundary state from a high-reward (or high-efficacy) variant into the matched low-value pass (expect length rise), and reverse for opportunity cost, at the Experiment-3 layer. Intervention B (steering): steer along the value/effort direction (difference-of-means high minus low value) to (a) cancel each axis's framing gap and (b) fix all framings to a common effort target; dose swept over 4 magnitudes. Intervention C (neuron ablation): ablate the candidate value neurons from Experiment 3 and test whether framing sensitivity collapses. Controls: matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems; comparison to a prompt-based fix (stripping framing) and to a scalar length-steering baseline. Systems compared: real patch/steer/ablation vs random-direction control vs no intervention vs prompt-strip vs scalar length steering. Decisive metric: fraction of the high-vs-low value length gap opened by patching (and closed by reverse patching), first; plus the reduction in the framing length gap under steering, with accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: patching moves length in the predicted direction closing >= 50% of the gap, steering shrinks the framing gap by >= 50% and ablating the value neurons removes >= 50% of framing sensitivity, while a matched-random direction does < 15%, monotone in dose, accuracy preserved. Indecision band: a 20-50% effect, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% effect, or the random control matching the value direction, means reasoning length is not causally carried by the value representation, refuting H2's causal claim and H3.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 modulators, combination, and transfer): Tests whether reward and efficacy combine as in human EVC and whether the value probe/steering transfer. Data: reuses Experiment 1 problems and derived vectors, plus a reward x efficacy factorial cell set and a monetary-reward framing ('you earn a stated bonus for a correct answer'). Transfer: apply the 7B-derived value probe and steering vector to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting; compare RL-tuned models (with explicit reward history) vs distilled models. Systems compared: reward-only vs efficacy-only vs combined cells; monetary vs importance framing; subtle vs explicit strength; in-model vs transferred vectors; RL-tuned vs distilled. Decisive metric: the interaction term between reward and efficacy on thinking length, first; plus transferred-vector gap-closing relative to in-model. Convincing: reward and efficacy combine at least additively (a significant positive joint effect), and transferred steering retains >= 70% of its in-model gap-closing effect. Indecision band: a transferred effect 40-70% of in-model, or an interaction within noise, is weak generalization. Negative result: no reward-efficacy combination and transferred effect < 40% means the phenomenon does not follow EVC structure and is idiosyncratic, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The framing effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences rather than motivational content per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, neutral baseline, and irrelevant-framing placebo isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. Effects may be small or absent in strongly instruction/safety-tuned models trained to behave identically regardless of stakes (a valuable boundary condition). The direction of some effects (especially opportunity cost) may not match human predictions - still a publishable characterization. The value/effort signal may be inseparable from a generic difficulty or sycophancy direction; the separability analysis, patching, value-neuron reuse, and difficulty-probe comparison address this, and overlap with the reported LLM value neurons would be a positive mechanistic finding rather than a confound. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Multiple framing axes and levels create a large prompt matrix; we subsample problems per cell and prioritize the reward and efficacy axes. Effects and their sign may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: isolation_induced_overthinking
Title: Alone With the Problem: Isolation-Induced Overthinking and the Attention-Fixation Mechanism Behind It
Short Hypothesis: The identical problem induces substantially more overthinking (reasoning tokens, self-doubt loops) when presented alone than when embedded among unrelated peer problems in the same context. We are explicit about what is already known versus new. KNOWN (behavioral): batch prompting reduces reasoning tokens at preserved accuracy. NEW (phenomenon): on matched targets, isolation vs peer-context is a controlled, length-dissociated overthinking effect, not just a throughput trick. NEW (mechanism, the core claim): the effect is causally driven by the model over-allocating attention to its lone input question, so that peers work by DILUTING attention-to-own-question and defusing the first-impression bias that drives redundant reflection. NEW (intervention): directly capping attention-to-own-question during isolated generation reproduces the peer-context token savings without peers, at equal accuracy. We narrow to two falsifiable claims — the length-controlled behavioral effect, and the attention-fixation causal mechanism — and preregister that the mechanistic claim (capping reproduces the savings; random-head/non-question caps do not) is the novel contribution even if the behavioral effect is merely replicated; conversely, if capping fails to reproduce the savings we conclude batch prompting works via a different route (e.g. pattern induction), an informative negative. Downstream, this implies reasoning-model benchmarks that test problems in isolation systematically over-estimate deployed (batched) overthinking, so evaluation protocols may need context-controlled or batched conditions; it benefits evaluation designers and inference-efficiency practitioners (same accuracy, fewer tokens, lower cost).
Related Work: We distinguish three candidate accounts and our delta. (1) Resource competition / batch prompting (Srivastava et al. 2025) empirically cuts reasoning tokens ~76% when queries share a context, attributed loosely to reduced per-query effort and hedging suppression, but offers NO mechanistic account and does not isolate which effect matters. (2) First-impression bias (The First Impression Problem, 2025) shows overthinking is triggered by an internal bias from the input question via EXCESSIVE ATTENTION to it, but only for a single isolated problem, never varying context composition. (3) Pattern induction — peers could teach a terse solving pattern rather than dilute attention — is the alternative mechanism our causal test adjudicates. We unify (1) and (2): peer context defuses the first-impression bias by diluting attention-to-own-question, and we causally test this against the pattern-induction alternative via same-question attention capping. Distinct from batch-prompting work (behavioral throughput trick), first-impression work (single isolated problem), and our prior overthinking proposals (within-single-problem dynamics under a fixed isolated prompt), our contribution is a matched-problem isolation phenomenon, an attention-fixation mechanism, and a training-free attention-dilution intervention.
Abstract: Reasoning models overthink—but almost all study of this assumes a problem is presented alone, exactly the format that may most inflate it. We identify a new phenomenon: isolation-induced overthinking. The identical problem, presented alone, provokes substantially more reasoning tokens and more self-doubt loops than when it is embedded among unrelated peer problems in the same context, even though its content, difficulty, and correct answer are unchanged. We further propose a mechanism unifying two disconnected findings—that batch prompting cheaply suppresses overthinking, and that overthinking is triggered by excessive attention to the input question: we hypothesize that peer context works by DILUTING the model's attention to its own question, defusing the first-impression bias that drives redundant reflection. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we hold the target problem fixed and vary only the number and nature of surrounding peer problems, measuring per-target reasoning tokens, self-doubt behavior, and accuracy. Mechanistically, we measure attention mass directed at the target's own question tokens as a function of peer count, test whether it predicts the overthinking reduction, localize the attention-fixation heads, and causally validate by directly capping attention-to-own-question during isolated generation—testing whether this reproduces the peer-context token savings without peers. We compare against batch prompting and length steering. Our work reveals that how a problem is packaged silently sets how hard a model overthinks it, and traces this to a manipulable attention-fixation mechanism.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B thinking mode); the reflection-direction classifier is the only trained linear component. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Targets come from existing sets used as-is: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). We CONSTRUCT matched contexts by embedding each target among peer problems drawn from a DIFFERENT topic/difficulty. Compute forces subsampling for the multi-context conditions: 400 GSM8K, 400 MATH500, all 60 AIME, all 198 GPQA, each presented in all peer conditions, 3 seeds. Per-target tokens and accuracy are parsed from the multi-problem response by answer delimiters.

Experiment 1 (H1 — isolation-induced overthinking): Tests whether the same target uses more reasoning tokens alone than among unrelated peers, at preserved accuracy. Data: each target presented (a) alone or (b) among N unrelated peers, N in {1,2,4,8}, target position randomized; plus an irrelevant-filler control (matched-length padding that is NOT peer problems). Measures on the target only: reasoning-token count, self-doubt/hedging events (lexical cues plus the reflection-direction classifier, validated on 200 held-out labeled steps with AUROC reported), and accuracy. Decisive metric FIRST: within-target reasoning tokens as a function of peer count, at matched target accuracy. Convincing result: target reasoning tokens decrease monotonically with peer count by >= 20% from N=0 to N=8 while target accuracy stays within 1 point, in >=3 of 4 models on >=3 of 4 datasets, AND peer problems reduce tokens more than the length-matched filler (isolating peer presence from length). Indecision band: token reduction 8-20%, or the peer-vs-filler gap CI overlaps 0 — a modest or length-driven effect, reported as limited. Negative result (no reduction, or filler matches peers): isolation-induced overthinking does not exist or is a pure length effect; H1 fails.

Experiment 2 (H1 — dissociation from length and position): Tests that the effect is peer-problem presence, not context length or serial position. Data: Experiment-1 conditions plus target-position variants (first/middle/last). Analysis: mixed-effects model of target reasoning length with random effect for target identity and fixed effects for peer count and raw context length. Decisive metric FIRST: the peer-count fixed effect after absorbing target identity and length. Convincing result: peer-count effect survives (CI excluding 0) with identity and length absorbed, and is not explained by target position. Indecision band: peer-count effect present but the peer-vs-length-matched-filler gap CI overlaps 0 — possibly length. Negative result (effect vanishes after controls): the phenomenon is a length/position artifact; H1 fails.

Experiment 3 (H1 — wasted vs genuine compute): Tests that peer context cuts WASTED tokens and self-doubt loops, not genuine reasoning. Data: 200 items/dataset with truncate-and-resume minimal-solve length per condition. Decisive metric FIRST: reduction in wasted tokens (beyond minimal solve) and self-doubt events with peer count, with accuracy preserved or improved. Convincing result: peer context reduces wasted tokens and self-doubt events (CI excluding 0) while minimal-solve length is unchanged and accuracy is preserved or improved. Indecision band: minimal-solve length itself drops with peers (5-15%) — peers may change genuine solving, reported as partly confounded. Negative result (peers cut minimal-solve or hurt accuracy): the savings are not clean overthinking reduction; the framing weakens.

Experiment 4 (H2 — attention-fixation mechanism): Tests that attention to the target's own question tokens is highest in isolation, dilutes with peers, and predicts the overthinking level. Data: attention traces during target reasoning across peer counts, 200 items/dataset. Measures: attention mass on the target's own question tokens vs peer count; head-attribution to localize the fixation heads. Decisive metric FIRST: the incremental R^2 of attention-to-own-question in predicting target reasoning tokens, over peer count and target difficulty. Convincing result: attention-to-own-question falls monotonically with peer count and adds >= 0.05 R^2 over peer count and difficulty (CI excluding 0), with a localizable head set carrying the effect. Indecision band: incremental R^2 0.02-0.05 — attention is a weak mediator, reported as suggestive. Negative result (attention does not track overthinking, or does not dilute with peers): the attention-fixation account is wrong; H2 fails (batch prompting may work by another route, e.g. pattern induction — an informative negative).

Experiment 5 (H2 causal — capping attention reproduces the savings): Tests that directly capping attention-to-own-question in ISOLATION reproduces the peer-context token savings without peers. Data: 300 targets generated alone. Intervention: cap/downweight attention to the target's own question tokens on the Experiment-4 fixation heads (attention masking/rescaling); frozen weights; dose-response over cap strength; plus a reverse test amplifying attention-to-own-question in a peer context. Systems compared: (i) no cap, (ii) fixation-head cap, (iii) cap on matched-random heads (no-effect control), (iv) cap on non-question tokens (specificity), (v) off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: reduction in isolated-generation reasoning tokens and self-doubt events under the fixation-head cap versus controls, accuracy preserved. Convincing result: the fixation-head cap reproduces >= half the peer-context token savings in isolation with CI excluding 0, monotone in cap strength, not reproduced by random-head or non-question caps, accuracy within 1 point; the reverse amplification restores overthinking. Indecision band: savings 20-50% of the peer effect, or random/non-question caps giving >=50% of it — causality not clean. Negative result (capping does not reproduce savings): attention fixation is not the causal route; H2's causal claim and the intervention (H3) fail.

Experiment 6 (H3 — intervention comparison and application): Tests that attention dilution cuts tokens without hurting accuracy and situates it against alternatives. Data: full evaluation sets, 3 seeds. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) peer-context (batch) prompting, (c) our attention-cap in isolation, (d) length/verbosity steering, (e) fixed truncation. Decisive metric FIRST: tokens-at-equal-accuracy on the target (overall and hardest strata), plus self-doubt-event reduction. Convincing result: both peer-context and the attention-cap cut tokens by >= 20% at accuracy within 1 point overall, without a >1-point accuracy drop on the hardest stratum (no induced underthinking). Indecision band: token savings 8-20%, or a 1-3 point accuracy drop on hard items — partial, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no token savings at equal accuracy, or hard items harmed): dilution does not deliver the free savings; H3 fails. We additionally report how much isolated single-problem benchmarking over-estimates overthinking relative to batched deployment.

Experiment 7 (generalization and peer relevance): Tests transfer without retraining and the role of peer relevance and scale. Data: attention-cap and fixation-head set fit on one set+model, applied unchanged to the others and across 1.5B->14B; unrelated vs same-topic peers. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-set token savings under the transferred cap, and whether unrelated peers dilute more than same-topic peers. Convincing result: transferred cap retains >= half its in-domain savings, and peer relevance modulates the effect as predicted, with a consistent scale trend. Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or no clear relevance effect — partial generalization. Negative result (no transfer): the mechanism and intervention are idiosyncratic per model/set, reported as a boundary characterization.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The peer-context effect could be a raw context-length artifact rather than peer-problem presence; the length-matched filler control and prompt-length covariate isolate this, and a null after controls (pure length effect) is itself an informative finding. Peers could interfere with target accuracy (cross-talk) or change difficulty perception; we randomize position, use unrelated peers, and verify per-target accuracy. Attention-to-own-question is a coarse mechanism proxy and may be entangled with generic difficulty attention; head localization, the regression against difficulty, and the causal attention-cap with specificity controls address this, and a failure of capping to reproduce the effect would falsify the mechanistic claim (still a valuable negative result showing batch prompting works via a different route, e.g. pattern induction). Attention masking can push activations off-distribution and degrade coherence; matched-random-head controls and sample-validity checks are included, and over-capping could cause underthinking on hard items (measured on hardest strata). Self-doubt detection is noisy; we validate with human spot-checks. Multi-problem responses require careful per-target parsing of tokens/accuracy. Effects may be model-family and scale specific, and require models with clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

Name: phantom_tool_offloading
Title: Phantom Offloading: Do Reasoning Models Think Less When a Tool Is Merely Available But Never Used?
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the cognitive-offloading literature from human decision science, we hypothesize that reasoning LLMs reduce their internal reasoning effort (fewer thinking tokens, shallower verification, and, on offloadable problems, lower accuracy) on the exact same problem when merely TOLD a relevant tool (calculator/code interpreter) is available, EVEN WHEN the tool is never actually invoked. This 'phantom offloading' is not justified by any real computation being outsourced; we test whether it is mediated by an offloading/effort-budget state set at the prompt boundary that steering can move to remove the disparity, rather than assuming such a representation.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here. (1) Human cognitive-offloading science shows people offload more as task complexity rises (Offloading Tools in Complex Decision-Making 2023), that offloading is value-based decision-making trading internal effort against tool cost (Cognitive Offloading as Value-Based Decision Making 2023), that offloading causes forgetting of offloaded content (the 'Google effect'), and that offloading can HURT performance yet still be chosen (When Calculators Lie 2019; Offloading Tools 2023). (2) AI work on tool-use decisions reads a meta-cognition/self-assessment signal to decide WHEN to call a tool (MeCo 2025) and studies whether reasoning enhancement amplifies tool hallucination (The Reasoning Trap 2025); efficient-reasoning interpretability reads pre-generation difficulty/effort signals to allocate compute (LLMs Encode Their Failures 2026; Efficiency Steering 2025). Crucially, ALL AI tool work studies decisions about ACTUAL tool invocation and its effect on accuracy/latency; none asks whether the mere BELIEF that a tool is available (with no invocation) changes how much INTERNAL reasoning compute the model spends. And all efficient-reasoning interpretability studies a fixed tool-free setting. We are the first to (a) transfer cognitive offloading to LLMs as a compute-allocation phenomenon triggered by phantom (unused) tool availability, (b) dissociate it from genuine difficulty and from real tool use, (c) show it can degrade accuracy (a Google-effect analog), and (d) locate and causally test an offloading effort-budget representation. This is orthogonal to my prior overthinking proposals, which all assume a neutral tool-free prompt.
Abstract: Human decision science shows that when people believe an external tool (a calculator, a search engine) is available, they invest less internal cognitive effort and sometimes remember and reason worse. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit an analog: do they think less when a tool is merely available but never used? Our narrow claim is that stated-but-unused tool availability reduces internal reasoning effort on the identical problem; the offloading representation is a hypothesized mechanism we test, not assume. We construct matched prompts that hold a math or science problem's content and correct answer fixed while varying only a stated affordance ('You may use a calculator/code interpreter' vs. no such statement), and -- critically -- analyze only traces in which the model never invokes any tool, isolating belief from real offloading; a pre-registered exclusion rule and a full-trace robustness check accompany this. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure internal reasoning-token count, verification behavior, and accuracy per condition, testing via a mixed-effects decomposition whether phantom availability reduces effort independent of true difficulty, with an irrelevant-tool placebo and controls separating 'available now' from 'generally exists' and 'not allowed here'. Mirroring the human 'Google effect', we test whether phantom availability degrades accuracy on exactly the problems whose computation would have been offloaded. Mechanistically, we seek evidence consistent with a separable offloading state via probing, activation patching, and steering with random-direction controls. For agent designers and safety researchers, a robust phantom-offloading effect would mean tool affordances silently lower reasoning quality even without invocation; we provide a training-free fix.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (problem, condition) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. A trace is included only if the model never emits a tool call or executable code block (verified by parsing for tool-call syntax and fenced code); the per-condition tool-invocation rate is reported so selection is transparent. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - phantom tool availability lowers internal reasoning effort without invocation): Tests whether merely stating a relevant tool is available reduces thinking tokens and verification on the identical problem, among traces where no tool is used. Data: constructed from existing sets - GSM8K test (1319; sample 400), MATH500 (500; all), AIME 2024+2025 (60; all), GPQA-Diamond (198; all); 1158 seed problems, chosen because each is expanded into 4 conditions x 5 seeds x 4 models. Each seed problem is rendered content-identical across four conditions: (a) no tool mentioned, (b) 'A calculator is available if you wish', (c) 'A Python code interpreter is available if you wish', (d) placebo mentioning an irrelevant tool ('a dictionary is available'). Content and gold answer are verified identical after stripping the affordance sentence. Verification depth is measured as the count of self-check/recheck steps via lexical cues plus a reflection-direction classifier. Systems compared: relevant-tool conditions (b,c) vs no-tool (a) vs placebo (d), within model, on never-invoked traces. Decisive metric: within-problem paired difference in mean thinking tokens between relevant-tool and no-tool conditions, as a median relative reduction, first; secondary verification-step reduction. Convincing: median relative token reduction >= 12% for (b/c) vs (a) with a paired Wilcoxon test (Holm-corrected), while the placebo (d) shows < 4% change (isolating relevance from mere tool mention). Indecision band: a 4-12% reduction, or a placebo effect of 4-12%, does not decide H1 and blocks the mechanism experiments. Negative result: < 4% reduction, or the placebo matching the relevant tool, means phantom availability does not reduce effort and H1 is rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the reduction is not justified by difficulty, and phantom availability harms accuracy on offloadable problems - the Google-effect analog): Tests dissociation from difficulty and the predicted accuracy harm. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces; problems are pre-tagged as calculation-heavy (arithmetic offloadable to a calculator) vs reasoning-heavy. Analysis 1 (dissociation): mixed-effects model of thinking length with a random intercept per problem identity (difficulty) and fixed effects for condition and raw prompt token count; supported by length-matched phrasings. Analysis 2 (accuracy harm): compare accuracy under phantom calculator availability vs no-tool, split by calculation-heavy vs reasoning-heavy; and on a 150-problem calculation-heavy subsample use truncate-and-resume to test whether errors concentrate in the offloadable subroutine (arithmetic mistakes) rather than in general reasoning. Systems compared: condition effect with vs without difficulty random effect; calculation-heavy vs reasoning-heavy accuracy deltas. Decisive metric: standardized condition coefficient on thinking length after controls, first; plus the accuracy drop under phantom calculator availability on calculation-heavy items. Convincing: the condition coefficient stays significant after controls, AND phantom calculator availability lowers accuracy on calculation-heavy items by >= 3 points more than on reasoning-heavy items, with resume analysis showing the errors are in the offloadable subroutine. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or a 1-3 point differential accuracy harm, is partial support. Negative result: coefficient vanishing under controls, or no differential accuracy harm, refutes the effort-artifact and Google-effect claims of H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - an offloading/effort-budget representation exists at the prompt boundary and is separable from difficulty and from a tool-decision signal): Tests whether the boundary residual stream encodes an offloading signal distinct from a difficulty probe and from a meta-cognition 'should-I-use-a-tool' probe. Data: final-prompt-token activations for the Experiment 1 problems across conditions, split 70/15/15 by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probes: ridge length probe (target = observed thinking length), logistic condition classifier (tool-available vs absent), true-difficulty probe (target = pass-rate), and a MeCo-style tool-decision probe (target = whether the model would call a tool, from a tool-allowed generation). Systems compared: for identical-content problems differing only in condition, does the length-probe prediction drop under phantom availability; and principal angles among the offloading, difficulty, and tool-decision directions. Decisive metric: held-out Spearman between length-probe prediction and phantom-availability on matched problems, first; plus principal angle to the difficulty direction and to the tool-decision direction. Convincing: Spearman <= -0.3 (p<0.01) at the best layer, condition classifier above the majority baseline, principal angle to difficulty >= 30 degrees, and the offloading direction adding significant R2 over both difficulty and tool-decision probes. Indecision band: |Spearman| 0.15-0.3, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: |Spearman| < 0.15 (classifier at chance) means no readable offloading signal, refuting H3's encoding claim; high overlap (angle < 20 degrees) with the tool-decision direction would reframe it as riding the meta-cognition signal rather than a distinct effort budget.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal + H4 - the offloading representation causally mediates the drop and steering removes it): Tests whether editing the boundary representation moves reasoning length and whether steering cancels the disparity. Data: 150 problems (subset of Experiment 1, calculation-heavy weighted) each with matched tool-available and tool-absent variants; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention A (patching): patch the boundary residual state from a tool-available variant into the matched tool-absent pass at the Experiment-3 layer and measure the thinking-length change. Intervention B (debiasing steering): derive an offloading direction (difference-of-means, tool-available minus tool-absent, on the train split) and steer tool-available prompts to cancel the effort reduction (dose swept over 4 magnitudes), or steer all prompts to a fixed effort target. Controls: matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems; comparison to a prompt-based fix (removing the affordance statement). Systems compared: real patch/steer vs random control vs no intervention vs prompt-strip. Decisive metric: for patching, fraction of the tool-available-vs-absent length gap reproduced by injecting the tool-available state, first; for steering, recovery of reasoning length and of calculation-heavy accuracy, with off-target accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: patching reproduces >= 50% of the length drop and steering restores >= 50% of both the lost tokens and the lost calculation-heavy accuracy, while the random control does < 15%, monotone in dose. Indecision band: a 20-50% effect, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% effect, or the random control matching the real direction, means the representation is correlational, refuting H3's causal claim and H4's fix.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 modulators and generalization): Tests where phantom offloading is strongest and whether it transfers. Data: reuses Experiment 1 problems and derived vectors. Factors: affordance strength (subtle 'tools available' vs explicit 'the calculator will handle the arithmetic'), reliability framing ('the tool may be inaccurate' - does stated distrust restore effort, mirroring humans?), and problem difficulty. We also vary availability scope, separating 'a calculator is available now' from 'calculators generally exist' and 'a calculator exists but you may not use it here', to test whether present, usable availability (not mere mention) drives the effect. Transfer: apply the 7B-derived probe and steering vector to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting; compare RL-tuned agentic models vs distilled models for effect size. Systems compared: strong vs subtle vs distrust-framed affordances; in-model vs transferred probe; agentic-tuned vs distilled. Decisive metric: change in the phantom-offloading token reduction across each factor, first; plus transferred-probe Spearman relative to in-model. Convincing: explicit affordances produce a significantly larger reduction than subtle ones, distrust framing significantly attenuates the reduction (human-analog), and the transferred probe retains >= 70% of in-model correlation. Indecision band: transferred correlation 40-70% of in-model, or factor effects within noise, is weak generalization. Negative result: no factor modulation and transferred correlation < 40% means the effect is idiosyncratic, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences between conditions rather than the affordance per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, and the irrelevant-tool placebo isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. Restricting to never-invoked traces may induce selection bias (problems where the model chooses not to call a tool may differ); we condition on matched problems and report the tool-invocation rate per condition. The effect may be small or absent in models trained to treat tool availability neutrally (a valuable boundary condition). The offloading signal may be inseparable from difficulty or from a generic meta-cognition/tool-decision direction; the separability analysis, patching, and comparison to a MeCo-style probe address this, and overlap would itself be an interesting mechanistic finding. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters, and detecting genuine (vs described-but-not-executed) tool use requires careful parsing; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Effects and their sign may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: narration_subspace_suppression
Title: Think in Shorthand: Separating a Narration Subspace from Computation to Suppress Performative Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models carry two largely separable residual-stream subspaces: a computation subspace that carries out and updates the latent answer, and a multi-dimensional narration subspace that governs verbose, human-facing presentation of already-computed results. Overthinking is over-activation of the narration subspace after computation is effectively done. The mathematical novelty over a single verbosity/length direction is that we construct a low-rank narration subspace ORTHOGONALIZED against the answer-carrying (computation) directions by construction, so suppression provably preserves the latent answer to first order; the pre-registered criterion for the idea collapsing into prior length steering is that the narration subspace's top direction aligns with a reproduced single verbosity direction (principal angle < 20 degrees) AND projecting out the extra dimensions adds < 5% token reduction at matched accuracy. Suppressing narration while leaving computation intact makes the model think in shorthand, cutting tokens more precisely than a single direction.
Related Work: Recent work establishes that CoT is often performative or unfaithful and that latent answers form early: Reasoning Theater (2026) probes performative CoT and early-exits; TTS / 'Can Aha Moments Be Fake?' (2025) labels steps decorative vs load-bearing and finds a single steerable TrueThinking direction; State over Tokens (2025) reframes tokens as externalized state; Causal Bypass / CMI (2026) shows answers can be causally independent of CoT text; functional-metacognition work decodes single state factors (uncertainty, difficulty, task-type) as separate directions. Efficiency-steering work (Manifold Steering, CREST, ThinkEdit, ASC) steers a single verbosity/length direction. The differences, by objective / intervention / causal claim: TTS labels steps and steers one direction; verbosity steering pushes one length direction; functional-metacognition reads single scalar factors; none constructs a MULTI-DIMENSIONAL subspace decomposition of the residual stream into a computation subspace that must be preserved and a separable narration subspace that can be projected out. Our contribution is (1) constructing and causally validating these subspaces via contrastive activation collection (terse vs verbose renderings of identical computations) plus explicit orthogonalization against the answer-probe directions - which yields a genuinely different object from a verbosity direction because it is defined relative to, and removed from, the computation subspace rather than to output length; (2) showing overthinking corresponds to sustained narration-subspace activation after computation completes; (3) a training-free projection intervention finer-grained than a single length direction.
Abstract: Reasoning language models routinely 'overthink,' generating verbose chains of thought long after they have effectively solved a problem, inflating tokens, latency, and serving cost. Prior interpretability work explains this as performative or decorative reasoning and either labels steps or steers a single verbosity direction. We propose a sharper, dimensional account: the residual stream contains two largely separable subspaces - a computation subspace that performs and updates the latent answer, and a multi-dimensional narration subspace that governs verbose, human-facing presentation of already-computed results. We hypothesize that overthinking is sustained narration-subspace activation after computation completes, and that suppressing narration while preserving the orthogonal computation subspace lets the model think in shorthand with minimal accuracy loss. We construct the narration subspace via contrastive activation collection - rendering identical computations tersely versus verbosely - followed by difference-of-means, SVD, and orthogonalization against the answer-probe directions, so it is by construction distinct from a length direction. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on DeepSeek-R1 distills (1.5B-14B) and Qwen3, we verify separability by testing that suppressing narration does not degrade a latent-answer probe while suppressing computation does, and that the effect holds on spontaneous chains of thought and production-style prompts, not only contrastively elicited ones. We show narration activation stays high during overthinking after residual work reaches zero, and intervene both mid-reasoning and at generation time. We report deployment value (tokens, wall-clock, cost) at equal accuracy against verbosity steering, TTS-style pruning, and reactive early-exit, with ablations isolating each construction step. The work reframes overthinking as an over-narration mode and offers a precise, interpretable efficiency mechanism.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear probes are trainable, interventions are activation projections. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into steps; analysis restricted to extractable-answer items (math / multiple-choice). Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198); a held-out 300-problem set (disjoint from evaluation) is used to build the subspaces. A subset of everyday/production-style prompts is included to test that effects are not artifacts of curated reasoning sets.

Experiment 1 (H1 - Constructing the narration subspace, with ablated construction): Collect contrastive activation pairs by prompting the model to render the SAME worked computation tersely vs verbosely on the held-out set; compute per-layer difference-of-means and assemble a low-rank narration subspace by SVD; orthogonalize against the answer-probe directions. Build an alternative narration signal from easy-vs-hard problems. Construction ablations: (a) terse-vs-verbose contrast only, (b) orthogonalization only, (c) random subspace of the same rank, (d) reproduced single verbosity direction. Decisive metric: variance explained and rank of the narration subspace, and principal-angle alignment between the terse/verbose subspace and the easy/hard subspace, plus alignment to the single verbosity direction (for the collapse criterion). Convincing: a low-rank (<= 10-dim) subspace captures the contrast and aligns with the easy/hard signal (principal angles < 45 degrees), while retaining >= 3 dimensions not aligned with the single verbosity direction. Indecision: alignment in [45, 60] degrees. Negative (no low-rank structure or > 60 degree misalignment): a stable narration subspace cannot be constructed.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Separability from computation): Train a linear latent-answer probe on 40% of held-out problems; evaluate on 60%. Compare probe accuracy under (a) projecting out the narration subspace, (b) a matched-rank random subspace, (c) the computation subspace (answer-probe weights). Report principal angles between narration and computation. Decisive metric: latent-answer probe accuracy drop under narration removal vs. computation removal. Convincing: narration removal drops probe accuracy < 3 points (comparable to random) while computation removal drops > 20 points, with narration/computation principal angles > 60 degrees. Indecision: narration-removal drop in [3, 8] points or angles in [45, 60] degrees. Negative (narration removal drops probe > 8 points or not near-orthogonal): the subspaces are not separable, refuting H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Narration stays high after computation completes, on spontaneous CoT): Read narration-subspace activation magnitude at each step of SPONTANEOUS (not contrastively elicited) chains of thought; measure residual work via truncate-and-resume. Decisive metric: out-of-sample 5-fold R^2 of the post-completion narration-activation integral predicting wasted tokens, minus best competitor among trace length, single verbosity-direction projection, and a confidence probe. Convincing: narration stays significantly elevated after residual work hits zero and its post-completion integral beats the best competitor by >= 0.10 R^2 on at least three datasets. Indecision: advantage in [0.02, 0.10]. Negative (<= 0.02 or no sustained activation): overthinking is not specifically sustained narration.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Mid-reasoning and generation-time projection: is narration truly post-hoc?): Subtract the projection onto the narration subspace at selected layers, applied (i) only at generation-time end-phase and (ii) DURING intermediate reasoning; if narration is post-hoc presentation, mid-reasoning suppression should cut tokens without harming the latent answer, whereas suppressing computation mid-reasoning should. Coefficient and layers selected on the held-out construction problems; full accuracy-vs-token Pareto reported. Systems compared on all four datasets: narration-subspace projection vs. (a) no intervention, (b) single verbosity/length steering (ASC/Manifold-style), (c) TTS-style post-hoc pruning, (d) Reasoning-Theater-style probe early-exit, (e) fixed truncation matched to mean budget. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy, with the key comparison whether narration projection Pareto-dominates the single verbosity direction (>= 5% more reduction at matched accuracy) - and the pre-registered COLLAPSE test (extra dimensions add < 5% over the single direction => idea reduces to length steering). Secondary: mean tokens, accuracy, wall-clock latency, per-query cost. Convincing: >= 25% token reduction within 1 point on GSM8K and MATH500, strictly above the single-direction frontier.
