Indecision: reduction in [10%, 25%] or within 5% of the single direction (collapse regime) - the separability analysis (Experiments 1-2) is then the standalone contribution. Negative (< 10% or worse than single direction): the subspace method adds nothing.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Qualitative: shorthand, not damage): Under narration suppression, an LLM-judge plus human spot-check (200 traces, two annotators) rate whether derivation steps are preserved while decorative narration/verification asides are dropped. Decisive metric: fraction of suppressed traces preserving all load-bearing derivation steps. Convincing: >= 85% preserve load-bearing steps while dropping narration, kappa > 0.6. Indecision: [70%, 85%]. Negative (< 70%): suppression damages computation.

Experiment 6 (H3 - Controls and underthinking): Control for prompt style, answer difficulty, and token budget; on the hardest quartile where narration may overlap genuine verification, measure accuracy drop vs. suppression strength. Decisive metric: hard-item accuracy drop at the deployed coefficient, and stability of savings across prompt styles/difficulty. Convincing: hard-item accuracy drops < 1 point at the coefficient delivering Experiment-4 savings, savings stable across prompt styles. Indecision: 1-3 point drop. Negative (> 3 point drop): narration suppression harms genuine verification, bounding H3.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 - Generality across data, scale, and family): Transfer the narration subspace across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models (>= 2 families) without recomputation. Decisive metric: separability asymmetry (Experiment-2 probe-drop) and token savings under a transferred subspace, relative to in-domain. Convincing: transferred subspace retains the separability asymmetry and >= 80% of in-domain savings on at least three scales. Indecision: 60-80% retention. Negative (< 60%): the narration subspace is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The clean separation of narration and computation may not hold - verification/narration can carry genuine computation, so suppression might harm hard problems; this trade-off is measured directly and a near-null separability result is itself informative. Contrastive terse/verbose prompting may not match spontaneous overthinking; we mitigate with an easy-vs-hard alternative signal and explicitly test on spontaneous CoT and production-style prompts. Latent-answer probes are reliable mainly for extractable answers, so we restrict to math/multiple-choice. The narration subspace may collapse into the single verbosity direction, in which case the pre-registered collapse criterion fires and the dimensional framing yields little gain over prior steering (the separability analysis remains a contribution). Projection at generation time can push activations off-distribution; coefficient sweeps and validity checks address this. Deployment adopters are reasoning-model servers and agent frameworks that pay per token; the mechanism must beat simpler early-exit/length steering to be adopted, which Experiment 4 tests head-on. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: conciseness_capability_entanglement
Title: The Conciseness Cliff: Why Global Brevity Steering Fails Because the Concise Direction Is Entangled with Difficulty-Appropriate Elaboration
Short Hypothesis: Training-free brevity steering has a sharp accuracy cliff not because the steering strength is mis-tuned, but because the 'concise-reasoning' direction is geometrically entangled with a 'difficulty-appropriate elaboration' capability in the same activation subspace: pushing toward brevity necessarily suppresses the model's own signal for when a problem needs more thinking. Disentangling brevity from this elaboration component yields steering that compresses easy reasoning while preserving hard-problem elaboration, eliminating the cliff.
Related Work: A wave of training-free brevity-steering methods treat conciseness as a single (often linear) direction to inject: ASC (steer residual stream, KL-bounded strength), Efficiency Steering (single contrastive direction), FlowSteer (nonlinear flow-matching transport), STU-PID (PID-controlled adaptive strength), and GLoRE (long-CoT is a general, transferable capability across domains). All of these either (a) assume brevity is a clean, universally-good direction and manage only its magnitude, or (b) add an external controller/classifier to modulate strength reactively. None asks WHY fixed steering has an accuracy cliff at the mechanistic level, nor whether the brevity direction is intrinsically coupled to the model's internal 'how much to elaborate' signal. GLoRE shows the long-CoT capability is a general encoded direction; we hypothesize the concise direction partially anti-aligns with a difficulty-appropriate elaboration capability, so global steering is not merely too strong but structurally destructive on hard problems. Our contribution is a mechanistic account of the failure mode (entanglement), a geometric measurement of it (principal angles / overlap between the brevity direction and an elaboration-capability direction), and a disentangled steering intervention that removes the harmful component — distinct from all prior 'steer harder / steer adaptively' methods.
Abstract: Training-free brevity steering promises to cut reasoning tokens with no retraining, but every method shares a fragile behavior: past a threshold, accuracy collapses sharply, especially on hard problems. Prior work manages this only by tuning or adaptively controlling the steering magnitude. We propose a mechanistic explanation: the 'concise-reasoning' steering direction is geometrically entangled with a difficulty-appropriate elaboration capability the model uses to decide how much to think, so pushing toward brevity does not merely shorten output -- it suppresses the internal signal that hard problems need more reasoning. We define elaboration operationally as a difference-of-means direction from correctness-conditioned contrasts (hard problems solved with long reasoning vs easy problems solved short) and require it to predict per-problem reasoning length beyond difficulty, confidence, and correctness probes; the entanglement hypothesis is pre-registered to be falsified if the brevity and elaboration directions overlap no more than a random-direction null. This predicts an asymmetric cliff (harmless on easy problems, destructive on hard ones). Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) reproduce the brevity direction (ASC/Efficiency-Steering) and map the accuracy-vs-strength cliff by difficulty; (2) measure geometric overlap/anti-alignment via principal angles; (3) causally test entanglement by component-wise steering -- the elaboration-parallel component alone should reproduce the cliff, the orthogonal component alone should compress without it; and (4) show disentangled steering compresses easy reasoning while preserving hard-problem elaboration, flattening the cliff versus ASC, Efficiency Steering, and STU-PID at matched token savings. Beyond one benchmark, this reframes the brevity-accuracy tradeoff as a general latent-capability entanglement problem and offers an interpretable, training-free fix that saves reasoning tokens at fixed accuracy.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only difference-of-means steering directions and linear probes are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per problem with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; accuracy is mean exact-match and length the mean thinking-token count. Difficulty strata are set by empirical per-problem pass-rate plus benchmark-provided levels: GSM8K and MATH500 (levels 1-2) as the easy strata, AIME 2024+2025 and GPQA-Diamond (and MATH500 level 5) as the hard strata. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - the brevity-steering accuracy cliff is asymmetric, hitting hard problems earlier): Tests whether a reproduced brevity direction produces a sharper, earlier accuracy cliff on hard problems than easy ones. Data: existing sets used as is - GSM8K test (1319; sample 400 for the easy stratum), MATH500 (500; all, stratified by level), AIME 2024+2025 (60; all), GPQA-Diamond (198; all). The brevity direction is extracted by difference-of-means over paired verbose/concise traces on a held-out 300-problem calibration set (ASC / Efficiency-Steering protocol), disjoint from the evaluation sets. Systems compared: increasing steering strength (a sweep of >= 8 magnitudes) within each difficulty stratum. Decisive metric: the steering strength at which each stratum's accuracy drops 5 points from its unsteered baseline (the cliff onset), first; plus the mean-token reduction at that strength. Convincing: the hard-stratum cliff onset occurs at a steering strength at least 2x smaller than the easy-stratum onset (the predicted asymmetry), replicated on at least the 7B and 14B models. Indecision band: a hard/easy onset ratio between 1.3x and 2x is weak asymmetry that does not firmly establish H1. Negative result: a ratio below 1.3x (the cliff hits both strata at similar strength) means the cliff is not difficulty-asymmetric, refuting H1 and pointing to a pure magnitude/off-distribution cause.

Experiment 2 (H2 location - an elaboration-capability direction exists and predicts difficulty-appropriate length): Tests whether a difference-of-means 'difficulty-appropriate elaboration' direction can be extracted and validated. Data: correctness-conditioned contrastive pairs from the Experiment 1 sets - hard problems solved correctly with long reasoning vs easy problems solved correctly with short reasoning - to isolate elaboration from mere errors; per layer difference-of-means gives the elaboration direction, with a 70/15/15 split by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Validation: (i) steering along the elaboration direction should lengthen reasoning preferentially on problems the model treats as hard; (ii) a probe along it should predict per-problem reasoning length beyond a raw difficulty probe (pass-rate). Systems compared: elaboration probe vs raw difficulty probe. Decisive metric: incremental R2 of the elaboration direction for predicting reasoning length over the difficulty probe on held-out problems, first; plus the hard-vs-easy differential lengthening when steering along it. Convincing: the elaboration direction adds >= 0.05 R2 over difficulty and lengthens hard-problem reasoning significantly more than easy-problem reasoning. Indecision band: incremental R2 0.02-0.05 is a present-but-weakly-distinct direction. Negative result: incremental R2 < 0.02 (the elaboration direction is indistinguishable from raw difficulty) undercuts the entanglement claim's second term and weakens H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 geometry - the brevity direction is anti-aligned with the elaboration direction): Tests whether the two directions overlap geometrically rather than being orthogonal. Data: the brevity direction (Experiment 1) and elaboration direction (Experiment 2) per layer on the 7B model (with 1.5B and 14B for stability). Systems compared: the brevity/elaboration principal angle (and signed cosine) against a matched-random-direction null distribution of equal dimension. We also decompose the brevity direction into its projection onto the elaboration direction (candidate harmful component) and its orthogonal complement (candidate benign compression component). Decisive metric: the cosine overlap (signed) between brevity and elaboration relative to the random-direction null, first. Convincing: the brevity direction is significantly anti-aligned with elaboration (negative cosine whose magnitude exceeds the 99th percentile of the random-null overlap) at the layers where steering is applied. Indecision band: an overlap magnitude between the 90th and 99th percentile of the null is weak entanglement. Negative result: overlap within the null (below the 90th percentile) means the directions are effectively orthogonal, refuting the entanglement mechanism of H2 (and implying the cliff is a pure magnitude effect).

Experiment 4 (H2 causal - the elaboration-parallel component of brevity causes the cliff): Tests whether the harmful damage comes specifically from the entangled component. Data: 200 problems spanning easy and hard strata (subset of Experiment 1); frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Systems compared, all at matched dose sweeps: (a) steering along the full brevity direction, (b) along the elaboration-orthogonal component only, (c) along the elaboration-parallel component only, plus matched-random-projection controls of equal norm. Decisive metric: hard-stratum accuracy drop per unit compression for each component, first (i.e., accuracy cost at matched token savings). Convincing: the parallel component (c) reproduces most (>= 60%) of the full direction's hard-stratum accuracy damage while giving little compression, and the orthogonal component (b) delivers comparable compression to the full direction with a hard-stratum cliff onset at least 2x later, both beyond the random-projection controls. Indecision band: the parallel component carrying 30-60% of the damage is partial support for the entanglement-causes-cliff claim. Negative result: the parallel component causing < 30% of the damage, or the orthogonal component not deferring the cliff, means the cliff is not driven by the entangled component, refuting the causal core of H2.

Experiment 5 (H3 - disentangled steering compresses easy reasoning while preserving hard elaboration, flattening the cliff): Tests the training-free fix. Data: full GSM8K sample (400), MATH500 (500), AIME (60), GPQA (198) on the 7B model (with 1.5B and 14B-subsample replications). Intervention: steer along the elaboration-orthogonal brevity component, optionally difficulty-gated using the elaboration probe. Systems compared: disentangled steering vs no steering vs full-direction ASC vs Efficiency Steering vs STU-PID vs fixed truncation (FlowSteer included only if reproducible in budget). Decisive metric: hard-stratum cliff position (steering strength at which hard-stratum accuracy drops 5 points) for disentangled vs full-direction steering, first; plus token-reduction-at-equal-accuracy overall and per stratum. Convincing: disentangled steering Pareto-dominates full-direction steering - at matched overall token savings its hard-stratum accuracy drop is smaller by >= 3 points and its cliff onset is >= 2x later - and it matches or beats STU-PID at equal accuracy. Indecision band: a 1-3 point hard-stratum accuracy advantage, or parity with (not beating) STU-PID, is a marginal win. Negative result: no Pareto improvement over full-direction steering (hard-stratum advantage < 1 point) means disentangling does not remove the cliff, refuting H3.

Experiment 6 (H3 generalization - the fix and the entanglement geometry transfer across datasets and scales): Tests whether the directions and intervention transfer without recomputation and whether the geometry is stable. Data: reuses Experiment 1-5 directions. Transfer: apply the 7B-derived brevity and elaboration directions and the disentangled intervention to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without recomputing them; measure the brevity/elaboration overlap across the four models. Systems compared: in-model vs transferred directions; overlap geometry across model families. Decisive metric: the disentangled intervention's cliff-flattening advantage under transferred directions relative to in-model, first; plus the cross-model consistency of the anti-alignment sign. Convincing: transferred directions retain >= 70% of the in-model hard-stratum advantage and the anti-alignment sign is consistent across all four models. Indecision band: transferred advantage 40-70% of in-model, or the sign consistent on three of four models, is weak generalization. Negative result: transferred advantage < 40% or an inconsistent anti-alignment sign means the entanglement geometry is model-specific and the fix does not transfer, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The brevity and elaboration directions may turn out to be largely orthogonal (no entanglement), refuting the mechanistic claim — this would be an informative negative result showing the cliff is purely a magnitude/off-distribution effect, and prior adaptive-strength methods (STU-PID) already suffice. The elaboration direction may be inseparable from a raw difficulty direction; we control by comparing predictive gain over a difficulty probe and by using correctness-conditioned contrasts. Projecting the brevity direction into a subspace may itself push activations off-distribution and reduce compression benefit, narrowing the Pareto gain; we sweep and report validity. Difficulty stratification for open math is noisy; we use empirical pass-rates and benchmark-provided levels. Reproducing FlowSteer/other baselines may be infeasible in an academic budget; we prioritize ASC, Efficiency Steering, and STU-PID as the core comparisons. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and the entanglement magnitude may vary with instruction/RL tuning. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters.

Name: notation_mode_economy
Title: Thinking in Prose When Symbols Would Do: A Notation-Mode Representation That Sets a Surface-Form Compute Tax in Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models default to a verbose natural-language 'narration mode' for computations that could be expressed in a far terser symbolic/equational mode carrying identical logical content, incurring a surface-notation compute tax independent of the problem's genuine reasoning depth. The novel, testable core is not that symbols save tokens (obvious) but that WHICH mode the model uses is set by a single linearly-decodable notation-mode representation at the prompt boundary, BEFORE any reasoning token is emitted, that is distinct from generic verbosity, output length, and difficulty directions and can be causally flipped. We therefore locate our contribution in three mechanistic claims — localization (a pre-generation mode direction), separability (it survives regressing out verbosity, length, and difficulty), and causal control (patching/steering it switches the surface notation) — with the primary value being phenomenon discovery rather than a systems win. Steering toward the symbolic mode on symbol-amenable problems cuts tokens with minimal accuracy loss, which matters where inference latency and cost dominate (high-throughput serving, long-context reasoning); on hard or non-symbol-amenable problems narration is load-bearing, delimiting a safe operating regime. If no separable pre-generation mode variable exists, the phenomenon collapses into existing verbosity work.
Related Work: Three families are closest; we state the exact delta against each. (1) Format/paradigm selection (HybridMind 2024; Chain-of-Reasoning 2025; H-STAR 2024; Adaptive LLM-Symbolic Reasoning 2025) uses EXTERNAL meta-selectors to pick a reasoning paradigm per problem and targets ACCURACY; our delta is an INTERNAL, pre-generation notation-mode representation that the model itself sets, measured as an inference-time COMPUTE tax, not an external accuracy selector. (2) CoT compression / token roles (Chain-of-Thought Tokens are Computer Program Variables 2025; KisMATH 2025) shows non-result 'glue' tokens are removable POST-HOC; our delta is that we identify a CONTROLLABLE internal mode that sets notation before generation, rather than pruning tokens after the fact. (3) Efficiency/verbosity steering (Efficiency Steering 2025; When More is Less 2025) shows verbose-vs-concise paths are linearly separable and steerable; our delta is that notation mode is a distinct axis from generic verbosity/length — we require it to survive regressing out those directions and to Pareto-dominate blunt verbosity steering. None frames the model's spontaneous surface-notation choice as a compute tax dissociable from reasoning depth, nor locates and causally controls a pre-generation notation-mode variable.
Abstract: Reasoning language models produce long chains of thought, and their length is assumed to reflect how much reasoning a problem requires. We identify a largely orthogonal source of waste: the SURFACE NOTATION the model chooses to think in. The same computation can be written as verbose narration ('First, we take the total number of apples...') or as a terse symbolic derivation ('42 - 12 = 30'), and we hypothesize models default to narration even when the symbolic mode carries identical logical content in a fraction of the tokens, a notation compute tax independent of reasoning depth. Our mechanistic claim is that which mode is used is set before generation by a linearly-decodable notation-mode representation at the prompt boundary, distinct from verbosity, length, and difficulty directions. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) quantify the notation tax via matched terse re-derivations that preserve the same answer and step structure; (2) dissociate it from reasoning depth via mixed-effects decomposition and truncate-and-resume minimal-solve length; (3) probe the pre-generation mode and show it survives regressing out verbosity, length, and difficulty, not just principal-angle separation; (4) causally flip it via activation patching; and (5) deploy a training-free mode steer, measuring tokens-at-equal-accuracy against verbosity steering and terseness prompting, and mapping where symbolic terseness starts to cost accuracy. The primary value is phenomenon discovery — a surface-notation compute tax with an identifiable, steerable pre-generation cause — with a practical corollary of cheaper inference on symbol-amenable problems.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B thinking mode); linear probes are the only trainable parameters. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Datasets used as-is: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). Chains are segmented into steps by native delimiters; each step is labeled narration / symbolic / mixed by regex (operators, equations, inequalities) plus an LLM-judge, with human spot-checks on 300 steps (report kappa; regex primary if kappa>=0.7). A per-problem 'symbol-amenability' label (does the solution reduce to a chain of equations/derivations?) is assigned by the same parser+judge.

Experiment 1 (H1 — notation compute tax): Tests whether models default to verbose narration on problems a terser symbolic derivation would solve with identical logical content. Data: all four sets, 3 generations each; for correct traces on symbol-amenable problems we build a matched terse symbolic re-rendering by prompting the model to rewrite ITS OWN correct solution as a compact symbolic derivation, keeping only rewrites the LLM-judge (plus human check on 200) certifies reach the same answer via the same step structure — rewrites that alter the reasoning are excluded (equivalence requires a one-to-one step alignment between narration and symbolic renderings and identical intermediate results, checked by symbolic evaluation where the derivation is arithmetic), and are not counted as savings. Decisive metric FIRST: notation tax = narration tokens minus matched-symbolic tokens, as a fraction of narration tokens, on symbol-amenable problems. Convincing result: median tax >= 30% on symbol-amenable problems in >=3 of 4 models, with models emitting narration-dominant traces on a majority of highly symbol-amenable problems. Indecision band: median tax 10-30% — a real but modest tax, reported as limited. Negative result (< 10%, or models already default to symbolic): there is no surface-notation tax; H1 fails and the remaining experiments are not warranted.

Experiment 2 (H2 — dissociation from reasoning depth): Tests that the tax is tokens-per-step notation overhead, not extra genuine steps. Data: Experiment-1 traces. Analysis: a mixed-effects regression of reasoning-token count with a random effect for problem identity (intrinsic difficulty / step count) and a fixed effect for realized notation mode; plus truncate-and-resume minimal-solve step count on 200 items/dataset as a proxy for genuine depth; plus a within-problem contrast of narration-heavy vs symbol-heavy sampled generations of the SAME problem at equal accuracy. Decisive metric FIRST: the fixed-effect coefficient of notation mode on token count after absorbing problem identity, and the within-problem token gap at equal accuracy. Convincing result: notation mode retains a significant token effect (CI excluding 0) after problem identity is absorbed, and narration-heavy generations use >= 25% more tokens than symbol-heavy ones on the same problems at equal accuracy, while minimal-solve step counts are indistinguishable between modes. Indecision band: notation-mode token effect present but < 10% of total variance explained, or within-problem gap 10-25% — dissociation weak, reported as partly entangled with depth. Negative result (no notation effect beyond problem identity, or step counts differ by mode): the tax is really reasoning depth in disguise; H2 fails and the phenomenon collapses into existing verbosity work.

Experiment 3 (H3 — pre-generation notation-mode representation): Tests that a linear direction at the prompt boundary (last prompt token, before any reasoning token) decodes the notation mode the trace will use, separably from difficulty and length. Data: prompt-boundary activations from Experiment-1 traces, labeled narration-dominant vs symbolic-dominant and by realized narration-to-symbol ratio; item-level 70/15/15 split; logistic-regression / ridge probe per layer, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Systems compared: notation-mode probe versus a difficulty probe (per-problem pass-rate) and a length probe (total token count), via principal angles, joint-model predictive gain, AND a residualization test — we regress the notation label on the verbosity, length, and difficulty probe readouts and test whether the notation direction still decodes above chance from the residual activations (surviving this, not merely principal-angle separation, is required). Decisive metric FIRST: AUROC for predicting narration-vs-symbolic mode from the pre-generation state. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70, principal angle to both the difficulty and length directions >= 30 degrees, and notation mode adds >= 0.03 AUROC beyond a difficulty+length model. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.70, or angle 15-30 degrees, or incremental gain 0.01-0.03 — decodable but entangled, reported as suggestive. Negative result (AUROC ~0.5, or collinear with difficulty/length): mode is not an independent pre-generation representation; H3 fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal — patching flips the mode): Tests that the notation-mode representation causally sets the surface notation. Data: 300 symbol-amenable problems with both a narration context and a symbolic-solved context. Intervention: activation-patch a symbolic-mode prompt-boundary state into the narration context for the same problem at the localized components; frozen weights; dose-response; plus the reverse patch (symbolic->narration) for bidirectionality. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) symbolic patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: drop in narration-to-symbol ratio (and token count) under the symbolic patch versus controls, with answer preserved. Convincing result: symbolic patch lowers the narration-to-symbol ratio by >= 30% and cuts tokens with answer preserved, monotone in dose, not reproduced by the random-direction patch, off-target accuracy within 1 point; reverse patch raises narration. Indecision band: ratio drop 10-30%, or random-direction patch giving >=50% of the effect — causality not clean. Negative result (no mode switch, or non-specific): the representation is not causal; H3's causal claim fails.

Experiment 5 (H4 — training-free notation-mode steer): Tests that steering toward symbolic mode cuts tokens with minimal accuracy loss on symbol-amenable problems. Data: full GSM8K/MATH500/AIME/GPQA, 3 seeds; steering direction = difference-of-means between symbolic-dominant and narration-dominant prompt-boundary states; applied at problem onset when the Experiment-3 probe predicts symbol-amenability; coefficient swept. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) blunt verbosity/length steering, (c) terseness prompting ('use compact symbolic notation'), (d) external paradigm-selection prompting, (e) fixed truncation, (f) our targeted notation-mode steer. Decisive metric FIRST: tokens-at-equal-accuracy on symbol-amenable problems, and whether the targeted steer Pareto-dominates blunt verbosity steering (fewer tokens at no worse accuracy). Convincing result: targeted steer cuts tokens by >= 20% at accuracy within 1 point of no-intervention on symbol-amenable problems, and Pareto-dominates blunt verbosity steering on the token-accuracy frontier. Indecision band: token savings 8-20%, or accuracy loss 1-3 points — a modest, non-dominant gain, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no token savings at equal accuracy, or dominated by verbosity steering): the steer offers no benefit over existing methods; H4 fails though the phenomenon (H1-H3) stands.

Experiment 6 (H4 boundary — where terseness costs accuracy): Tests the claim's scope limit that steering helps on symbol-amenable problems by mapping where symbolic terseness hurts. Data: hard AIME/GPQA and non-symbol-amenable MATH500 problems. Decisive metric FIRST: accuracy drop vs steering strength across symbol-amenability strata. Convincing result: accuracy loss stays within 1 point on symbol-amenable easy/medium problems but grows on hard/non-amenable ones, delimiting a safe operating regime and showing narration is load-bearing where symbolic terseness fails. Indecision band: accuracy loss 1-3 points on symbol-amenable problems — the safe regime is narrow, reported as such. Negative result (accuracy loss large even on symbol-amenable easy problems): the intervention is unsafe to deploy; the scope of H4 shrinks to near-empty.

Experiment 7 (H3/H4 generalization and scale): Tests transfer without retraining and whether stronger models already default to terser notation. Data: probe/steer fit on one set+model, applied unchanged to the others and across 1.5B->14B. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-set mode-decoding AUROC and cross-set tokens-at-equal-accuracy under transferred steering, plus the trend of the Experiment-1 notation tax across model scale. Convincing result: transferred AUROC within 0.05 of in-domain, transferred token savings >= half the in-domain effect, and a monotone decline of the notation tax with scale (a notation analog of simplicity bias). Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or a non-monotone but downward scale trend — partial generalization. Negative result (no transfer, flat scale trend): mode and tax are idiosyncratic per model/set, reported as a boundary characterization.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Classifying notation mode (narration vs symbolic vs mixed) is noisy; we mitigate with parsing plus LLM-judge and human spot-checks, reporting agreement. Producing a matched terse symbolic rendering that provably carries the IDENTICAL computation is nontrivial and could drop genuinely necessary reasoning; we verify same-answer and same-step-structure via LLM-judge and human validation, and treat cases where symbolic rendering changes the reasoning as excluded. The notation-mode signal may be inseparable from a difficulty or length signal (harder problems may genuinely warrant narration), which would collapse the phenomenon into existing verbosity work; the separability analysis, mixed-effects dissociation, and causal patching directly test this, and a null separability result is itself an informative finding. Narration may be load-bearing on hard problems (it scaffolds intermediate state), so steering toward symbolic terseness could cause underthinking; the boundary analysis and per-stratum accuracy quantify this trade-off and may show the intervention only helps symbol-amenable, easy-to-medium problems. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Intervention gains may not exceed strong verbosity-steering baselines on tokens alone, but the mechanistic reframing (a surface-notation compute tax with a decodable, steerable pre-generation mode representation) is a standalone contribution. Reasoning-length/notation measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume and matched re-rendering are compute-heavy, so we subsample. Effects may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: answer_oscillation_settling
Title: Settling Time: Overthinking as Under-Damped Oscillation in the Model's Latent Answer Trajectory
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models often overthink because their internal latent answer does not converge monotonically but oscillates - repeatedly returning to previously-visited candidate answers - before settling. We define oscillation precisely (not as a metaphor) as a discrete switch process in which the step-wise decoded latent answer revisits an earlier candidate at least once, and we fit a damping coefficient to the decay of switch amplitude/spacing over trace time. Overthinking is largely the settling time of this under-damped process; the damping coefficient carries predictive power for wasted tokens even after controlling for switch count and step-wise entropy; and a settling detector that stops only once the answer has entered a low-amplitude converged regime (no predicted future revisit) beats one-shot stability exit.
Related Work: Prior work reads a single latent-answer or confidence signal and treats stabilization as a one-time event (Chain-of-Probe on early answering; Beyond the Last Answer on subthought answer distributions; commitment/uncertainty probes). Backtracking/hesitation work characterizes when models revise: Emergent Search and Backtracking (2026) documents exploration-commitment-backtracking phases but for non-verbal latent transformers, with no efficiency intervention; hesitation-loop and self-doubt accounts describe revision qualitatively. Overthinking-cause work attributes it to internal bias/first-impression conflict or a verbosity direction (Manifold Steering, CREST, First Impression Problem). The precise deltas: backtracking measures whether the model revises at all, whereas we measure a RETURN structure (revisiting prior candidates) and its damping; early-answering/stability work measures a one-shot commitment point, whereas we measure settling time and the danger of premature stability; latent-reasoning work studies continuous non-verbal models, whereas we study deployable verbal reasoning models step-by-step. To show this is not a rebranding of backtracking or hesitation, we compare, on the SAME trajectories, whether the damping coefficient predicts wasted tokens beyond a raw backtracking/switch-count measure and beyond entropy. The contribution is a dynamical-systems reframing with an identifiable oscillation model, an estimator, and a damping-aware invariant, plus a flip-aware settling detector targeting the documented failure of naive early-exit (exiting during a lull before the answer flips back).
Abstract: Existing interpretability accounts of overthinking read a single latent signal (a committed answer, a confidence, a verbosity direction) and treat the moment it stabilizes as the point past which reasoning is wasted. But models frequently stabilize on a wrong answer, flip, restabilize, and flip again, so one-shot stability is a dangerous stopping criterion. We propose a dynamical-systems view: the model's step-wise latent answer follows a trajectory that is often under-damped, oscillating among a small set of competing candidates before settling. We give an explicit oscillation model - a discrete switch process with a damping coefficient fit to switch amplitude over trace time, with a pre-registered estimation procedure - and distinguish it from generic backtracking by requiring returns to previously-visited candidates. Using logit-lens and trained linear probes, we decode the implicit answer at every step on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA across DeepSeek-R1 distills (1.5B-14B) and Qwen3, and report oscillation prevalence upfront. We test our key invariant: settling time and the damping coefficient predict wasted tokens (via truncate-and-resume) better than one-shot stability, absolute confidence, trace length, raw switch count, and entropy - and remain predictive after controlling for switch count and entropy, showing the damping signal is not a rebranding of backtracking. We build a training-free settling detector that exits only when the latent answer has entered a low-amplitude, converged regime, and compare cost-accuracy curves against one-shot stability exit, confidence/abstention early-exit, and verbosity steering, reporting failure modes where it hurts. We localize candidate-switching heads via activation patching (exploratory). The work reframes a slice of overthinking as under-damped answer dynamics and yields a flip-aware efficiency mechanism.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear probes are trainable. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into steps by newline/step delimiters; analysis restricted to extractable-answer items (math / multiple-choice). Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). Oscillation model (pre-registered): decode a candidate answer per step; a 'switch' is a change in decoded candidate; an 'oscillation' requires at least one RETURN to a previously-visited candidate; the damping coefficient is the fitted decay rate of a regression of |amplitude of successive switches| (or inter-switch spacing) on step index, fit only on traces with >= 2 switches, with the fit form and outlier rules fixed before analysis.

Experiment 1 (H2 - Step-wise latent answer is decodable): Decode the current implicit answer per step via (a) logit-lens and (b) a trained linear probe predicting the eventual answer (40/60 split by problem). Ablate probe type (linear vs small MLP), decoding layer, and trajectory length sensitivity. Decisive metric: held-out probe accuracy for the eventual answer and logit-lens/probe trajectory agreement. Convincing: probe accuracy >= 0.70 by mid-trace and agreement >= 0.7. Indecision: accuracy in [0.55, 0.70] or agreement in [0.5, 0.7]. Negative (< 0.55 or agreement < 0.5): the trajectory is not reliably decodable.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Trajectories are oscillatory, prevalence reported upfront): Characterize each trace: number of distinct candidates, switch count, share of switches that are returns (oscillatory), dominant switch-pair identity, and damping coefficient. Decisive metric: fraction of correctly solved traces with >= 2 switches AND >= 1 return, and, among those, the share of switches confined to the top-2/3 candidates. Convincing: >= 40% of correctly solved traces oscillate with >= 70% of switches confined to 2-3 candidates. Indecision: 20-40% oscillating - we frame the paper as characterizing a subset of failures, not a universal theory. Negative (< 20% oscillating or diffuse drift): overthinking is not characteristically oscillatory, refuting H1.

Experiment 3 (H1 KEY INVARIANT - damping predicts waste beyond switch count and entropy): Settling time = tokens from first commitment to the final flip. Wasted tokens via truncate-and-resume. Compare out-of-sample 5-fold R^2 of predictors of wasted tokens: settling time, damping coefficient, one-shot stability point, absolute confidence, trace length, RAW switch count, and mean step-wise entropy. The decisive test is the incremental R^2 of the damping coefficient AFTER partialling out switch count and entropy (the anti-rebranding control). Decisive metric: damping/settling advantage over the best competitor, and damping's incremental R^2 over a switch-count+entropy model. Convincing: settling/damping beats the best competitor by >= 0.10 R^2 on at least three datasets AND damping retains >= 0.05 incremental R^2 over switch-count+entropy. Indecision: advantage in [0.02, 0.10] or incremental R^2 in [0.01, 0.05]. Negative (advantage <= 0.02 or incremental R^2 < 0.01): the dynamical invariant adds nothing over backtracking/entropy, collapsing the novelty.

Experiment 4 (H3 - One-shot stability is dangerous): Quantify how often the answer is stable for k steps then flips. Decisive metric: expected accuracy loss of a naive k-step one-shot exit, k in {2,3,5}. Convincing: naive exit at k=3 forfeits >= 5 accuracy points on at least one hard dataset (AIME/GPQA). Indecision: 2-5 points. Negative (< 2 points): one-shot stability is already safe, and the flip-aware criterion adds little (informative negative for H3's motivation).

Experiment 5 (H1 - Switching is head-mediated, exploratory): Activation patching / head attribution at switch onsets to find heads driving candidate switching; ablate and measure change in switch count and settling time. Labeled EXPLORATORY: it supports but is not required for the dynamical claims. Decisive metric: change in mean switch count under top-head vs. equal-count random ablation. Convincing: top-head ablation changes switch count by >= 30% (vs. < 10% random) with accuracy within 3 points. Indecision: [10%, 30%]. Negative (< 10%): switching is not cleanly head-mediated; the dynamical characterization stands independently.

Experiment 6 (H3 - Settling detector: cost-accuracy curves, strong baselines, failure modes): Online, decode step-wise answer; a lightweight residual-stream probe (trained on Experiment-2 trajectories, 40/60 split) predicts P(future return); exit only when the answer is stable for k steps AND predicted return probability < tau. k, tau swept to trace the FULL cost-accuracy curve. Systems compared on all four datasets: settling detector vs. (a) no intervention, (b) one-shot k-step stability exit, (c) confidence early-exit, (d) abstention/verification-style stopping, (e) verbosity/manifold steering, (f) fixed truncation matched to detector budget. Controls: match competitors on confidence, entropy, switch count, and early-stability duration so the detector must add unique signal. Decisive metric: token/compute reduction at equal accuracy across the whole Pareto curve, with the detector required to specifically beat one-shot stability exit; report missed-flip rate and the operating points where the detector HURTS. Secondary: mean tokens, wall-clock latency, per-query cost. Convincing: >= 20% token reduction within 1 point on GSM8K and MATH500 with missed-flip rate >= 30% lower than one-shot exit at matched tokens, dominating on the cost-accuracy frontier. Indecision: reduction in [10%, 20%] or missed-flip within 10% of one-shot exit - the dynamical characterization (Experiments 1-5) is then the standalone contribution. Negative (< 10% or no missed-flip improvement): no usable flip-aware advantage.

Experiment 7 (H2/H3 - Generality across data, scale, and family): Transfer probes and detector across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining, spanning at least two model families and both math and multiple-choice problem types. Decisive metric: transferred-probe accuracy relative to in-domain and detector savings retention. Convincing: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain probe accuracy on at least three scales/families; savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision: retention in [60%, 80%]. Negative (< 60%): the oscillation signal is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Step-wise latent-answer decoding is only reliable for extractable answers, so we restrict to math/multiple-choice. Oscillation may be rare in some models/datasets, making settling-time a weak predictor; we report prevalence upfront and, if rare, frame the paper as characterizing a subset of failures rather than a universal theory. The future-return probe may be hard to calibrate and could exit prematurely on hard problems where a late flip is corrective (underthinking); the missed-flip metric and tau tuning make this trade-off explicit, and we report operating points where the detector hurts. Damping-coefficient fitting on discrete, short trajectories is noisy; the estimator and outlier rules are pre-registered and we report robust summary statistics. Head patching is labeled exploratory so a weak circuit result does not undercut the dynamical claims. The key risk to novelty - that damping merely restates backtracking/entropy - is tested head-on by the incremental-R^2 control in Experiment 3. Detector gains may not exceed strong steering/abstention baselines, but the flip-aware criterion targets a documented failure of one-shot exit and is a standalone contribution. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: decorative_step_router
Title: Skip the Filler: A Mechanistic Router that Predicts and Suppresses Decorative Reasoning Steps Before They Are Generated
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning LLMs interleave a small number of causally-load-bearing 'true-thinking' steps with many 'decorative' steps that have near-zero causal influence on the answer. Our single, falsifiable primary claim is: the residual stream at a reasoning-step boundary linearly encodes whether the UPCOMING step will be decorative or load-bearing, before that step is generated, with prospective held-out AUROC well above lexical and confidence baselines. The novelty is not the existence of decorative steps (already known) but this pre-step predictability and the proactive generation-time control loop it enables; if true, a lightweight probe-based router can skip decorative steps at generation time, cutting tokens without harming accuracy.
Related Work: Our positioning is best summarized as retrospective/reactive vs. prospective. True Thinking Score / TTS (2025) shows only a tiny fraction of CoT steps causally drive predictions and finds a steerable TrueThinking direction, but scores each step POST-HOC by corrupting an already-generated step. Thought Anchors (2025) measures per-step counterfactual importance RETROSPECTIVELY by resampling generated steps. NLDD / Reasoning-Horizon (2026) shows late steps (70-85% mark) lose causal influence but only measures this after the fact. Think Clearly (2025) prunes redundant tokens using attention-to-end-of-thinking, but REACTIVELY: it must generate the tokens first, then evict and resume, and is content-agnostic. Length-based methods (When More is Less, 2025) target a global optimal length, not which specific steps to keep. The exact one-line delta against each: TTS/Thought Anchors score existing steps, we predict the next step's status before emission; Think Clearly removes tokens after generation, we prevent their generation; length methods pick how long, we pick which steps. We therefore do not claim to be the first to find decorative steps; we claim the specific, testable result that decorative-vs-load-bearing status is prospectively encoded in the pre-step residual and can drive a proactive router. If the prospective signal is absent, the correct conclusion is that reactive pruning (Think Clearly) is the right default, which we state plainly.
Abstract: Large reasoning models produce long chains of thought in which only a small minority of steps causally affect the final answer; the rest are 'decorative.' Prior interpretability work identifies decorative steps only retrospectively, by corrupting or resampling steps after generation, and existing efficiency methods either prune tokens reactively or target a single global length. We ask a sharper mechanistic question with a single primary endpoint: at the boundary just before emitting a reasoning step, does the residual stream already encode whether that step will be load-bearing or decorative? We first quantify per-step causal influence via resample-ablation (drop in answer log-probability when a step is removed) to label steps across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on DeepSeek-R1 distills (1.5B-14B) and Qwen3. We then train lightweight probes on the pre-step boundary residual to predict the UPCOMING step's label, benchmarking prospective AUROC against lexical, hidden-state-norm, entropy, and next-token-confidence baselines and against a retrospective upper bound. Using the probe as a training-free router, we skip predicted-decorative steps at generation time and report full accuracy-vs-token Pareto curves and wall-clock/cost against reactive pruning, length-aware filtering, and TTS-style post-hoc baselines. We localize the circuit behind the prediction via activation patching (supporting, not required) and characterize when the signal fails (e.g., near the reasoning horizon). The result reframes overthinking as a per-step, predictable planning decision and, if it holds, turns a diagnostic finding into a proactive efficiency mechanism useful to API providers, agent frameworks, and reasoning-model deployers who pay per token and per unit latency.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, all weights frozen; only linear probes are trainable. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. Step-boundary protocol (pre-registered): CoT is segmented into steps by newline/step delimiters plus sentence splitting; a boundary is the token position immediately before the first token of a step; the pre-step probe reads only residuals at or before that position and never any token of the step it predicts (leakage control). Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). Unless stated, analysis is on correctly solved traces; train/eval split is by problem (40/60).

Experiment 1 (H1 - Load-bearing steps are sparse): Quantify per-step causal influence via resample-ablation: replace the step with a semantically neutral connector, and separately delete-and-resume, then measure the normalized drop in final-answer log-probability. A step is 'load-bearing' if the drop exceeds theta, fixed a priori as the drop that changes the argmax answer with probability 0.5 on a 200-step calibration subset. Decisive metric: median decorative fraction per dataset. Robustness: label agreement (Cohen's kappa) between the two ablation variants, plus a resampling-stability report (variance of labels across 3 resamples). Convincing: median decorative fraction > 0.5 on all four datasets with kappa > 0.6. Indecision: fraction in [0.35, 0.5] or kappa in [0.4, 0.6]. Negative (fraction < 0.35 or kappa < 0.4): the premise is undercut.

Experiment 2 (H2 PRIMARY ENDPOINT - Decorative status is prospectively encoded): Test whether a linear probe on the pre-step residual predicts the upcoming step's label before it is generated. Systems compared: (i) prospective linear probe on the boundary residual, (ii) bag-of-words baseline on preceding text, (iii) hidden-state-norm baseline, (iv) next-token entropy baseline, (v) next-token confidence/logit-margin baseline, (vi) a small MLP probe (capacity control), (vii) a retrospective probe that sees the generated step (upper bound). Decisive metric: prospective held-out AUROC for the upcoming-step label. Report calibration (ECE) and layer/head/position sweep. Convincing: prospective linear AUROC >= 0.75 on at least three datasets and >= 0.10 above the strongest of the bag-of-words/norm/entropy/confidence baselines, with the MLP giving < 0.03 further AUROC. Indecision: AUROC in [0.62, 0.75] or advantage over the best baseline in [0.03, 0.10] - weak or partly lexical/confidence-driven signal; the router is unlikely to help much and we say so. Negative (AUROC < 0.62 or no advantage over the baselines): decorative status is not linearly pre-encoded, refuting H2 - an informative negative that validates reactive pruning as the correct default.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Circuit behind the prediction, supporting not required): Localize components that determine the probe's prediction via activation patching and head attribution; identify whether a consistent head/feature family (not just a diffuse direction) distinguishes decorative from load-bearing planning; ablate top components and test whether the model emits fewer/different decorative steps. Decisive metric: change in decorative fraction under top-component ablation vs. equal-count random ablation. Convincing: top-component ablation changes decorative fraction by >= 10 points while random changes < 3, with accuracy preserved within 3 points, and the top components recur across at least three datasets. Indecision: change in [3, 10] points. Negative (< 3 points or accuracy collapse): the prospective signal is not tied to an identifiable circuit; the utility claim (Experiment 4) stands independently.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Proactive router: full Pareto and cost): Use the Experiment-2 probe as a training-free generation-time router: at each boundary, if predicted decorative with confidence > tau, force continuation past the step. tau swept to trace the whole accuracy-vs-token Pareto curve (not a single target); reporting on held-out problems. Systems compared on all four datasets: router vs. (a) no intervention, (b) fixed truncation matched to router mean budget, (c) length-aware voting (When More is Less), (d) reactive attention pruning (Think Clearly), (e) post-hoc TTS pruning. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy plus the dominated-area comparison of full Pareto curves. Secondary: mean tokens, accuracy, wall-clock latency, and estimated per-query serving cost (tokens x price) under a realistic inference setting. Convincing: router lies on or above every baseline's frontier and achieves >= 25% token reduction within 1 accuracy point on GSM8K and MATH500. Indecision: reduction in [10%, 25%] or Pareto-tie with the best reactive baseline - the standalone contribution is then the mechanistic finding (Experiments 1-3). Negative (< 10% or > 1 point loss): the signal does not convert into a usable router.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Failure and safety analysis): Measure router accuracy vs. tau separately on the final 15-30% of the chain (reasoning horizon) and on the hardest quartile (by base pass-rate); audit false-skip cases. Decisive metric: accuracy drop attributable to skips in the final 30% vs. the first 70% at the deployed tau. Convincing: no region shows > 2 points extra loss, so a single tau is safe. Indecision: 2-5 points extra in a region - a horizon-aware tau schedule is reported. Negative (> 5 points concentrated loss): the router needs step-position gating, bounding H3.

Experiment 6 (Controls and generality across data and scale): Report the full control battery: label-noise sensitivity (relabel at 2x/0.5x theta), calibration, sequence-length confound (partial out trace length from the AUROC), task-difficulty stratification, and cross-family transfer. Transfer the probe/router across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain (after partialling out length) and router token-savings retention. Convincing: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC across at least three scales, savings hold within 10 relative percent, and the AUROC survives length-partialling. Indecision: retention in [60%, 80%] - partly model-specific; scoped to per-model probes. Negative (< 60% retention, or AUROC vanishes after length-partialling): prospective decorative-encoding is idiosyncratic or a length artifact, contradicting the shared-signal claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Step boundaries may be ambiguous for models without clean delimiters, complicating labeling; mitigated by consistent newline/step segmentation plus sentence splitting and a reported resampling-stability check. Resample-ablation labels are noisy proxies for causal influence and depend on the neutral replacement; validated with two ablation variants. Decorative status may only be weakly predictable in advance (the model may decide mid-step); this is an informative negative that would validate reactive pruning as the right default. Skipping steps could disrupt downstream coherence or trigger error cascades on hard problems (underthinking); the confidence threshold and horizon-aware analysis address this. The prospective signal could be a length or difficulty artifact; the length-partialling and difficulty-stratified controls test this. Router gains may not exceed strong reactive baselines, but the mechanistic finding (prospective encoding of step utility) stands independently and is separated from the utility claim throughout. Results may be model-family specific.

Name: compute_conservation_under_compression
Title: Conservation of Compute: Forced Terseness Pushes Reasoning from Token Space into Activation Depth
Short Hypothesis: We formalize 'conservation of compute' as a single, falsifiable causal claim with a measurable coefficient rather than a general theory. Define, on content-matched computation steps, the compute-conservation coefficient k = the increase in per-token activation-space computation density (logit-lens convergence depth or shallow-head KL) per token removed under forced compression. The claim: (1) when a standard reasoning model is forced to be terse (via prompted terseness or a length-steering direction), k > 0 on matched tokens -- surviving tokens undergo measurably DEEPER processing, distinguishing this from architectural depth-length redistribution because it happens in an unmodified, off-the-shelf model at inference; (2) this compensation saturates at an activation-space ceiling, and proximity to that ceiling predicts, per problem, where compression crosses the accuracy cliff (a decision threshold: compress until the predicted ceiling, then stop); (3) blocking depth (forced early-exit) during compression causally collapses accuracy, and conversely adding recurrent latent depth restores it. The falsifier: k <= 0 on matched tokens, or saturation failing to predict the cliff, would refute conservation and support a pure token-space account.
Related Work: Token Complexity (Lee et al. 2025) shows an information-theoretic floor of tokens per problem and a universal length-accuracy tradeoff, but treats computation as living purely in token space and studies prompt-based compression only behaviorally, with no internal measurement. MTD / Divergence Steering (2025) and 'Sparse or Dense?' (2026) introduce per-token computation-density estimators (KL between full model and a shallow head; mechanistic density) and find density tracks difficulty and rare tokens, but never manipulate output length and never ask whether density RESPONDS to compression. 'Think Deep, Not Just Long' (2025) is the closest: it argues depth can substitute for length and redistributes compute between depth and token count. We are not a re-run of it: that work redistributes compute in settings that add or train depth and studies it as a design choice, whereas our claim is that an UNMODIFIED, off-the-shelf reasoning model SPONTANEOUSLY performs this trade at inference when merely instructed or steered to be terse, that the trade has a measurable per-problem coefficient k and a ceiling, and that hitting the ceiling is the mechanistic CAUSE of the accuracy-compression cliff -- a causal, instance-level, training-free result rather than an architectural depth-vs-length demonstration. Latent-reasoning architectures (Coconut, ETD, Think-at-Hard, looped transformers, Heima) establish depth/token interchangeability in principle but require retraining new architectures and do not test spontaneous inference-time compensation. Our contribution is thus the first inference-time, training-free test that forced terseness in standard models is compensated by rising per-token density, with a formalized coefficient and a ceiling that gauges safe compression.
Abstract: Reasoning language models spend many tokens 'thinking,' and a universal tradeoff links shorter chains of thought to lower accuracy, usually explained purely in token space: fewer tokens mean less computation. We propose a formalized, testable alternative -- conservation of compute. We define a per-problem compute-conservation coefficient k: the rise in per-token activation-space computation density per token removed under forced compression, measured on content-matched computation steps. We hypothesize (1) k > 0 in unmodified, off-the-shelf reasoning models when forced to be terse (surviving tokens are processed more deeply), (2) compensation saturates at an activation ceiling whose proximity predicts, per problem, the accuracy-compression cliff, and (3) blocking depth causally collapses accuracy under compression while adding recurrent latent depth restores it. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure density via logit-lens convergence depth and a shallow-head KL estimator, validated first as an instrument. We estimate k under prompted terseness and length-steering with content-matched controls (so rising density is not just dropped narration), test whether k plus saturation predicts lossless-compressibility better than Token-Complexity and raw length, and causally probe the ceiling by depth-capping and by recurrent latent iteration, reporting FLOP-adjusted gains. The user-facing payoff is an adaptive CoT-shortening policy with an accuracy safety bound: compress each problem until its predicted density ceiling, then stop. We reframe the length-accuracy tradeoff as token-vs-depth compute allocation and yield an interpretable, deployable gauge of safe compression.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup — Per-token computation-density instrumentation is valid): Validates the two density measures all later experiments rely on. Data: GSM8K (500-problem sample), MATH500 (500), AIME 2022-2024 (90), GPQA-Diamond (198); natural-length traces. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Method: at each generated token compute (a) logit-lens convergence depth (earliest layer after which the argmax matches and holds the final token) and (b) MTD, the KL between the full-model next-token distribution and an early-layer logit-lens distribution. Decisive metric: correlation of each density measure with known difficulty proxies (answer/numeric tokens vs narration, rare vs common tokens, harder vs easier problems) and agreement between the two measures. Convincing result: both measures are higher on answer/numeric and rare tokens and on harder problems (Spearman >= 0.3 with token rarity/difficulty) and correlate with each other at Spearman >= 0.5 — the instrument is meaningful. Indecision band: inter-measure agreement in [0.3, 0.5) means the proxies are only loosely consistent and later results must be reported under both separately; below 0.3 the instrument is unreliable and must be revised before proceeding. Negative result would invalidate the density readout and halt the mechanistic program.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Compression raises per-token density on retained tokens: conservation of compute): The core test. Data: the four datasets above; for each problem a baseline natural-length trace plus compressed traces via (i) prompted terseness at several strengths ('use as few words as possible', 'answer in <= N tokens') and (ii) steering along a length/verbosity direction (difference-of-means of short vs long traces), the steering variant being content-lighter. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B, frozen. Method: on retained / semantically-matched tokens (aligned to the same computation steps via an LLM-judge alignment so density is compared on comparable work, not just dropped narration) measure mean per-token density vs trace length, and fit the compute-conservation coefficient k = density increase per token removed. Systems compared: baseline vs each compression strength; raw vs content-matched density estimates. Decisive metric: k (density gain per token removed), tested > 0 on matched tokens. Convincing result: k is significantly positive on the content-matched comparison for a majority of problems (median k such that removing 30% of tokens raises matched per-token density by >= 15%), and the effect survives in the content-lighter steering condition. Indecision band: a matched-token density rise in [5%, 15%) at 30% compression is weak conservation; below 5%, or a rise present only in the raw (unmatched) estimate, means the apparent compensation is just dropped easy tokens and H1 fails. Negative result (no density rise on matched tokens) would refute conservation and support the pure token-space account.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Compensation saturates at a ceiling that predicts the accuracy cliff): Tests that k and density saturation predict which problems compress losslessly. Data: the four datasets, compression-strength sweep tracing each problem's accuracy-length curve and its accuracy cliff (the compression point where accuracy drops sharply). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen. Method: for each problem compute k and a saturation indicator (per-token density plateauing near maximum layers), then predict lossless-compressibility (no accuracy drop beyond noise at a target compression). Systems compared: the k+saturation predictor vs Token-Complexity, raw token count, and a difficulty probe. Decisive metric: AUROC for predicting lossless-compressibility. Convincing result: the k+saturation predictor reaches AUROC >= 0.75 and beats each baseline by >= 0.05 AUROC, with problems near the density ceiling being the ones that break. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.75), or an edge over baselines in [0.02, 0.05), is weak — the ceiling carries some but not decisive predictive value; AUROC < 0.65 or no edge over Token-Complexity means saturation does not predict the cliff and H2 fails. Negative result would sever the link between the activation ceiling and the accuracy cliff.

Experiment 4 (H2/H3 — Blocking depth causally collapses accuracy under compression): Tests that retained accuracy under compression depends on activation-space compensation. Data: held-out problems across the four datasets. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is capping per-token depth by forcing early exit through the LM head at a chosen layer during generation, applied at baseline length and under compression. Systems compared: the accuracy vs (cap-layer x compression-strength) interaction; control = capping only on narration tokens; a clean per-token-only cap and a KV-approximated variant (given skipped layers' missing KV). Decisive metric: the interaction effect — the additional accuracy loss from depth-capping under compression beyond its loss at baseline length. Convincing result: depth-capping causes >= 2x more accuracy loss under compression than at baseline length, and capping narration tokens hurts far less than capping answer-relevant tokens — the compressed model was relying on depth. Indecision band: an interaction where compression-time capping loss is 1.2x-2x the baseline-length loss is weak causal support; < 1.2x means depth-capping hurts equally regardless of compression and the ceiling is not causally implicated. Negative result would refute the causal role of activation depth in compression tolerance.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Adding activation depth restores accuracy lost to compression): The substitutability test. Data: compressed-generation runs on problems that fell off the accuracy cliff in Experiment 3. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is training-free recurrent latent iteration (looping a subset of reasoning-relevant middle layers k times at inference) during compressed generation. Decisive metric: accuracy recovery under compression as a function of the number of loops, reported FLOP-adjusted (added depth costs FLOPs). Convincing result: added depth recovers >= half of the accuracy lost to compression at a FLOP cost below the baseline-length generation's FLOPs — token-space and depth-space compute are substitutable off the shelf. Indecision band: a recovery of [25%, 50%) of lost accuracy, or recovery only at FLOP cost exceeding baseline-length generation, is a weak/uneconomical positive; below 25% means depth does not substitute for tokens. Negative result would mean compression loss is not recoverable via depth, bounding the conservation claim.

Experiment 6 (H1 — Localization of where compensation happens): Tests that compressed reasoning shifts answer-relevant computation deeper. Data: 300 matched baseline/compressed trace pairs. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen. Method: layer-wise logit-lens to test whether answer-relevant computation moves to later layers under compression, and activation patching of compressed-trace late-layer activations into an uncompressed run. Decisive metric: the shift in the layer at which the answer becomes decodable under compression, and whether patching compressed late-layer activations transfers the compressed answer. Convincing result: answer-decodable layer shifts later by >= 2 layers under compression, and patching compressed late-layer activations transfers the answer on >= 50% of cases. Indecision band: a layer shift of 1 layer or transfer in [25%, 50%) is weak localization; no shift and < 25% transfer means compensation is not localized to later layers. Negative result would leave the mechanism unlocalized while the behavioral H1 stands.

Experiment 7 (H2 — Practical payoff: k as a safe-compression gauge, and generalization): Tests the applied value and transfer. Data: GSM8K/MATH500/AIME/GPQA held-out. Model: 7B and 14B, frozen; use per-problem k to set adaptive length budgets. Systems compared: k-guided adaptive compression vs uniform terseness vs Token-Complexity-guided compression. Decisive metric: tokens-at-fixed-accuracy (median token reduction at accuracy within noise), reported both token-adjusted and FLOP-adjusted. Secondary: whether the density measures, coefficient, and predictor transfer across datasets and scales without retraining. Convincing result: k-guided compression saves >= 15% tokens at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point, beating uniform terseness and matching or beating Token-Complexity, and the predictor retains >= two-thirds of its AUROC on transfer. Indecision band: token savings in [5%, 15%), or transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds), is a modest/partial outcome; below those means k offers no practical edge or does not transfer. Negative result would confine the contribution to the mechanistic findings without a deployable gauge.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The compensation may be small or absent—models may just do less compute when compressed (pure token-space story), which would refute the hypothesis but is itself an informative, publishable negative result clarifying the Token-Complexity picture. Matching 'retained tokens' across compressed and full traces is nontrivial; density could appear to rise merely because compression drops easy narration tokens, inflating the average—we mitigate with content-aligned comparison and by measuring density on matched computation steps, and report both raw and matched estimates. Logit-lens convergence depth and MTD are proxies for computation; we cross-validate with two measures and with causal depth-capping. The depth-capping experiment faces the standard early-exit KV-consistency issue (skipped layers' KV missing for future attention); we report both a clean per-token-only cap and a KV-approximated variant and interpret cautiously. Adding recurrent depth increases FLOPs, so 'restoring accuracy under compression' trades tokens for compute—we report FLOP-adjusted, not just token-adjusted, gains. Effects are likely model-family and scale specific, and the conservation coefficient may not transfer across very different tokenizers. Compression via prompting may change reasoning content, not just length, confounding density readings; the steering-based compression provides a content-lighter alternative.

Name: shallow_token_depth_skip
Title: Most Reasoning Tokens Are Shallow: Training-Free Adaptive Depth via a Cheap Deep-Thinking Predictor
Short Hypothesis: In a reasoning model's chain of thought, the vast majority of generated tokens (connectives, narration, formatting, easy continuations) reach their final prediction in early-to-middle layers ('shallow tokens'), while only a sparse set of 'deep-thinking' tokens require the full stack. We frame the contribution as CHARACTERIZATION + DEPLOYMENT rather than a new early-exit algorithm: (1) the mechanistic finding that deep-thinking need in reasoning CoT is sparse and category-structured (concentrated on computation/answer tokens, not narration) and this structure survives controls for token frequency, entropy, position, and difficulty; (2) that this need is predictable online from mid-layer activations; (3) a fully training-free adaptive-depth decoder for existing reasoning models via a self-speculative check, whose realized wall-clock gains under realistic serving are measured, not just FLOP proxies.
Related Work: Adaptive-depth architectures (Mixture-of-Depths, Mixture-of-Recursions, Inner Thinking Transformer, Think-at-Hard, adaptive latent CoT) REQUIRE training routers/adapters or fine-tuning. Interpretability on depth usage (Guess-then-Refine 2025; Concept Depth 2024; Demystifying LLM Layers 2025) shows tokens converge at different depths but builds no deployable decoder. 'Think Deep, Not Just Long' (2026) measures deep-thinking tokens and uses the deep-thinking ratio to SELECT samples (test-time scaling), not to allocate per-token depth during generation. MTD/Divergence Steering (2025) measures computation density via a shallow-head KL and steers text style, not depth. Classic/early-exit LMs (CALM) and layer-skip routers (TIDE, LiteStage, FlexiDepth) use confidence thresholds or trained routers for general LM. The checkpoint/router-level deltas: CALM early-exits on a confidence threshold but typically needs calibration training and does not characterize which token TYPES are deep; TIDE/LiteStage/FlexiDepth train or tune routers; none exploit the specific mechanistic structure that reasoning CoTs are dominated by shallow narration tokens with deep need concentrated on computation/answer tokens. We do not claim a fundamentally new early-exit mechanism; we claim a mechanistic characterization of reasoning-CoT depth structure, that it is training-free-predictable mid-stack, and that a self-speculative training-free decoder built on it is complementary to step-level stopping - with honest wall-clock accounting that prior FLOP-proxy claims often omit.
Abstract: Reasoning language models generate long chains of thought, but not every token is computationally hard. Building on the guess-then-refine view of transformer depth, we hypothesize that in reasoning traces the overwhelming majority of tokens - connectives, narration, formatting, easy continuations - converge to their final prediction in early-to-middle layers, while only a sparse set of deep-thinking tokens (arithmetic results, logical commitments, answer tokens) need the full stack. We first characterize this structure across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on DeepSeek-R1 distills (1.5B-14B) and Qwen3: using logit-lens saturation and prediction-revision-in-deep-layers, we measure per-token convergence depth and show deep-thinking need is sparse and concentrated on specific token categories rather than narration, testing this against token-frequency, entropy, position, and local-difficulty confounds. We then test whether deep-thinking need is decidable online from mid-layer signals, comparing a cheap mid-layer confidence/agreement check with a lightweight linear probe. Finally we build a fully training-free adaptive-depth decoder: run to a mid-layer checkpoint, and if the prediction is confidently stable, exit through the LM head, skipping remaining layers, else complete full depth, with a self-speculative verify step guarding accuracy. We evaluate compute-at-fixed-accuracy against uniform full depth, fixed-layer early exit, and CALM-style confidence exit, reporting BOTH a FLOP proxy and true wall-clock under realistic decoding with the KV-consistency caveat handled explicitly, and show the method is complementary to step-level early stopping. We frame the contribution as a mechanistic characterization plus a deployable, interpretable efficiency mechanism, and show the characterization changes the depth-allocation decision rather than merely confirming intuition.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only a lightweight linear depth-probe is trainable, the decoder itself training-free. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B (L layers each). Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). Splits by problem (40/60). All wall-clock is measured under a realistic serving setup (batched decode, standard KV cache) and reported separately from the FLOP proxy.

Experiment 1 (H1 - Deep-thinking need is sparse and category-structured, vs confounds): For sampled traces, apply logit-lens at every layer and record each token's convergence depth (earliest layer after which the argmax equals the final output and stays stable); cross-check with prediction-revised-in-deep-layers. Categorize tokens (function/connective, narration, numeric/operator, answer-region) via POS + regex. Decisive metric: fraction of tokens converging by layer 2L/3, and the share of late-converging (deep) tokens in numeric/logical/answer categories vs narration - reported after controlling for token frequency, next-token entropy, position, and local difficulty (perplexity) via a logistic model, so the category effect must survive these confounds. Convincing: >= 70% of tokens converge by 2L/3, >= 60% of deep tokens are numeric/logical/answer, the two depth definitions agree (rank correlation > 0.5), AND token category retains a significant effect on depth after partialling out frequency/entropy/position/difficulty. Indecision: convergence-by-2L/3 in [50%, 70%], or category concentration in [45%, 60%], or category effect marginal after controls. Negative (< 50% converge, deep tokens spread evenly, or category effect vanishes under controls): reasoning tokens are not predominantly shallow or the category structure is a confound, refuting H1.
