Experiment 2 (H2 - Deep-thinking need is decidable online mid-stack): Predict late-convergence from mid-layer state via (a) training-free mid-layer logit-lens top-1 margin/entropy and adjacent-layer agreement, and (b) a lightweight linear probe on the mid-layer residual. Split 40/60 by problem; checkpoint layer swept; report calibration and threshold robustness. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC for late-convergence at the best mid-layer checkpoint. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.80 at a checkpoint no deeper than 2L/3, with the training-free confidence check within 0.05 AUROC of the probe. Indecision: [0.65, 0.80]. Negative (< 0.65): not predictable mid-stack, so the decoder cannot exit safely, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Training-free adaptive-depth decoder: FLOP AND wall-clock at fixed accuracy): Decode to checkpoint layer c; if the checkpoint LM-head prediction is confident (margin > tau) and agrees with layer c-1, exit and emit, else run full depth; a self-speculative safeguard periodically re-verifies exited tokens at full depth and adjusts tau. tau, c on the Experiment-2 training split. Systems compared on all four datasets with implementation parity: adaptive-depth decoder vs. (a) uniform full depth, (b) fixed exit at c for all tokens, (c) CALM-style confidence exit, (d) confidence-only policy without the category structure, (e) random exit at matched rate. Decisive metric: average layers per token (FLOP proxy) at fixed accuracy AND true wall-clock speedup under realistic serving, reported for both a KV-recompute variant and a checkpoint-KV-reuse variant (per the KV-consistency caveat). Secondary: fraction early-exited, accuracy. Convincing: >= 30% reduction in average layers within 1 point on GSM8K and MATH500, beating fixed-layer exit and matching/beating CALM at equal accuracy, WITH a measurable (>= 15%) wall-clock speedup in at least one KV variant. Indecision: layer reduction in [15%, 30%], a CALM-tie, or FLOP savings that do not translate to wall-clock (< 5% speedup) - the mechanistic characterization (Experiments 1-2) remains the standalone contribution. Negative (< 15% layer reduction or > 1 point loss): no usable savings.

Experiment 4 (H1 - Causal category check, precise counterfactual): Verify early-exited tokens are dominantly narration/connective and that forcing early exit on answer-region tokens is harmful. Intervention: force early exit (emit the checkpoint-layer argmax) on a chosen token category at matched exit rate; counterfactual: the same tokens at full depth. Falsifier stated: if forcing exit on answer-region tokens costs no more than on narration, the sparse-deep-thinking-on-computation hypothesis is false. Decisive metric: accuracy drop when early exit is forced on answer-region vs. narration tokens at matched exit rate. Convincing: forcing exit on answer-region tokens costs >= 10 points while equal narration exits cost < 2. Indecision: answer-region cost in [3, 10] points. Negative (< 3 points): depth is not causally concentrated on computation tokens, weakening H1's mechanistic claim.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Complementarity with step-level stopping): Combine the token-wise depth decoder with a step-level early-stopping baseline and measure additive savings. Decisive metric: compute (FLOP proxy) and wall-clock at fixed accuracy for the combination vs. either alone. Convincing: the combination saves >= 10% more compute at matched accuracy than the better single method on the Pareto frontier. Indecision: [3%, 10%] additive. Negative (< 3% additive or accuracy loss combined): the two axes are redundant.

Experiment 6 (H3 - Sensitivity and hard-item safety): Sweep tau and checkpoint layer to trace the accuracy-vs-compute curve; report AIME accuracy and calibration drift across datasets under transferred (not retuned) thresholds. Decisive metric: AIME accuracy drop at the tau/c delivering Experiment-3 savings on GSM8K/MATH500. Convincing: < 1 point under transferred thresholds. Indecision: 1-3 point drop (per-dataset retuning reported). Negative (> 3 point drop): thresholds do not transfer, bounding H3.

Experiment 7 (H2/H3 - Generality across data and scale, with CIs): Transfer the depth probe and thresholds across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining; report bootstrap CIs on savings and AUROC. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain and decoder compute-savings retention. Convincing: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales; savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision: [60%, 80%]. Negative (< 60%): the shallow-token signal is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Standard transformer forward passes are not trivially layer-skippable at decode time because later layers' KV entries would be missing for future attention; we exit only the current token's residual through the head while still computing (or approximating/caching) skipped-layer KV - this may limit realized speedup and is measured carefully with both a FLOP proxy and true wall-clock and a checkpoint-KV-reuse variant. If KV inconsistency degrades downstream attention, gains shrink (an informative systems finding). Deep-thinking need may be only weakly predictable at the checkpoint, yielding modest exit rates - still a publishable characterization. Logit-lens convergence depth is a proxy and may misclassify tokens; we cross-validate with two definitions and control for frequency/entropy/position/difficulty so the category claim is not a confound. Forcing early exit could cascade errors on hard problems; tau sweeps and the self-speculative safeguard address this. Gains may not exceed CALM-style baselines; we therefore frame the contribution as characterization + training-free, complementary deployment, and show the characterization changes the depth-allocation decision. The operational setting is a serving operator running an existing reasoning model who wants token-level compute savings without training a router. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: hawthorne_effort_effect
Title: The Hawthorne Effort Effect: Do Reasoning Models Think Harder When They Believe They Are Being Tested?
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models allocate more thinking compute (more tokens, more verification) to the exact same problem when the prompt signals an evaluation/test context than when it signals casual real-world deployment, even though difficulty and the correct answer are identical. This is a new dependent variable (reasoning effort) layered on the known, linearly-encoded, steerable evaluation-awareness representation rather than a new mechanism; we test whether steering the awareness signal moves reasoning length, decoupled from difficulty, under format-matched and random-direction controls.
Related Work: A recent cluster shows evaluation/test awareness is linearly represented and steerable in LLMs and ties it to SAFETY outcomes: 'The Hawthorne Effect in Reasoning Models' (2025) and 'Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness' (2025) probe/steer test-awareness activations and study sandbagging and harmful-compliance; 'Evaluation Awareness Scales Predictably' (2025) gives a scaling law. All of these measure the effect of evaluation awareness on ANSWER correctness, compliance, or capability concealment. Separately, efficient-reasoning interpretability reads a scalar length/difficulty signal to allocate compute (When More is Less 2025; Overclocking LLM Reasoning 2025; ThinkEdit 2025; S3-CoT 2026) but always in a fixed prompt framing and treats length as difficulty-driven. Crucially, NO prior work connects evaluation awareness to reasoning COMPUTE ALLOCATION: none asks whether test framing makes a reasoning model think LONGER on identical problems, dissociates this from genuine difficulty, or shows the reasoning-length change is causally carried by the evaluation-awareness representation. Our contribution is (1) a new behavioral phenomenon — a Hawthorne effect for reasoning effort; (2) its dissociation from difficulty; and (3) a mechanistic account showing it rides the known evaluation-awareness direction and can be causally steered. This is distinct from all my prior overthinking proposals (which assume a neutral, single framing) and from prior evaluation-awareness work (which targets safety/accuracy, not compute). If confirmed, it means published benchmark efficiency numbers are systematically biased and real users receive less careful reasoning.
Abstract: Reasoning language models are almost always measured on benchmarks -- but benchmarks announce themselves as tests. We ask whether this framing changes how hard a model thinks. Our contribution is a narrow new dependent variable, reasoning effort, layered on the known and already-steerable evaluation-awareness representation -- not a new mechanism. Transferring the Hawthorne effect, we hypothesize a Hawthorne effort effect: on the identical problem, a reasoning model spends more thinking tokens and does more self-verification under an evaluation/test framing than under a casual real-world deployment framing. The single primary endpoint is total thinking tokens under a length-matched test-vs-deployment comparison. We construct matched prompts holding the math or science problem's content and correct answer fixed while varying only contextual framing -- explicit test cues ('Question 4 of this exam', 'for benchmark scoring') versus deployment cues (a casual user) versus neutral. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure reasoning tokens, verification, and accuracy, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate framing from genuine difficulty. Mechanistically, we test whether the prompt-boundary evaluation-awareness direction predicts reasoning length beyond a difficulty probe, and via activation patching and steering whether editing it moves length -- reported as consistent with mediation only if format-matched and random-direction controls hold. We separate the measurement-validity implication (benchmark efficiency numbers are inflated relative to deployment, biasing rankings and cost estimates) from the broader deployment-equity claim, which we test rather than assert. We target eval-validity and reasoning-efficiency researchers and provide a training-free debiasing intervention.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (problem, framing) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - test framing inflates reasoning effort on identical problems): Tests whether an evaluation/test framing yields more thinking tokens and more self-verification than a deployment framing on the identical problem. Data: constructed from existing sets - GSM8K test (1319; sample 300), MATH500 (500; all), AIME 2024+2025 (60; all), GPQA-Diamond (198; all); 1058 seed problems, since each is expanded into 3 framings x 5 seeds x 4 models. Each seed problem is rendered content-identical across three framings that change only context: (a) explicit test cues ('This is question 4 of a graded exam'; 'Your answer will be scored on a benchmark'; 'You are being evaluated'), (b) deployment/casual cues (a hurried user asking for help in chat), (c) neutral no-framing baseline. Content and gold answer are verified identical after stripping the framing. Verification depth = count of self-check/recheck steps via lexical cues plus a reflection-direction classifier. Systems compared: test vs deployment vs neutral framing, within model. Decisive metric: within-problem paired difference in mean thinking tokens between test and deployment framing, as a median relative increase, first; secondary verification-step increase; accuracy reported to confirm the extra effort is not merely correcting errors. Convincing: median relative token increase >= 12% (test over deployment) with a paired Wilcoxon test (Holm-corrected across models) and accuracy equal-or-higher under test framing. Indecision band: a 4-12% increase does not decide H1 and blocks the mechanism experiments. Negative result: below 4%, or the sign reversing consistently (deployment overthinking), refutes the stated direction of H1 (a reversal is still a reportable measurement-validity finding but rejects the hypothesis as written).

Experiment 2 (H1 dissociation - the effort gap is not driven by difficulty or prompt length): Tests that the framing effect survives removal of intrinsic difficulty and raw prompt length, and that the extra tokens are wasted rather than needed. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces. Analysis 1 (dissociation): mixed-effects model of thinking length with a random intercept per problem identity (difficulty) and fixed effects for framing and raw prompt token count; supported by length-matched phrasings. Analysis 2 (wasted vs genuine): on a 150-problem subsample use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length per framing and test whether test framing inflates the beyond-minimal (wasted) portion rather than the minimal-solve length. Systems compared: framing coefficient with vs without difficulty random effect and prompt-length covariate. Decisive metric: standardized framing coefficient on thinking length after both controls, first; plus the share of test-framing extra tokens in the wasted portion. Convincing: the framing coefficient stays significant (95% CI excludes 0) with most of its raw effect surviving controls, and >= 60% of extra tokens fall in the wasted portion. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or 30-60% wasted share, is partial support. Negative result: the coefficient vanishing under controls, or extra tokens being genuine (< 30% wasted), means the gap is difficulty/length-driven, refuting the dissociation part of H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - the effort gap rides on the linearly encoded evaluation-awareness representation): Tests whether the boundary residual stream carries an evaluation-awareness direction that predicts reasoning length beyond a difficulty probe. Data: final-prompt-token activations for the Experiment 1 problems across framings, split 70/15/15 by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep (prior work localizes awareness to early-to-middle layers). Probes: (i) a linear evaluation-awareness probe trained on test vs deployment framing (reproducing prior work), (ii) a ridge length probe (target = observed thinking length), (iii) a true-difficulty probe (target = pass-rate). Systems compared: does the length-probe prediction rise under test framing for identical problems; does the awareness direction predict length beyond difficulty; principal angle between awareness and difficulty directions. Decisive metric: incremental R2 of the evaluation-awareness direction for predicting reasoning length over the difficulty probe on held-out problems, first; plus held-out Spearman between length-probe prediction and framing on matched problems and the awareness/difficulty principal angle. Convincing: the awareness direction adds >= 0.05 R2 over difficulty (significant), length-probe Spearman with framing >= 0.3 (p<0.01), and principal angle to difficulty >= 30 degrees (awareness not collinear with difficulty). Indecision band: incremental R2 0.02-0.05, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: incremental R2 < 0.02, or the awareness direction collinear with difficulty (angle < 20 degrees), means the length change is not carried by a distinct awareness representation, refuting H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 - steering the awareness direction causally moves reasoning length, decoupled from difficulty): Tests whether editing the awareness representation changes reasoning length as predicted. Data: 150 problems (subset of Experiment 1) each with matched test and deployment variants; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention A (patching, both directions): patch the boundary state from a test variant into the matched deployment pass (expect effort to rise) and, reversed, patch deployment state into a test pass (expect effort to drop), at the Experiment-3 layer. Intervention B (steering): steer along the evaluation-awareness direction (difference-of-means test minus deployment, or the awareness-probe weight) to (a) cancel the framing effort gap and (b) fix all framings to a common effort target; dose swept over 4 magnitudes. Controls: matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems; comparison to a prompt-based fix (stripping framing). Systems compared: real patch/steer vs random-direction control vs no intervention vs prompt-strip. Decisive metric: fraction of the test-vs-deployment length gap opened by injecting the test state (and closed by injecting deployment), first; plus the reduction in the framing length gap under steering, with accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: patching moves length in the predicted direction for both patch directions closing >= 50% of the gap, and steering along the awareness direction shrinks the framing gap by >= 50% while a matched-random direction does < 15%, monotone in dose, accuracy preserved. Indecision band: a 20-50% effect, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% effect, or the random control matching the awareness direction, means reasoning length is not causally carried by the awareness representation, refuting H3.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 modulators, scaling, and transfer): Tests where the effort gap is strongest and whether it scales and transfers. Data: reuses Experiment 1 problems and derived vectors. Factors: framing strength (subtle vs explicit test cues), high-stakes framing ('this determines your deployment'), and domain (GPQA/medical items). Scaling/transfer: apply the 7B-derived awareness probe and steering vector to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting, and test whether the framing token gap grows with model scale (as predicted by the evaluation-awareness scaling law) and whether RL-tuned models show larger gaps. Systems compared: subtle vs explicit vs high-stakes framing; 1.5B vs 7B vs 14B; in-model vs transferred probe/steering. Decisive metric: change in the framing token gap across each factor and across scale, first; plus transferred-vector effect relative to in-model. Convincing: explicit/high-stakes framing yields a significantly larger gap than subtle framing, the gap grows monotonically with scale, and transferred steering retains >= 70% of its in-model gap-closing effect. Indecision band: transferred effect 40-70% of in-model, or a non-monotone scale trend, is weak generalization. Negative result: no factor or scale modulation and transferred effect < 40% means the effect is idiosyncratic and does not follow the awareness scaling law, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences between framings rather than the evaluation-awareness cue per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, and neutral baseline isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Framing may be small or absent in models trained to behave identically regardless of context (a valuable boundary condition, and one that would itself matter for eval validity). The reasoning-length signal may be inseparable from difficulty or from a generic sycophancy/instruction-following direction; the separability analysis, patching, and comparison to a difficulty probe address this, and overlap with the known evaluation-awareness direction is in fact the mechanistic prediction we test. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. The direction of the effect could reverse in some families (deployment overthinking) — still a novel, publishable measurement-validity finding. Results may be model-family and scale specific.
